entries.name: The Classical Western
entries.description: The settlement argument stated at full strength, with violence presented as the price of the law that follows it.
entries.principle: The classical western asserts three things and needs all three: that the country is available, that the violence which takes it is regrettable and necessary, and that the man who does the violence cannot live in the town he makes possible. It is not naive — it usually knows the third claim costs something, and the cost is where its best work happens. What it does not do is doubt the first two.
entries.example: Ford's Stagecoach (1939) runs the whole argument through a coach full of people the town has already expelled. Schaefer's Shane (1949) and Stevens's film of it (1953) put the cost of the third claim in front of a child. Wister's The Virginian (1902) supplies the moral grammar the rest inherits, including the walk-down as a legitimate court.
entries.application: Write the myth at full strength before writing any correction of it. A reader who cannot state what your story believes about the land has nothing to watch you take apart.

entries.name: The Psychological Western
entries.description: The 1950s turn inward, where the gun hand becomes a symptom and the plot becomes a diagnosis.
entries.principle: The psychological western keeps the classical machinery and relocates the conflict inside the protagonist, so the question stops being whether he can win and becomes what winning has already done to him. Bazin named the mode the sur-western in 1955 and meant it as a complaint: a western embarrassed by being a western and reaching for justification outside the genre. The complaint is worth keeping as a test.
entries.example: Henry King's The Gunfighter (1950) makes reputation itself the antagonist. Anthony Mann's Winchester '73 (1950) and The Naked Spur (1953) put a man's grievance where the landscape used to be. Zinnemann's High Noon (1952) is the mode's most argued case, though two separate objections are usually run together: Bazin's aesthetic complaint that the film reaches outside the genre for its seriousness, and the political objection Hawks and Wayne made to the marshal's appeal for help.
entries.application: Beware the term. This is not the paperback adult western that emerged in the mid-1970s and ran for decades, which is a shelf category defined by sex and violence quotas; see subgenre-16. If your western needs a psychiatric vocabulary to explain its climax, ask whether the genre is carrying the story or apologising for it.

entries.name: The Revisionist Western
entries.description: The classical machinery kept intact and its moral polarity reversed.
entries.principle: Revision is not arrival from outside. It reverses who the violence serves while leaving the form's engineering — the ride-in, the escalation, the walk-down — fully operational, which is why revisionist westerns are still satisfying as westerns. The tell is that the classical structure delivers a conclusion the classical version would have refused.
entries.example: Ford was revising Ford by 1956: The Searchers builds Ethan Edwards out of precisely the competence the genre admires and then makes it inseparable from his hatred. Peckinpah's Ride the High Country (1962) and The Wild Bunch (1969) keep the professional ethic and strip it of any civic result. Eastwood's Unforgiven (1992) restores the walk-down in order to charge for it.
entries.application: If you are revising, keep the machinery. A story that dismantles the form and the structure at once has nothing left to disappoint the reader with, and disappointment is the mechanism.

entries.name: The Anti-Western
entries.description: An attack on the form itself, rather than a reversal inside it.
entries.principle: The anti-western withholds the satisfactions the machinery exists to deliver — the competent man, the decisive violence, the settlement that means something — and it withholds them structurally rather than thematically. Where the revisionist western pays out in the wrong direction, the anti-western declines to pay out. Conflating the two is the commonest error in writing about the genre.
entries.example: Altman's McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971) denies its gunfight any staging that would let a viewer enjoy it. Penn's Little Big Man (1970), from Berger's 1964 novel, alternates modes rather than blending them, so the parody and the massacre sit in the same film without reconciling. Cimino's Heaven's Gate (1980) refuses legibility itself.
entries.application: Decide which of the two you are writing before Chapter One. An anti-western that flinches into a satisfying climax has become a revisionist western with a bad third act.

entries.name: The Elegiac Western
entries.description: A revision that forgives, set at the moment the country closes.
entries.principle: The elegiac western agrees with the revisionist reading of what the frontier cost and declines to prosecute, because its subject is obsolescence rather than guilt. Its structural marker is that the antagonist is time — fences, railways, automobiles, actuarial age — and that the protagonist's skills are correct and no longer wanted. Forgiveness is the mode's characteristic risk and its characteristic power.
entries.example: Peckinpah's Ride the High Country (1962) is the form in miniature, two old men and a payroll. Ford's The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962) elegises the very legend it is exposing. Swarthout's The Shootist (1975) and Siegel's film (1976) put a cancer where the closing frontier goes; McMurtry's Lonesome Dove (1985) spends eight hundred pages earning the same ending.
entries.application: Watch the forgiveness. Elegy is the easiest mode in the genre to write badly, because mourning a world excuses you from asking who was in it.

entries.name: The Acid Western
entries.description: The frontier as a hallucination, and the genre's furniture used as symbolic rather than historical material.
entries.principle: The acid western abandons the settlement argument's realism while keeping its iconography, treating the West as a landscape of the mind in which the journey is initiatory and the violence is ritual rather than instrumental. It is the one mode where the genre's imagery is explicitly severed from any claim about American history, which is what distinguishes it from the anti-western's refusal.
entries.example: Jodorowsky's El Topo (1970) is the founding case, and Pauline Kael coined the label for it in The New Yorker in November 1971. Jonathan Rosenbaum theorised the mode in 1996 around Jarmusch's Dead Man (1995). Monte Hellman's The Shooting (1966) reaches it early and by subtraction rather than excess.
entries.application: Establish your rules of causation in the first ten pages. An acid western that starts realist and drifts reads as a failure of control rather than a change of register.

entries.name: The Cavalry Western
entries.description: The Indian Wars told from inside the institution that fought them.
entries.principle: The cavalry western is organised by command rather than by gunfighting, so its recurring problems are orders, competence, garrison boredom and the gap between a colonel's understanding and a scout's. It is the subgenre in which the settlement argument is least deniable, because the protagonists are the instrument of policy and the policy has a name. That is also why it produced the genre's earliest internal criticism.
entries.example: Ford's Fort Apache (1948), She Wore a Yellow Ribbon (1949) and Rio Grande (1950) build the institution lovingly and, in the first of them, indict its commander. Aldrich's Ulzana's Raid (1972) rebuilds the same machinery to argue the opposite case with the same professional respect.
entries.application: Decide whose competence the story admires, then check whether the campaign's purpose is anywhere on the page. A cavalry story that only knows tactics has made policy invisible, which is a craft failure before it is anything else.

entries.name: The Outlaw Western
entries.description: The claim made against the law rather than through it, and the sympathy that requires.
entries.principle: The outlaw western has to solve a problem the lawman western does not: it must make theft and killing legible as a claim, usually by supplying a prior dispossession — the war, the railroad, the bank, the fence. Where that prior claim is missing the mode collapses into crime fiction with horses, which is the boundary the pack hands to mystery-crime-thriller.
entries.example: Hansen's The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford (1983) treats the legend and the killing as the same industry. Walter Hill's The Long Riders (1980) casts brothers as brothers to make a point about clan. George Roy Hill's Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969), written by William Goldman, shows the mode's other move: charm standing in for warrant, with the dispossession barely mentioned.
entries.application: Name the dispossession that licenses your outlaw, and put it on the page rather than in the backstory. If you cannot, you are writing a heist.

entries.name: The Trail Drive and the Cattle Empire
entries.description: The journey as a survey of a whole country, and the herd as the thing that owns everyone.
entries.principle: The trail drive converts the western into a logistics story with a moving population, which is why it produces the genre's best ensemble writing and its best labour writing. The cattle empire is the same subject after arrival: a claim that has succeeded and now has to be inherited. In both, the contested ground is often not contested by a named antagonist at all — the opposition is distance, weather, market and time.
entries.example: Adams's The Log of a Cowboy (1903) is the procedural baseline, written by a man who had done it. Hawks's Red River (1948) turns the drive into a succession crisis. McMurtry's Lonesome Dove (1985) spends the whole route arguing that the destination was never worth it, and Ferber's Giant (1952) takes the empire two generations on.
entries.application: Work out the money and the days before you write the weather. This is the subgenre where a reader who knows the material will catch you first, and the working-west collection exists for exactly this.

entries.name: The Town and the Marshal
entries.description: Jurisdiction as the subject, and the town's willingness to be governed as the real question.
entries.principle: The town western moves the contest from land to authority: who may hold office, what the office can actually compel, and whether the citizens will stand behind it. Its characteristic structure is a deadline rather than a journey, and its characteristic revelation is that the community is the antagonist. The office is small and its limits are specific, which is what gives the mode its pressure.
entries.example: Zinnemann's High Noon (1952) makes the town's refusal the plot. Hawks's Rio Bravo (1959) was made in explicit disagreement with it and answers with professional sufficiency. Hall's Warlock (1958) puts a hired gun and an elected office in the same street to ask which is law, and Milch's Deadwood (2004) shows a camp with no jurisdiction at all inventing one.
entries.application: Establish what your officer can and cannot legally do, and to whom, before the deadline starts. A marshal with unlimited authority is a superhero, and the subgenre's tension is entirely in the limits.

entries.name: The Range War
entries.description: Two lawful claims to the same ground, and the violence that arbitrates between them.
entries.principle: The range war is the purest form of the pack's organising claim, because both sides can state a warrant and neither is simply criminal: open range against enclosure, cattle against sheep, corporation against homesteader. Its moral clarity is usually manufactured — by scale, by hired guns, by making one side's warrant older — and noticing how a given story manufactures it is the most useful thing a writer can do with the mode.
entries.example: Schaefer's Shane (1949) hands the homesteaders the sympathy and the cattlemen the prior use, then imports a specialist to settle it. Cimino's Heaven's Gate (1980) takes the Johnson County war and refuses to manufacture clarity at all. Costner's Open Range (2003) restores it, on purpose and late.
entries.application: Write both warrants out in full before you choose. If one of them cannot be stated in a sentence the character would recognise, you have a villain rather than a claimant.

entries.name: The Mountain Man and the Fur Trade
entries.description: The pre-settlement West, where the economy is extraction and the protagonist has left society rather than founded it.
entries.principle: The fur-trade story runs before the genre's usual clock and therefore before the settlement argument, which frees it and limits it in the same move: there is no town to secure and no law to arrive, so the material has to generate its own stakes from survival, exchange and the terms on which a white trapper lives among people whose country it is. Its recurring hazard is treating those terms as scenery.
entries.example: Guthrie's The Big Sky (1947) is the mode's central novel and knows exactly what its protagonist destroys. Manfred's Lord Grizzly (1954) and Punke's The Revenant (2002) work the Hugh Glass material forty-eight years apart. Pollack's Jeremiah Johnson (1972), from Fisher's Mountain Man (1965), turns withdrawal into a career.
entries.application: Get the trade right — what is exchanged, at what rate, with whom, and who sets it. The economics are the plot here in a way they are not in the settled West.

entries.name: The Gold Rush and the Boom Camp
entries.description: A town with money and no institutions, and the short window before either arrives.
entries.principle: The boom camp gives the genre a setting where property is unstable by design: claims are staked rather than titled, the population is transient and unusually mixed, and the absence of law is a fact about paperwork rather than about wilderness. It is the western's most reliable setting for writing labour, women's work and non-white presence without special pleading, because the historical camp actually contained them.
entries.example: Harte's The Luck of Roaring Camp (1868) invents the sentimental version and the market for it. Altman's McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971), from Naughton's McCabe (1959), replaces the sentiment with a balance sheet. McCunn's Thousand Pieces of Gold (1981) writes the camp from a Chinese woman's position in it, and Milch's Deadwood (2004) shows the institutions arriving as a hostile takeover.
entries.application: Decide what a claim is worth and how it is recorded, because that is your story's property law. The camp is the one western setting where you can write the paperwork and keep the tension.

entries.name: The Zapata Western
entries.description: The Italian cycle's revolutionary strain, where the contested ground is a country and the outsider is a mercenary.
entries.principle: Defined and popularised by Christopher Frayling in 1981, the Zapata western pairs a Mexican revolutionary with a European or American professional and makes the political education of the professional the plot. Its distinguishing move is that the settlement argument is explicitly about power rather than land, and the film knows which side of the exchange it is on — which is why the mode carries left politics that the American form generally does not.
entries.example: Damiani's Quién sabe? (1966) sets the template of peon and gringo. Sollima's Faccia a faccia (1967) inverts it by converting the professor rather than the mercenary. Corbucci's Il mercenario (1968) plays it as farce with real stakes, and Leone's Giù la testa (1971) turns it against revolution itself.
entries.application: If your outsider ends the story unchanged, you have written a mercenary picture rather than a Zapata western. The conversion, in either direction, is the form.

entries.name: The Captivity Narrative
entries.description: The genre's oldest layer, where the contested ground is a person and the border runs through a family.
entries.principle: The captivity narrative predates the western by a century and a half and supplies it with its most durable and most dangerous plot: a white woman or child taken, a rescue attempted, and a return that may not be wanted. It is the form in which the genre's fear of contact is most nakedly stated, and the point at which a writer's choices about Indigenous peoples become unavoidable rather than incidental.
entries.example: Rowlandson's 1682 narrative establishes the shape and the theology. Cooper's The Last of the Mohicans (1826) makes it romance. Le May's The Searchers (1954) and Ford's film (1956) make the rescuer the problem, and Johnson's short story A Man Called Horse (1950) reverses the direction of travel.
entries.application: Ask what the captive wants, and let the answer be allowed to be inconvenient. The narratives that survive as literature are the ones where return is a loss.

entries.name: The Dime Novel, the Story Paper and the Paperback Line
entries.description: The industrial prose West, from Beadle's list to the men's-adventure shelf, and the market logic that shaped the genre's conventions.
entries.principle: The western's conventions were manufactured at speed for a mass market before they were anything else, and the constraints of that market — fixed length, series continuity, a required quota of incident — did more to fix the form than any single author. Treating this material as beneath notice reproduces the class distaste David Lusted diagnosed in critical writing about the form, and it also loses the historical explanation for why the genre looks the way it does.
entries.example: Beadle's Dime Novels began in 1860. Edward L. Wheeler invented Deadwood Dick for the story papers in 1877, and the traffic then ran backwards: Nat Love, Richard Clarke and others claimed the name afterwards, so the franchise manufactured the real men rather than the other way round. Mulford's Hopalong Cassidy stories from 1904 were rebuilt as a family screen property from 1935, against their author's harder original. The Longarm line from 1978 is the same machine running under different quotas, and is the genre's actual commercial floor for a working writer today.
entries.application: If you are writing for a series line, get the line's specification and honour it, because the specification is the form. If you are not, read the specification anyway — it is the clearest available statement of what the genre's audience has always been buying.

entries.name: The B-Western, the Singing Cowboy and the Serial
entries.description: The genre by volume — six-day shoots, series stars, a song, and a tie-in economy that paid for all of it.
entries.principle: From the mid-1930s to the early 1950s the studios released B-unit westerns built around a contracted star persona in very large numbers, and their economics rather than their scripts explain most of what they are: the running time, the recycled stock footage, the interchangeable plots and the songs that sold records. They are second-mode westerns almost without exception, circulating the iconography rather than arguing about the land, and they are where most of the audience actually met the genre.
entries.example: Autry's Republic pictures from 1935 built a merchandising business with a film attached. The Hopalong Cassidy screen series from 1935 turned Mulford's hard character into a family brand. Roy Rogers inherited and industrialised the model, and the serial format carried the same furniture to a juvenile audience week by week.
entries.application: Do not write these as if they were failed A-pictures. If you are working in the mode, the persona is the text and the plot is the delivery mechanism — and if you are writing about the genre, this is the output your generalisations have to survive.

entries.name: Iconography in Circulation
entries.description: The second mode — the settlement argument's furniture reproduced without the argument.
entries.principle: A great deal of the genre uses the hat, the standoff, the frontier town and the drifter as a working vocabulary for stories about something else entirely, and it is a mode rather than a failure. The pack's organising claim covers it explicitly: the work stands inside the iconographic system without contesting any ground. What makes it worth carding is that iconography is most legible when detached, so these works are the best evidence of what the furniture actually means.
entries.example: Crichton's Westworld (1973) makes the detachment its subject by building a literal simulation. Whedon's Firefly (2002) runs the whole vocabulary on a spaceship. Nightow's Trigun (1995) does it in manga, and Verbinski's Rango (2011) does it as a children's film that knows its sources exactly.
entries.application: Know which mode you are in and be consistent. The commonest failure here is a story that borrows the iconography for two acts and then reaches for the moral weight of a settlement argument it never set up.

entries.name: The Neo-Western
entries.description: The same claims, the same country, and a date after the genre's clock has stopped.
entries.principle: The neo-western keeps the contested claim to ground and the force that settles it, moves them into the twentieth or twenty-first century, and derives its charge from the mismatch between a frontier moral vocabulary and a landscape that now has banks, oil leases, highways and jurisdictions. Its recurring subject is a man whose code has outlived its applicability, which makes it the elegiac western's descendant rather than a separate invention.
entries.example: McMurtry's Horseman, Pass By (1961) and Ritt's film Hud (1963) put the code and the market in the same family. McCarthy's No Country for Old Men (2005) and the Coens' film (2007) hand the country to an economy that does not negotiate. Mackenzie's Hell or High Water (2016) makes the bank the land-grabber, and Sheridan's Yellowstone (2018) restores the cattle empire as a going concern.
entries.application: The anachronism is the engine — make sure something in the story is genuinely incompatible with the present rather than merely nostalgic about the past.

entries.name: The Borderland and Narco Western
entries.description: The line itself as the contested ground, and an economy that crosses it in both directions.
entries.principle: The borderland western takes the pack's claim and makes the boundary the object rather than the setting: what the line means, who may cross it, what it is worth to move something over it, and whose law stops where. It is the mode in which the genre's Mexican material stops being scenery, because the plot cannot function without the other side having its own interests, institutions and grievances.
entries.example: McCarthy's All the Pretty Horses (1992) sends its riders south and lets Mexico have a legal system that beats them. Winslow's The Power of the Dog (2005) writes the trade as a forty-year institutional history. Villeneuve's Sicario (2015) makes jurisdiction itself the horror, and the mode's crime-fiction half is handed to mystery-crime-thriller at subgenre-40.
entries.application: Give the far side of the line its own institutions and its own reasons. A borderland story in which Mexico is a condition rather than a country has written half a setting.

entries.name: The Indigenous Counter-Western
entries.description: The form worked from inside the communities it was built to write out, using its machinery deliberately.
entries.principle: The Indigenous counter-western is not a corrective appended to the genre but a body of work that takes the same country, the same century and often the same iconography and holds the camera or the sentence from the other position. Its distinguishing move is specificity: a named nation with its own protocols, obligations and internal disagreements, in place of the pan-Indian composite the classical form runs on. It is recent, real, and the first thing an Anglophone survey drops.
entries.example: Mourning Dove's Cogewea, the Half-Blood, drafted around 1912 and published in 1927, is the founding prose case; her collaborator Lucullus Virgil McWhorter edited it heavily and scholars remain divided on how far his hand went, which is itself part of the subject. Eyre's Smoke Signals (1998), from Alexie's stories, uses road-movie structure against the captivity plot. Kunuk's Atanarjuat (2001) works entirely in Inuktitut and refuses the genre's arrival premise; Harjo's Reservation Dogs (2021), co-created with Taika Waititi, inherits all of it as comedy.
entries.application: Name the nation, and find out what that nation has said about outside use before you write a word of ceremony. Specificity is not a courtesy here; it is the difference between this subgenre and the thing it is answering.

entries.name: The Black West
entries.description: The Black presence the genre's vocabulary writes out, and the fiction and film that puts it back.
entries.principle: The most-cited estimates put roughly a quarter of the working cowhands on the great drives as Black and a further eighth as Mexican; Richard Slatta notes these are the highest figures on offer and rest on thin documentation, but no estimate supports an all-white range, and Black settlement, soldiering, homesteading and lawkeeping are documented in detail. The classical western's whiteness is a selection rather than a record. The mode's craft problem is that restoring the presence is not enough: the story still has to give its Black characters a claim to ground and an interest of their own rather than a corrective walk-on.
entries.example: Oscar Micheaux wrote Black homesteading from experience in his novels of 1913 and 1917 and filmed The Homesteader in 1919, while the genre was still forming. Jenkins's Night Song (1994) writes the Tenth Cavalry as romance with the settlement history intact. Samuel's The Harder They Fall (2021) assembles documented figures into a genre picture on purpose.
entries.application: Give the claim, not the cameo. And handle the Bass Reeves material carefully: the link between Reeves and the Lone Ranger is Art T. Burton's hypothesis, not an established fact, and it circulates almost everywhere as though it were.

entries.name: The Women's Western and the Cowgirl Tradition
entries.description: The genre read against its own gender arrangement, and the tradition that never accepted it.
entries.principle: Jane Tompkins argued that the western is constitutively a flight from the sentimental novel and from the domestic authority of women, which makes the women's western a structural counter-tradition rather than a variant: it restores the interior, the household and the labour the form defined itself against. Its strongest work does not simply put a woman in the gunfighter's position but changes what the country is for.
entries.example: Cather's My Ántonia (1918) makes the prairie a working life rather than a frontier. Reichardt's Meek's Cutoff (2010) puts the wagon train's decisions in the hands of people denied a vote in them. Purcell's The Drover's Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson (2021) rewrites a national short story as a claim, and Kent's The Nightingale (2018) refuses the revenge structure the material invites.
entries.application: Ask what the women in your story are doing when they are not being looked at. The mode's test is whether the domestic economy exists on the page as work.

entries.name: The Queer Western
entries.description: The form's homosociality read straight, and the desire the classical version keeps just below the surface.
entries.principle: The western has always been a genre of men in intense proximity with women structurally excluded, and the queer western does not import anything — it declines to look away from what the arrangement already contains. Its craft interest is that the genre's own conventions of reticence, unspoken loyalty and physical closeness are unusually well suited to a story about what cannot be said, which is why the mode's best work is formally conservative.
entries.example: Proulx's Brokeback Mountain (1997) uses the genre's economy of speech as the mechanism of concealment. Savage's The Power of the Dog (1967) makes a rancher's performance of hardness the whole architecture, and Campion's film (2021) keeps it. Zhao's The Rider (2017) sits adjacent, on the cost of a masculinity its subject cannot put down.
entries.application: Use the reticence rather than solving it. A queer western that becomes explicit about its own subject in Act One has given up the genre's most useful inherited tool.

entries.name: The Weird Western
entries.description: The settlement argument run with a supernatural or fantastic engine, and what that engine is standing in for.
entries.principle: The weird western keeps the claim to ground and the force that settles it and makes one of the parties non-human, which turns the genre's anxieties into literal antagonists. It works when the fantastic element is doing the settlement argument's work — the land as genuinely hostile, the dead as genuinely unquiet about what happened on it — and fails when it is a costume change with monsters.
entries.example: Lansdale's Dead in the West (1986) is the pulp baseline played straight. Jones's The Only Good Indians (2020) makes a broken hunting obligation the whole causal engine. Zahler's Bone Tomahawk (2015) is the mode's most argued case precisely because of what it makes its antagonists, and McCarthy's Blood Meridian (1985) is the boundary the pack keeps just outside it.
entries.application: Make the fantastic element carry the claim. If your ghost could be removed without changing who owns the valley, you have written a horror story in a hat, and horror-reference owns it.

entries.name: The Italian Cycle
entries.description: The American form played straight by people who never believed its contract, with money in the place of land.
entries.principle: The Italian cycle strips the settlement argument out and leaves the iconography running without it, which is why its violence has no civic justification and its landscapes have no destination. The exchange is documented and litigated: Leone's Per un pugno di dollari (1964) is an unlicensed transposition of Kurosawa's Yojimbo (1961), Toho sued, and the settlement reportedly gave it fifteen per cent of worldwide receipts and distribution rights across Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. It is the one case in the genre where the borrowing was established in court rather than argued in criticism.
entries.example: Leone's Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo (1966) makes a treasure hunt of the Civil War and lets the war be removable. Corbucci's Django (1966) substitutes a coffin of gold for any claim to ground, and his Il grande silenzio (1968) sets the same machinery in snow and refuses the payout. C'era una volta il West (1968) is the cycle answering the American form directly, with Ford's own iconography quoted back.
entries.application: If your scene's morality is supplied by the audience's memory of other westerns rather than by anything present, you are working inside this cycle whether or not you meant to be.

entries.name: The Ostern
entries.description: The Eastern Bloc's westerns, in two distinct traditions that Anglophone accounts routinely merge.
entries.principle: There are two Osterns and they are not the same object. The East German DEFA Indianerfilme relocate sympathy to the Indigenous side and deliver explicitly anti-colonial content — while casting a Serbian actor as the Native lead across most of the cycle, which is a fact the card states alongside the politics rather than instead of them. The Soviet Ostern proper is mostly not about Native America at all: it moves the form to the Russian Civil War and Central Asia, where the contested authority is revolutionary rather than juridical.
entries.example: DEFA's cycle opens with Die Söhne der großen Bärin (1966), adapted from Liselotte Welskopf-Henrich's novels and built as an answer to the West German Karl May films. Motyl's Beloye solntse pustyni (1970) and Keosayan's Neulovimye mstiteli (1966) are the Soviet line; Mikhalkov's Svoy sredi chuzhikh, chuzhoy sredi svoikh (1974) is its most controlled example, and Lipský's Limonádový Joe (1964) is the Czechoslovak parody that proves the vocabulary had fully arrived.
entries.application: Say which Ostern you mean. And if you are writing about the DEFA films, hold both facts at once — the anti-colonial argument and the casting — because dropping either one misdescribes the cycle.

entries.name: The Australian Western
entries.description: A frontier with its own dispossession, its own outlaw legend, and a bush that answers to none of the American conventions.
entries.principle: Australia has the genre's other great settler frontier and reached it independently, through the bushranger legend and the squatter's run rather than through the cattle town, so the iconography differs while the claim is identical. The tradition's centre of gravity has moved decisively toward Indigenous authorship, which makes it the international tradition where the counter-western is strongest rather than marginal.
entries.example: Boldrewood's Robbery Under Arms (1888) establishes the bushranger as the outlaw form. Hillcoat's The Proposition (2005), written by Nick Cave, imports the American revisionist grammar deliberately and says so. Thornton's Sweet Country (2017) and Sen's Mystery Road (2013) work the same country from Kaytetye and Gamilaraay positions, and Purcell's The Drover's Wife (2021) rewrites the national canon from inside it.
entries.application: Do not transplant American furniture. The legal instruments, the pastoral economy and the terms of dispossession are all different, and the differences are where the material is.

entries.name: The Nordestern and the Latin American Western
entries.description: The Brazilian sertão and its cangaço banditry, where the antagonist is the landowner and the drought.
entries.principle: The nordestern inverts the American form's antagonist. The threat is not an Indigenous nation or an outlaw but the latifundio, the colonel and the weather, so the bandit is a figure of resistance rather than of criminality and the ballad-singing narrator is a structural device rather than decoration. It shares the American western's iconography — the horse, the rifle, the hard sun, the walk down a dirt street — and almost none of its politics.
entries.example: Barreto's O Cangaceiro (1953) is the founding commercial case and took the Best Adventure Film prize at Cannes that year, which is what exported the form. Rocha's Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol (1964) makes the cantador's ballad the narrative frame; his O Dragão da Maldade contra o Santo Guerreiro (1969) answers Leone's iconography directly. Mendonça Filho and Dornelles's Bacurau (2019) restages the whole tradition against a foreign hunting party.
entries.application: Find out who owns the land before you write who fires first. In this tradition the landlord is the plot, and a story that makes the bandit merely criminal has adopted the enemy's account.

entries.name: Japanese Chanbara and the Two-Way Traffic
entries.description: The exchange that runs in both directions, and the wandering swordsman who is the western's opposite number.
entries.principle: The traffic between the western and Japanese period film is documented on both sides and is genuinely reciprocal, which is why neither can be treated as the other's source. The relevant Japanese material is not jidaigeki as a whole — that is the entire category of period drama — but chanbara and the matatabi-mono wandering-gambler film, whose masterless swordsman occupies the structural position the western gives its drifter: skill without a place, arriving where he is needed and unable to stay.
entries.example: Sturges's The Magnificent Seven (1960) reached the screen through a rights chain rather than a studio licence — Lou Morheim acquired the remake rights reportedly for two hundred and fifty dollars and they passed to Yul Brynner, and Anthony Quinn sued over the arrangement and lost. Yojimbo (1961) went back the other way as Per un pugno di dollari (1964), and that one was settled in court. Miike's Sukiyaki Western Django (2007) closes the loop by making the borrowing its subject.
entries.application: When you borrow across this line, borrow the structure and not the costume. What transfers is the masterless professional and the town that needs him; what does not transfer is a legal and social order the western's audience will read wrongly.

entries.name: The Northern
entries.description: The Canadian frontier, where the law arrives first and the genre's central premise is therefore inverted.
entries.principle: The Northern was for decades a rival label rather than a subgenre, and its organising premise is the sharpest available contrast to the American form: that the Mounted Police reached the west ahead of large-scale settlement, so the story cannot turn on the absence of law. Historians of the North-West Mounted Police qualify that heavily, and the tradition is best read as running on the premise rather than on the record. What replaces it is a frontier of extraction and endurance where the antagonist is climate and distance, and where the moral question is obedience rather than jurisdiction.
entries.example: London's Yukon stories, from The Call of the Wild (1903) to To Build a Fire (1908), fix the endurance frontier for a mass audience. Curwood's novels and the long screen life they had build the Mountie as a type. Borsos's The Grey Fox (1982) imports an American outlaw into a country that is already administered, which is the tradition's premise dramatised.
entries.application: If you set a western in Canada, work out what the law already is before Chapter One. Writing the Northern as an American west with snow is the tradition's characteristic misuse.

entries.name: The Dacoit Film and the Indian Western
entries.description: The Chambal ravines, the bandit gang and the village that hires protection — India's own frontier form.
entries.principle: The dacoit film is an independent tradition with its own banditry, landscape and social grievance, which in the 1970s absorbed the American and Italian westerns and produced something neither could have made alone. Its characteristic structure is a village under predation hiring outsiders, so the settlement argument arrives as a question about protection and vengeance rather than about title.
entries.example: Khosla's Mera Gaon Mera Desh (1971) is the immediate precursor. Sippy's Sholay (1975), written by Salim–Javed, carries its acquisitions on the surface — the hired-defenders structure of Shichinin no samurai, the iconography and scoring of the Italian cycle, and set-pieces answering C'era una volta il West — and became the defining commercial success of its era on that synthesis.
entries.application: Treat the borrowing as a two-way claim rather than a derivation. Sholay is not a western with songs; it is a dacoit film that took what it needed and kept its own moral economy.

entries.name: The Charro Film and the Mexican West
entries.description: Mexico's own screen West, which was Hollywood's direct rival across Latin America and predates most of what borrowed from it.
entries.principle: The comedia ranchera built a national screen West around the charro — a horseman with a codified dress, music and social position that has no American equivalent — and paired it with a revolutionary cinema that took the same country seriously as history. Both traditions supply the northern-Mexico material that American borderland westerns use as backdrop, which is the single strongest reason for a Western pack to card them.
entries.example: De Fuentes's Allá en el Rancho Grande (1936) is the form's commercial breakthrough and the film that exported it across the continent; his Vámonos con Pancho Villa (1936) does the opposite job on the Revolution. Negrete and Infante turn the charro into a star system, and the Fernández–Figueroa partnership gives the landscape a visual language the Italian cycle later quotes.
entries.application: If your story crosses into Mexico, find out what the charro already means there. Using the figure as decoration in a story about Americans reproduces exactly the erasure the pack's presence floor exists to prevent.

entries.name: The Historical Western
entries.description: A western whose primary contract is a claim about the documented past — owned by historical-reference.
entries.principle: This story-type is handed off to the historical-reference pack, which owns the craft of reconstruction and already holds the frontier's revisionist material. Historical asks what claim the book makes about the past and what the record will bear; Western asks what makes a claim to ground legitimate and what the force that settles it costs. The overlap is the largest in the library and both packs card the same works from different contracts.
entries.example: Mantel's method applied to the Johnson County war would be a historical novel; Cimino's Heaven's Gate (1980) is a western, because its argument is about legitimacy rather than about evidence. McMurtry's Lonesome Dove (1985) is carded in both packs and answers to both questions.
entries.application: When the claim about the documented past is the point, work in the historical pack; when the claim to ground and the force settling it are the point, hold the western contract and hand the record across.

entries.name: The Indian Wars and the Cavalry Novel
entries.description: A frontier campaign told as military experience — owned by war-military-reference.
entries.principle: This story-type is handed off to the war-military-reference pack, which owns command, friction and what combat does to the people inside it. War asks what the fighting does to soldiers; Western asks what the campaign was for and whose claim it enforced. The pack notes that war-military currently holds no card on the Indian Wars in any form, so this hand-off is written alongside a reciprocal card into that pack.
entries.example: A novel that lives in the column, the supply line and the officer's nerve is War's. Aldrich's Ulzana's Raid (1972) uses all of that machinery to ask what the policy is, which makes it Western's.
entries.application: When the subject is the conduct and cost of the fighting, work in the war pack; when the subject is the warrant behind the campaign, hold the western contract and hand the soldiering across.

entries.name: The Literary Western
entries.description: A western whose primary contract is formal and interpretive — owned by literary-reference.
entries.principle: This story-type is handed off to the literary-reference pack, which owns prose, consciousness and the sentence as a unit of meaning. Literary asks what the manner of telling does that the material alone cannot; Western asks what claim is contested and what settles it. Literary already cards McCarthy, Erdrich and Blood Meridian and carries no Western hand-off of its own, so this card is written alongside a reciprocal one.
entries.example: McCarthy's Blood Meridian (1985) is carded in three packs and is genuinely all three things. Proulx's Brokeback Mountain (1997) survives the western collapse test and is handed across, with Western keeping the cowboy as its own figure of unfitness.
entries.application: When prose and consciousness exceed what the events supply, work in the literary pack; when the contested ground is the engine, hold the western contract and hand the manner across.

entries.name: The Space Western
entries.description: The frontier argument restaged off Earth — owned by sf-reference.
entries.principle: This story-type is handed off to the sf-reference pack, which owns extrapolation and already cards colonisation and frontier SF. SF asks whether the extrapolation holds; Western asks whether the claim to ground is contested and what force settles it. Many space westerns are second-mode works in this pack's terms, circulating the iconography without arguing about any land, and those are SF's outright.
entries.example: Corey's Cibola Burn (2014) is carded in SF as a water-rights war restaged under alien ruins, and the western structure is the point of it. Whedon's Firefly (2002) is carded here at subgenre-18 as iconography in circulation, because the settlement argument is furniture rather than subject.
entries.application: When the speculative premise is doing the work, work in the SF pack; when a contested claim to ground is doing it, hold the western contract and hand the extrapolation across.

entries.name: The Western Parodied
entries.description: Comic treatment of the form, which requires the form to be fixed enough to recognise — owned by comedy-reference.
entries.principle: This story-type is handed off to the comedy-reference pack, which owns parody and pastiche and requires that a borrowed form be reproduced competently before it is altered. Comedy asks who pays for the laugh and whether the joke lands; Western asks what the form being reproduced actually asserts. Comedy wrote its half of this hand-off before this pack existed, naming this pack's iconography and moral-structure cards as the source a parodist reproduces from.
entries.example: Brooks's Blazing Saddles (1974) is carded in comedy and parodies the genre and the industry that made it at once. Lipský's Limonádový Joe (1964) does the same job from inside the Eastern Bloc, which is why it is also carded here at subgenre-27.
entries.application: When the comic contract is primary, work in the comedy pack; when what the form asserts is primary, hold the western contract and hand the joke across.

entries.name: The Western Romance
entries.description: The West as the setting for a central love story with a guaranteed ending — owned by romance-reference.
entries.principle: This story-type is handed off to the romance-reference pack, which owns the central promise and already holds Western and Americana as one of its own subgenres. Romance asks whether the relationship's arc is earned and the promise kept; Western asks whether a contested claim to ground is settled by force. The mail-order bride, the marriage of convenience and the rancher hero are romance's property, and the commercial line is substantial.
entries.example: Jenkins's Night Song (1994) is carded in romance and is also a Black West work this pack cards at subgenre-22 from the other contract. A homesteading novel whose ending turns on title rather than on the couple is Western's.
entries.application: When the promise to the reader is the relationship, work in the romance pack; when it is the claim to the ground, hold the western contract and hand the courtship across.

entries.name: The Borderland Crime Novel
entries.description: Crime and investigation on the line, where the procedure is the contract — owned by mystery-crime-thriller-reference.
entries.principle: This story-type is handed off to the mystery-crime-thriller-reference pack, which owns investigation, procedure and the crime's solution. Crime asks how the thing is solved and what solving it costs; Western asks what claim to ground the violence is settling. MCT holds Hillerman's Navajo procedurals, Winslow's cartel history and Grann's Osage material, and — a gap this pack notes — cards Elmore Leonard purely as a crime writer, with his substantial western period unmentioned anywhere in the library.
entries.example: Hillerman's Dance Hall of the Dead (1973) is carded in MCT because the investigation is the contract. Leonard's Hombre (1961) is Western's, and this pack claims his western period as its own.
entries.application: When the case is the spine, work in the crime pack; when the spine is who may hold the ground, hold the western contract and hand the investigation across.

entries.name: Establish Whose Ground It Is Before Anyone Rides In
entries.description: The genre's first question is not who is dangerous but who is entitled, and the answer must exist before the plot needs it.
entries.principle: A western's conflict is legible only against a settled account of who holds what and on what basis, so the writer has to know the ownership situation of every location in the story before a rider crosses it. This is not exposition; almost none of it reaches the page. It is the substrate that lets a scene of trespass, hospitality or refusal carry weight, because the reader can feel that something is at stake in a doorway.
entries.example: Schaefer's Shane (1949) can stage an entire film around a fence line because the homesteaders' patents and the cattleman's prior use are both fixed before the story opens. Hall's Warlock (1958) knows exactly which authority each of its three armed men derives from, which is why their standoff is a constitutional argument rather than a brawl.
entries.application: Write the ownership situation out for yourself as a paragraph per location, then delete it. If you cannot say who holds a piece of ground and how they came to, your antagonist has no warrant and your protagonist has no grievance.

entries.name: A Warrant Is a Sentence the Claimant Would Say Out Loud
entries.description: Every party to the dispute must be able to state their entitlement in words they believe.
entries.principle: The test of a claim is whether the person holding it could state it, in one sentence, without irony and without the author's editorial showing through. A warrant the character would not recognise is not a warrant but a verdict, and readers can tell the difference immediately: villains who know they are villains are the genre's most common structural failure.
entries.example: Cimino's Heaven's Gate (1980) lets the Stock Growers' Association state its position at full strength, which is what makes its actions monstrous rather than merely wicked. Ford's Fort Apache (1948) gives Thursday a doctrine he genuinely holds, so the disaster follows from a belief rather than from stupidity.
entries.application: Write each claimant's sentence in the first person before drafting. If one of them comes out as an admission of guilt, you have not found their warrant yet.

entries.name: Name the Basis: Purchase, Treaty, Conquest, Labour, Prior Occupancy
entries.description: The five warrants the genre actually runs on, and what each one commits your story to.
entries.principle: Claims in the western rest on a small number of bases and they are not interchangeable. Purchase invites the question of who sold and whether they could. Treaty invites the question of whether it was kept, which in this genre is usually answerable. Conquest is honest and hard to sympathise with. Labour — I built this, I worked it, I bled here — is the genre's most emotionally powerful warrant and its least legally durable. Prior occupancy is the strongest of all and the one the classical form is built to make invisible.
entries.example: McMurtry's Lonesome Dove (1985) runs almost entirely on labour: the drive earns the claim, and the book spends eight hundred pages asking whether that is enough. Le May's The Searchers (1954) has a prior-occupancy claim standing behind the whole plot that the rescue narrative is structured never to examine.
entries.application: Name the basis for each party in one word. If two parties share a basis, your conflict is about facts; if they differ, it is about law, and those are different stories.

entries.name: The Uncontested Claim Is Still a Claim
entries.description: Some of the genre's best work has no antagonist holding the other end of the argument.
entries.principle: A western does not require a rival claimant. The opposition can be distance, drought, market price, an institution with no face, or time — and in those stories the claim is tested rather than disputed. The craft demand shifts accordingly: with no antagonist to externalise the stakes, the cost has to be made visible in labour, attrition and the passage of seasons, which is why this mode produces the genre's best writing about work.
entries.example: Kelton's The Time It Never Rained (1973) sets a rancher against a drought and a federal programme and gives him no enemy to shoot. Adams's The Log of a Cowboy (1903) has no villain at all and holds attention on procedure. Reichardt's Meek's Cutoff (2010) makes the contested thing a direction of travel.
entries.application: If you have no rival claimant, put a clock on the claim — a debt, a season, a herd that has to reach a railhead. Without one the mode drifts, and drift is what gets it called slow.

entries.name: Two Lawful Claims Beat One Lawful and One Criminal
entries.description: The genre's strongest conflicts are between parties who are both entitled.
entries.principle: Where one party is simply a criminal, the western collapses into a crime story with horses and the moral work is done before the story starts. Where both hold real entitlements — open range against enclosure, grazing against water, an old grant against a new patent — the reader has to decide, and the story can afford to let its protagonist be wrong. This is the structural reason the range war is the genre's most durable plot.
entries.example: Costner's Open Range (2003) is weaker than its material because it makes one side hired thugs. Cimino's Heaven's Gate (1980) is harder to watch and more honest because it does not. Hall's Warlock (1958) gives three armed men three legitimate sources of authority and lets them cancel one another out.
entries.application: Before you assign sympathy, check whether the losing side could win a hearing. If they could not, you are writing about crime, and the crime pack owns it.

entries.name: Put the Paperwork On the Page
entries.description: Deeds, patents, brands, water rights and filings are dramatic objects, not research.
entries.principle: The instruments that record a claim are physical, forgeable, losable and burnable, which makes them among the most useful props the genre has. A story that keeps its legal situation entirely in dialogue wastes the fact that in this period ownership was a piece of paper in a box in a town that might burn down. The paperwork also disciplines the writer: you cannot fudge a claim you have had to describe.
entries.example: Milch's Deadwood (2004) makes the absence of any recognised title the engine of a whole season, because the camp is on land the United States has not yet taken. Ferber's Giant (1952) tracks an empire across generations through what is on the documents and what is not.
entries.application: Give at least one claim in your story a physical instrument, and put it somewhere it can be lost. If your plot cannot survive the deed burning, the deed was decorative.

entries.name: Standing Is a Claim — the Right to Be Somewhere at All
entries.description: Not every contested claim is to property; many are to presence, passage or belonging.
entries.principle: The pack's organising claim covers ground in the broad sense, and a large part of the genre is about the right to be in a place rather than to own it: to ride through, to drink in the saloon, to hold office, to stay after dark, to be buried in the cemetery. These claims are cheaper to establish than title and they cut closer, because they are enforced socially rather than legally and the enforcement is visible in every scene.
entries.example: McCunn's Thousand Pieces of Gold (1981) turns on whether a Chinese woman may be present in a mining town on her own terms. Jenkins's Night Song (1994) makes a Black cavalry garrison's standing in a white town the constant condition of the romance. Zinnemann's High Noon (1952) is a story about whether an officer may ask anything of a town at all.
entries.application: Ask what your characters are permitted to do in each location by custom rather than by law, and who enforces it. The genre's sharpest scenes usually happen at that boundary.

entries.name: The Warrant That Is Only Arrival
entries.description: The genre's default and weakest warrant — we are here, therefore it is ours — and what to do when it is the one your story rests on.
entries.principle: A great deal of the classical form runs on a claim with no stated basis at all: the country is described as waiting, the settlers arrive, and the entitlement follows from presence. It is the move the whole revisionist tradition takes apart, and a writer working today has three honest options — state it as the character's belief, let the story test it, or write a work that is knowingly reproducing the myth. What does not work is deploying it while pretending to be neutral.
entries.example: Wister's The Virginian (1902) supplies the model, with Wyoming rendered as available. Penn's Little Big Man (1970) puts a named people into the same country and the availability evaporates. Thornton's Sweet Country (2017) shows the same warrant operating in Australia with the paperwork stripped away entirely.
entries.application: If your story uses this warrant, decide on page one whether the story knows it is a warrant. A narrator who does not notice is making a claim on the author's behalf.

entries.category: Violence, Its Staging and Its Cost
entries.name: Decide What the Violence Buys Before You Stage It
entries.description: In this genre killing is a transaction, and the writer has to know the price and the purchase.
entries.principle: The western uses violence as its mechanism of resolution, which means every killing settles something — a claim, an office, a debt, a question of who may stay. If you cannot say what a given death purchases and for whom, the scene is spectacle, and spectacle in this genre reads as endorsement whether or not you meant it. The classical form is very clear about the purchase; the revisionist form makes the purchase worthless; the anti-western refuses to complete the transaction.
entries.example: Eastwood's Unforgiven (1992) restores the walk-down specifically so it can present the invoice. Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch (1969) stages a battle on a scale the genre had not attempted in order to buy nothing at all, which is the argument.
entries.application: Write the purchase in the margin beside every killing in your outline. Any death with a blank beside it is either doing work you have not identified or should not be there.

entries.category: Violence, Its Staging and Its Cost
entries.name: Who Pays, and Is the Payer On the Page
entries.description: The genre's characteristic erasure is a craft failure before it is an ethical one.
entries.principle: Settlement in the western is paid for by people the form is very good at keeping out of frame — the dispossessed, the labourers, the women who bury the dead, the town that has to live with what was done in its name. When the payer is absent the story loses its stakes as well as its honesty, because a cost nobody visibly bears is not a cost. This is the single most productive question in the pack.
entries.example: Ford's The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962) keeps its payer in the frame for decades and makes the whole film an account of the debt. Clark's The Ox-Bow Incident (1940) puts the price in a read-aloud letter and refuses to let the posse leave before it is paid.
entries.application: For each act of violence, name the person who bears the consequence and put them in a scene. If the only people affected are the shooter and the shot, the story has understated its own subject.

entries.category: Violence, Its Staging and Its Cost
entries.name: Camera Distance and the Ethics of the Kill
entries.description: How close you stand to a killing is an argument about it, on the page as much as on screen.
entries.principle: Proximity confers intimacy and intimacy confers consent — the closer and slower the rendering, the more the work asks the audience to participate rather than witness. Distance, brevity and refusal are equally available and equally legible. Neither is automatically the moral choice: a killing rendered at a cold distance can be a dismissal, and one rendered closely can be an indictment. What matters is that the choice is a choice.
entries.example: Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch (1969) uses multiple cameras and intercut slow motion to make death take longer than the audience wants; the technique reached him through his editor Lou Lombardo and the example of Bonnie and Clyde (1967) rather than, as is often claimed, directly from Kurosawa. Altman's McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971) declines to stage its killing for pleasure at all. Zahler's Bone Tomahawk (2015) is the genre's most argued case in the other direction.
entries.application: On the page, control distance with sentence length and with whose senses you are inside. If the reader is enjoying it and the story does not know that, you have made the choice by accident.

entries.category: Violence, Its Staging and Its Cost
entries.name: The Aftermath Is the Scene
entries.description: The genre's real material is the ten minutes after the shooting, not the shooting.
entries.principle: Gunfights are short and, in craft terms, largely self-executing; what distinguishes a western is what the story does with the body, the widow, the horse, the town's silence and the legal aftermath. Writers new to the genre put their effort in the wrong place, and the tell is a story that ends on a gunshot. The best work treats the exchange of fire as a hinge and gives the weight to what it opens onto.
entries.example: Clark's The Ox-Bow Incident (1940) is entirely aftermath and is the strongest anti-lynching novel the genre produced. Swarthout's The Shootist (1975) knows its subject is dying rather than shooting. Milch's Deadwood (2004) reliably cuts to the disposal of the body and the negotiation that follows.
entries.application: Draft the scene that follows your climactic violence before you draft the violence. If the story has nothing to say afterwards, the violence was the point, and that is a different genre.

entries.category: Violence, Its Staging and Its Cost
entries.name: Count the Rounds and the Reload
entries.description: The genre's technical floor, and the place a knowledgeable reader catches you first.
entries.principle: The weapons of the period have hard limits and those limits generate scenes: a single-action revolver carried safely holds five, a reload is one cartridge at a time through a loading gate, a rifle out-ranges a pistol by an order of magnitude, and black powder leaves a cloud that tells everyone where you are. Getting this right is not pedantry — it is where the tension in a gunfight actually lives, because a man who is empty has a problem the audience can count.
entries.example: Eastwood's Unforgiven (1992) makes competence with a weapon rare, difficult and mostly absent, which is what gives its violence weight. The genre's B-unit tradition ran on the opposite convention, and its bottomless revolver is the most recognisable single marker of the second mode.
entries.application: Track ammunition in your outline as you would track time of day. The working-west collection carries the specifications; the craft point is that the limits are dramatic gifts rather than constraints.

entries.category: Violence, Its Staging and Its Cost
entries.name: Massacre Is Not a Set Piece
entries.description: Rendering a documented mass killing carries obligations that a fictional gunfight does not.
entries.principle: The genre's history includes Sand Creek, the Washita, the Marias, Bear River and Wounded Knee, and a story that stages one of them is making a claim about a real event with descendants living. The craft requirements are specific: name the event and the nation, do not invent participants who stand in for real ones, do not resolve it, and do not let the sequence deliver the satisfactions of an action scene. Historical's own cards on reconstructed massacre and on depicting atrocity are the standing library craft here.
entries.example: Nelson's Soldier Blue (1970) stages Sand Creek as spectacle and is argued about for exactly that reason. Penn's Little Big Man (1970) reaches the Washita through a structure that has been alternating registers all film, so the sequence arrives as rupture rather than climax.
entries.application: If you are staging a documented massacre, write it without any character achieving anything. The moment a protagonist's arc is served by it, you have made a set piece.

entries.category: Violence, Its Staging and Its Cost
entries.name: The Body Recovers on a Schedule
entries.description: Wounds in this period have a timetable, and honouring it changes your plot.
entries.principle: Before antisepsis a survivable wound is a slow event with a fever in the middle of it, and that timetable is a structural resource: it strands characters, forces dependence, puts a competent man in someone else's hands and generates the genre's best two-hander scenes. Writers who let a shoulder wound heal in a scene transition throw away a week of story and a change in the power relations of the cast.
entries.example: Punke's The Revenant (2002) is entirely built on the schedule of a body repairing itself in the open. Portis's True Grit (1968) puts its climax on the wrong side of an injury and makes the return journey the real test.
entries.application: Give every significant wound a duration in days and put it in the outline. Then ask who is obliged to stay.

entries.category: Violence, Its Staging and Its Cost
entries.name: Violence That Settles Nothing
entries.description: The hardest mode to sustain, and the one the genre's most serious work reaches for.
entries.principle: If violence is the western's mechanism of settlement, then violence that settles nothing is the form arguing against itself, and it is structurally difficult because the machinery keeps promising resolution the story intends to withhold. Sustaining it requires removing the usual compensations — no competent professional, no legible antagonist, no aftermath that redistributes anything — and it fails the moment the writer relents and lets one killing mean something.
entries.example: McCarthy's Blood Meridian (1985) never permits an exchange of fire to alter the moral situation. Corbucci's Il grande silenzio (1968) builds an entire film toward a walk-down and then refuses the outcome the form demands.
entries.application: If you are writing this mode, audit every act of violence for a payoff you did not intend to give. One relented scene converts the whole book into a revisionist western with an unearned ending.

entries.category: Landscape, Music and the Genre's Sensory Signature
entries.name: The Country Is a Party to the Dispute
entries.description: Landscape in a western is not setting; it is one of the claimants.
entries.principle: The western's country has interests — it withholds water, it hides people, it kills the unprepared and it rewards the knowledgeable — and treating it as a backdrop wastes the genre's most distinctive asset. The practical test is whether the landscape ever changes what a character decides. If every scene could happen on a different piece of ground with no consequence, the country is scenery and the story is a costume drama.
entries.example: Guthrie's The Big Sky (1947) makes knowledge of the country the difference between the men who live and the men who do not. Reichardt's Meek's Cutoff (2010) shoots in a nearly square frame so the horizon is denied to the audience as it is to the party.
entries.application: Take one decision in each act and make the terrain the reason for it. Then check that a reader could draw a rough map from the text.

entries.category: Landscape, Music and the Genre's Sensory Signature
entries.name: Weather Is a Deadline
entries.description: Season and weather are the genre's most reliable source of structural pressure.
entries.principle: Drives have to reach railheads before the market moves, passes close, rivers rise, herds cannot be held through a winter and drought does not negotiate. Weather in the western is therefore a clock rather than an atmosphere, and using it that way solves the pacing problem the genre's open landscapes create. The corollary is that weather deployed purely for mood is a missed opportunity twice over.
entries.example: Kelton's The Time It Never Rained (1973) makes a drought the antagonist and lets it win on its own timetable. McMurtry's Lonesome Dove (1985) is organised by the seasons a herd can be moved in, and its worst losses arrive on schedule.
entries.application: Put the weather in your outline as dates, not as description. If nothing in the story would change if the season were different, the setting is doing no work.

entries.category: Landscape, Music and the Genre's Sensory Signature
entries.name: Distance Is the Real Antagonist
entries.description: How far things are from each other governs plot, and most writers get it wrong by a factor of three.
entries.principle: The western's country is crossed at the speed of a horse or a wagon, and that speed is slower and more constrained than instinct suggests: a day's ride is a working figure, not an approximation, and it determines who can arrive in time, how far help is, how long a body lies undiscovered and whether a threat is credible. Distance is also the genre's supply of dread, because a threat two days away is a different story from one two hours away.
entries.example: Zinnemann's High Noon (1952) works because the audience knows exactly how long the train takes. Portis's True Grit (1968) makes a journey's length the measure of a girl's determination and never shortens it for convenience.
entries.application: Draw the map and put times on the routes before you write the chase. The working-west collection carries the day-rates; the craft point is that they are plot, not colour.

entries.category: Landscape, Music and the Genre's Sensory Signature
entries.name: Description Earns Its Place by Knowing the Work
entries.description: Landscape prose in this genre survives on specificity of labour, not on adjectives.
entries.principle: The difference between western description that lands and description that reads as postcard is whether the land is known from inside a working life — what grazes there, what it costs to cross, what the soil will take, where the water is in August. Naming plants, tools and stock correctly does more than any amount of atmospheric writing, because it signals that the narrator belongs to the place rather than visiting it.
entries.example: Cather's My Ántonia (1918) writes the prairie almost entirely through cultivation and season and is the standing model. Adams's The Log of a Cowboy (1903) is unliterary on purpose and gets its authority from procedure. Proulx's Wyoming stories work the same seam a century later.
entries.application: In every landscape paragraph, name one thing that only a person who worked that ground would know. Cut every adjective that could apply to any wide country anywhere.

entries.category: Landscape, Music and the Genre's Sensory Signature
entries.name: The Score Announces the Genre Before the First Line
entries.description: Few genres are identifiable from four bars of score; this one is, and that is a craft fact.
entries.principle: The genre's scoring conventions are strong enough to function as a claim about the material — the wide orchestral Americana of the studio era asserts national epic, the whistle, twang, ocarina and wordless soprano of the Italian cycle assert that the whole thing is being quoted. A writer working in prose should still know this, because the reader arrives with the sound already in their head and the story is either using that or fighting it.
entries.example: Moross's The Big Country (1958) and Bernstein's The Magnificent Seven (1960) set the American convention. Morricone's C'era una volta il West (1968), with Edda Dell'Orso's wordless vocal, sets the other one and makes the borrowing audible.
entries.application: Decide which sound your reader is hearing and write with or against it deliberately. In screen work, the score is a statement of allegiance before a single frame of argument.

entries.category: Landscape, Music and the Genre's Sensory Signature
entries.name: The Ballad Over the Titles
entries.description: The sung summary that tells the audience what the story means before it begins.
entries.principle: The title ballad is a genuine structural device, not a marketing appendage: it states the moral of the film in advance, which converts the plot into the demonstration of a proposition the audience already holds. That is why it belongs to the classical and elegiac modes and sits awkwardly in revisionist work. Its prose equivalent is the epigraph or the framing narrator who tells you the ending first.
entries.example: Tiomkin and Washington's ballad for High Noon (1952), sung by Tex Ritter, states the marshal's dilemma before the story does, and took the Oscar for Best Song. Bacharach and David's The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance is associated with Ford's 1962 film, does not appear in it, and was a hit for Gene Pitney in May 1962 regardless — a useful reminder that the convention had a life outside the pictures.
entries.application: If you open with a statement of the moral, commit to demonstrating it. A ballad promising a lesson followed by a story that undercuts it is a tonal fracture, not an irony.

entries.category: Landscape, Music and the Genre's Sensory Signature
entries.name: The Corrido and the Cantador Are Structure, Not Colour
entries.description: In the borderland and Brazilian traditions the song is the narrator, and it carries a counter-history.
entries.principle: Both the Mexican corrido and the Brazilian cantador's ballad are narrative forms in their own right — they name the hero, state the grievance, and transmit an account of events the official record contradicts. When a story in these traditions uses song it is not adding atmosphere but citing a rival source, and treating the music as texture drops the entire point.
entries.example: Paredes's With His Pistol in His Hand (1958) reconstructs the corrido of Gregorio Cortez and shows the ballad preserving what the Texas record suppressed. Rocha's Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol (1964) hands the narration to a cantador outright, so the film is structured as a ballad being sung.
entries.application: If your story crosses into this material, work out what the song claims and whether the story agrees with it. A corrido that merely sounds authentic has been used as decoration.

entries.category: Landscape, Music and the Genre's Sensory Signature
entries.name: Silence and the Withheld Line
entries.description: The genre's inherited reticence is a tool, and it is the tool most often thrown away.
entries.principle: The western's characters famously do not explain themselves, and the convention is worth more than its reputation for laconic cool: it forces meaning into action, gesture and the gap between what is said and what is meant, and it makes a single spoken admission enormous. The failure mode is a story that mistakes silence for depth. Reticence works only when the audience knows there is something specific being withheld.
entries.example: Proulx's Brokeback Mountain (1997) makes the genre's inarticulacy the mechanism of concealment and the source of the loss. Ford's The Searchers (1956) withholds Ethan's central motive so completely that critics still argue about it, and the film is stronger for refusing to settle it.
entries.application: For each withheld line, write the version where the character says it, and check that you know exactly what it would have been. Silence you have not filled in privately reads as vagueness.

entries.category: Structure — Wright's Four Plots and the Set Pieces
entries.name: Wright's Classical Plot: The Stranger the Society Cannot Absorb
entries.description: The first of Will Wright's four structures, and the one the whole genre is measured against.
entries.principle: In Sixguns and Society (1975) Will Wright derived four plot structures from the genre's commercially successful films, and the classical is the base case: an outsider of unknown ability arrives at a society, the society is threatened, his ability is revealed, he defeats the threat and is offered a place. Its engine is the gap between the skill the society needs and the standing it will grant.
entries.example: Stevens's Shane (1953) is Wright's own classical exemplar and the structure at its purest, with the offered place withheld at the end. Note that Wright's corpus is box-office films rather than novels, and that he classes Ford's Stagecoach (1939) under the vengeance variation rather than here — a reminder to check a film against his functions rather than against its reputation.
entries.application: Use it when your story's question is whether a community can accept what saves it. Wright's four are the most usable tool in the criticism because he stated his method — check your plot against all four before you assume you are writing this one.

entries.category: Structure — Wright's Four Plots and the Set Pieces
entries.name: Wright's Vengeance Plot: The Hero Who Leaves
entries.description: The variation in which the protagonist starts inside the society and steps out of it to settle a wrong.
entries.principle: Wright's vengeance structure inverts the classical: the hero begins as a member, is wronged, leaves the society in order to act, and the society then tries to hold him back. The moral pressure runs the other way — the community is an obstacle rather than a prize — and the ending turns on whether revenge is completed, abandoned or completed at a cost that makes return impossible.
entries.example: Ford's The Searchers (1956) runs it for five years and makes the return the unanswerable part. Mann's The Naked Spur (1953) puts the wrong and the bounty in the same man so the motive cannot be cleanly stated.
entries.application: Decide early whether the society is right to try to stop him. If it is, you are writing a critique of the revenge; if it is not, you are writing an endorsement, and audiences read the difference instantly.

entries.category: Structure — Wright's Four Plots and the Set Pieces
entries.name: Wright's Transition Plot: The Society That Turns
entries.description: The structure in which the community is the antagonist and the protagonists end outside it.
entries.principle: In Wright's transition structure the protagonists begin inside the society and can see something it refuses to see; the society turns on them; they hold to a value it has abandoned; and they end outside it, having won the argument and lost the place. It is the genre's mechanism for social criticism, which is why it clusters in the 1950s, and it is structurally harder than the other three because it must make the community's refusal plausible rather than merely cowardly.
entries.example: Zinnemann's High Noon (1952) is the case Wright builds the category on. Clark's The Ox-Bow Incident (1940) runs it to the bleakest available ending, with the value held only by men who cannot enforce it.
entries.application: Give the community a reason a decent person could hold. A town that refuses out of pure cowardice makes the protagonist correct too cheaply, and the structure needs the refusal to cost the reader something.

entries.category: Structure — Wright's Four Plots and the Set Pieces
entries.name: Wright's Professional Plot: The Group That Serves Itself
entries.description: The late structure, in which the society is irrelevant and loyalty runs sideways.
