entries.principle: Wright's professional plot replaces the individual with a group who are already skilled, already known to one another, and hired rather than called. Society is weak, absent or corrupt, and the moral centre is the group's internal code — competence, loyalty, the job finished. It dominates the genre from the late 1950s and it is the structure most easily emptied out, because a code with nothing outside it to serve becomes an aesthetic.
entries.example: Hawks's Rio Bravo (1959) is the structure arriving. Brooks's The Professionals (1966) names it. Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch (1969) runs it to the point where the code is all that is left and shows what that costs.
entries.application: Ask what the group's code is for. If it serves nothing beyond the group, say so on purpose — that is the mode's real subject and its most interesting failure.

entries.category: Structure — Wright's Four Plots and the Set Pieces
entries.name: The Ride-In
entries.description: The genre's opening move, and the information it is obliged to deliver.
entries.principle: An arrival scene has four jobs and they are all load-bearing: establish the country, establish the society's condition before the story disturbs it, establish what the arriving figure can do, and establish what the society sees when it looks at him. The convention is so fixed that a reader will supply the missing pieces if you skip them, which is exactly the risk — they will supply the classical defaults.
entries.example: Ford's stagecoach coming down into Monument Valley does all four in a single sequence. Altman's McCabe & Mrs. Miller (1971) subverts each of them deliberately, arriving in rain with a reputation the man has not earned.
entries.application: Write the ride-in even if you cut it. If you cannot say what the town looked like the day before your protagonist arrived, the story has no baseline to disturb.

entries.category: Structure — Wright's Four Plots and the Set Pieces
entries.name: The Walk-Down
entries.description: The formal duel as a court of law, and the most heavily conventionalised scene in the genre.
entries.principle: The walk-down is a legal procedure disguised as a fight: the parties agree to it, witnesses attend, a verdict is delivered and the community accepts the result. That is why it satisfies, and why the revisionist tradition attacks it by removing the procedure — the shot from cover, the shot in the back, the man who will not draw. Understanding it as a court is what lets a writer break it usefully rather than merely dirtily.
entries.example: Wister's The Virginian (1902) establishes the form as a settlement the town endorses. Eastwood's Unforgiven (1992) restores every element of the ritual and then narrates what the ritual is actually for.
entries.application: Decide what verdict your walk-down delivers and who accepts it. If the town does not care about the outcome, the scene is a fight, and fights are much less interesting than trials.

entries.category: Structure — Wright's Four Plots and the Set Pieces
entries.name: The Ride-Out
entries.description: The ending the genre reaches for, and the question of whether it has been earned.
entries.principle: The departure ending states the genre's central proposition in one image: the man whose skills secured the place cannot live in it. It is powerful and it is nearly automatic, which makes it the ending most often used to avoid a harder one. The test is whether the story has established a specific incompatibility — something this man did that this town cannot hold — rather than a general aura of unbelonging.
entries.example: Schaefer's Shane (1949) earns it by making the child's need and the man's function the same thing. Ford's The Searchers (1956) closes a door on it. Swarthout's The Shootist (1975) refuses it, because its subject is a man with nowhere to ride to.
entries.application: Before you write the ride-out, write the version where he stays and find out what breaks. If nothing does, you have not earned the ending.

entries.category: Structure — Wright's Four Plots and the Set Pieces
entries.name: The Set-Piece Inventory, and When to Refuse One
entries.description: The genre's fixed sequences are a resource with a cost, and the refusal is also a move.
entries.principle: The western has a short, fixed inventory — the ride-in, the saloon confrontation, the card game, the river crossing, the stampede, the ambush, the siege, the hanging, the walk-down, the ride-out — and audiences know all of them. That knowledge is capital: it lets you compress, and it lets you generate tension purely by delay. It is also a trap, because a story assembled from the inventory has structure without argument.
entries.example: Hawks's Rio Bravo (1959) uses almost the whole inventory and earns it by making each one a test of the group's code. Reichardt's Meek's Cutoff (2010) refuses nearly all of it and generates its tension from the refusal.
entries.application: List the set pieces in your outline and mark each one with the story reason it exists. Any set piece you cannot justify twice is decoration, and the ones you refuse should be refused visibly.

entries.category: Voice, Idiom and Which Language the Scene Is In
entries.name: The Vernacular Narrator
entries.description: The genre's most distinctive prose resource — a narrator whose speech is the region's.
entries.principle: Western prose gets much of its authority from a voice that belongs to the country rather than describing it, and the technique is grammatical rather than decorative: sentence rhythm, the refusal of certain constructions, and a vocabulary tied to work. The failure mode is phonetic spelling, which slows reading and patronises the speaker. The successful version changes syntax and leaves orthography alone.
entries.example: Portis's True Grit (1968) builds Mattie Ross out of a refusal of contractions and a King James cadence, and never spells a word oddly. Twain established the terms a century earlier, and Proulx's Wyoming stories work the same seam with a modern ear.
entries.application: Write one paragraph of your narrator's voice with all dialect spelling removed and see whether it still sounds like the person. If it does not, the voice was an accent rather than a character.

entries.category: Voice, Idiom and Which Language the Scene Is In
entries.name: Period Idiom Without Costume Dialogue
entries.description: Sounding of the period without writing a pastiche of previous westerns.
entries.principle: Most of what reads as western dialogue is not nineteenth-century speech but mid-twentieth-century screen convention, so a writer aiming at period accuracy and a writer aiming at genre familiarity are pursuing different targets and should know which. Real period idiom is more formal, more biblical and more legalistic than the screen version, and using it is a strong choice with a cost in accessibility.
entries.example: Milch's Deadwood (2004) writes an elaborate, formal, near-Jacobean register precisely because the flat screen-western idiom would have sounded modern by comparison. Hall's Warlock (1958) keeps the period's legal formality and gets its tension from it.
entries.application: Decide whether you are writing the period or the genre, and be consistent. Mixing them produces the register most readers describe as sounding like a television western, which is a verdict rather than a description.

entries.category: Voice, Idiom and Which Language the Scene Is In
entries.name: Which Language Is the Scene In
entries.description: The West was multilingual, and a story that renders everything in English has made a choice it should make deliberately.
entries.principle: The country the genre is set in ran on Spanish, on dozens of Indigenous languages, on German and Chinese and Norwegian, and the classical form's monolingual English is a convention rather than a record. Deciding scene by scene which language is being spoken changes who understands what, who is excluded, and where the story's power sits — and it converts translation itself into a plot mechanism.
entries.example: Costner's Dances With Wolves (1990) subtitles its Lakota rather than dubbing it, which was the decision that made the film's Lakota characters people rather than obstacles. Kunuk's Atanarjuat (2001) works entirely in Inuktitut. Thornton's Sweet Country (2017) uses Arrernte and English to mark exactly who is permitted to be understood.
entries.application: Mark each scene in your outline with the language it is actually in before you write a line of it. Then decide what the reader is allowed to understand, and why.

entries.category: Voice, Idiom and Which Language the Scene Is In
entries.name: Rendering a Language You Do Not Speak
entries.description: The technical obligations when a scene is in a language the writer has to source.
entries.principle: Getting a language wrong on the page is not a small error, because the speakers will read it and the mistake is permanent. The requirements are specific: a fluent speaker as consultant, credited and paid; attention to register, dialect and period; and awareness that many Indigenous languages mark gender, kinship and formality in ways a translated script will silently flatten.
entries.example: The Lakota dialogue in Dances With Wolves (1990) is the standing cautionary case: Doris Leader Charge coached the cast, and Russell Means was among those who observed afterwards that male characters were speaking grammatically female forms, which Lakota speakers heard immediately and non-speakers did not. Trachtenberg's Prey (2022) released a full Comanche-language version, dubbed in post-production by the returning cast, with Jhane Myers — a Comanche and Blackfeet producer — credited on the film.
entries.application: Budget for a consultant before you write the scene, not after. If you cannot, write the scene so the language is present and untranslated rather than rendered badly.

entries.category: Voice, Idiom and Which Language the Scene Is In
entries.name: Subtitles, Dubbing and the Polyglot Shoot
entries.description: How the international traditions handled language, and what it means for anyone quoting them.
entries.principle: The Italian cycle was shot with international casts speaking their own languages on set and dubbed entirely in post, which is why the performances have their characteristic detachment and why no version of these films is the original. This is a craft fact rather than a trivium: it explains the cycle's reliance on faces, gesture and music, and it is part of what a writer is borrowing when they borrow that style.
entries.example: Leone's films exist in Italian and English versions that differ in dialogue and running time, and neither is authoritative. The DEFA Indianerfilme were made for an audience reading a different politics into the same iconography, and travel accordingly.
entries.application: If you are quoting the Italian style, notice you are quoting a sound produced by post-synchronisation. On the page, the equivalent is dialogue that carries no regional texture at all — which can be a deliberate effect and is usually an accident.

entries.category: Voice, Idiom and Which Language the Scene Is In
entries.name: What the Story Calls People
entries.description: Naming is a position, and the narrator's vocabulary is the author's argument.
entries.principle: There is a difference between what a character calls someone, what the narrator calls them, and what they call themselves, and in this genre that difference is where the story's politics are visible. Period-accurate slurs in a character's mouth are a legitimate craft choice with obligations attached; the same words in the narrator's mouth are an authorial position. The specific and correctable version of this is naming: a nation has a name it uses for itself.
entries.example: Berger's Little Big Man (1964) puts period vocabulary in a period narrator and makes the narration itself the subject. Hillerman's novels use Navajo and Diné terms with the precision the Navajo Nation later recognised him for.
entries.application: Audit every instance of a group name in your manuscript and mark whether it is character, narrator or author. Then check the narrator's list against what the people concerned call themselves.

entries.category: Voice, Idiom and Which Language the Scene Is In
entries.name: Profanity, Register and the Deadwood Problem
entries.description: Period-accurate obscenity does not read as obscene, and the workaround is a real craft decision.
entries.principle: Nineteenth-century American profanity was overwhelmingly blasphemous rather than sexual or scatological, and rendered accurately it reads to a modern audience as quaint — which is the opposite of the intended effect. Every writer in the genre has to choose between accuracy that misfires, modern obscenity that is anachronistic but lands, and elision. There is no correct answer, only a choice that should be made once and held.
entries.example: Milch's Deadwood (2004) chose modern obscenity deliberately and has discussed the reasoning, arguing the coarseness as a marker of a place outside law; the further claim that period profanity would simply have read as quaint is a commentator's gloss rather than his. Most studio-era westerns chose elision, and the genre's reputation for laconic dignity is partly an artefact of the Production Code.
entries.application: Make the decision at the outline stage and write it down. The failure is not either choice; it is a manuscript that drifts between them.

entries.name: Name the Nation, Not the Category
entries.description: The single most correctable failure in the genre, and the one with the highest return.
entries.principle: The classical western runs on a composite that has no referent — a pan-Indian figure assembled from Plains dress, Southwest geography and invented ceremony — and the correction is not sensitivity but specificity. Nations differ in language, kinship, subsistence, governance, religion and their relations with one another and with the United States, and those differences generate plot. Naming the nation is where the research starts, not where it ends.
entries.example: Hillerman's Navajo procedurals are set inside Diné legal and ceremonial specifics, and in 1987 the Navajo Nation named him a Special Friend of the Dineh for authentically portraying the strength and dignity of traditional Navajo culture. Jones's The Only Good Indians (2020) turns a specific Blackfeet hunting obligation into the causal engine of a horror novel, which a composite could not have supplied.
entries.application: Write the nation's name at the top of your outline. If your story would work identically with a different nation substituted, you have written the composite.

entries.name: Research Order: Community First, Ethnography Second
entries.description: The sequence matters, because the most-cited sources are often the ones the community objects to.
entries.principle: The obvious research path — the standard ethnography, the university library, the well-indexed monograph — frequently leads to material gathered under pressure from informants who did not consent to its circulation. Communities today publish their own histories, language resources, protocols and, often, explicit statements about what outsiders may use. Reading those first changes what you do with the ethnography, and sometimes tells you not to use it.
entries.example: Kluckhohn's Navaho Witchcraft (1944) is a standard outside source on its subject and records material many Diné hold should not be discussed with outsiders at all; how far its informants were willing participants is itself disputed. A writer who reads the community's own position first knows that before they build a plot on it.
entries.application: Search for what the nation has published about outside use before you search for what anthropologists published about the nation. It is usually findable, and it is usually specific.

entries.name: Consultation, Credit and Payment
entries.description: The standard the genre almost never meets, stated plainly enough to meet it.
entries.principle: Consultation means a named person with standing in the community, engaged early enough to change the story, credited in the finished work and paid at a professional rate. Anything less is a courtesy read at the end for reassurance, which is the industry's normal practice and is not the same thing. The distinction is visible in the result: a consultant engaged early changes plot, and one engaged late changes vocabulary.
entries.example: Hillerman's sustained consultation over decades is the prose benchmark, and the Navajo Nation's 1987 Special Friend of the Dineh recognition is the rare case of a community saying so itself. Jhane Myers's credited producer role on Prey (2022) is the screen equivalent, engaged on the production rather than consulted on a finished script.
entries.application: Ask whether your consultant can change the plot. If the answer is no, do not describe the work as consulted.

entries.name: What Is Not Yours to Put on the Page
entries.description: Some material is restricted by the community that holds it, and the restriction is not negotiable by argument.
entries.principle: Ceremony, song, sacred narrative, medicine practice and certain names are held under protocols that determine who may know them, who may speak them and in what circumstances — and those protocols do not lapse because a text has been published. The craft consequence is that a plot which requires restricted material to function is a plot that needs redesigning, and redesigning it is ordinary work rather than censorship.
entries.example: The genre's standing failure is the invented ceremony that resolves an act. Jones and other Indigenous writers routinely build stories on obligation, kinship and consequence rather than on ceremony, which is both safer and better, because obligations generate plot and rituals generate spectacle.
entries.application: If your climax needs a ceremony, replace it with an obligation. You will almost always find the scene improves, because an obligation has two parties and a ritual has an audience.

entries.name: Writing a Character Whose Interiority You Do Not Share
entries.description: The craft problem underneath the ethical one, and the techniques that address it.
entries.principle: The genre's characteristic failure is not malice but thinness — characters whose interior life consists of their relation to the settler protagonist. The technical fixes are ordinary: give the character interests that predate the plot, relationships the protagonist never sees, disagreements with people of their own community, and a scene in which the protagonist is absent. Whether to write the interiority at all is a separate and genuinely disputed question, and the pack does not settle it.
entries.example: Erdrich's novels give whole communities internal politics that the outside world barely touches. Eyre's Smoke Signals (1998) is built almost entirely of intra-community disagreement, which is exactly the texture the classical form removes.
entries.application: Write one scene between two characters from the community with no settler present and no reference to the main plot. If you cannot, you do not know them well enough to write them.

entries.name: The Equivalence Test
entries.description: A single question that catches most of what the other cards in this block are for.
entries.principle: Take the treatment you have given a tradition, a community or a belief, and apply it to one you belong to or know intimately. If the result reads as caricature, as extraction, or as a story that uses people you know as furniture, the treatment is the problem rather than your sensitivity to it. The test is crude and it is quick, and it catches the majority of failures before a reader does.
entries.example: The genre's zombie-adjacent history is instructive here: horror's own record of turning a functioning religion into a monster is the case the library's Horror pack carries, and the western's ancient-burial-ground device is the same move on different material.
entries.application: Run the test on the finished draft, not the outline. And run it on the smallest details as well as the premise, because that is where the failures accumulate.

entries.name: When the Answer Is Not to Write It
entries.description: A legitimate outcome, and the one the genre's incentives make hardest to reach.
entries.principle: Some stories are not yours to tell, and deciding not to write one is a craft judgement rather than a failure of nerve. The useful version of this is not a prohibition but a redirection: the material that drew you is usually available from a position you can legitimately occupy — the settler who benefits, the institution that acts, the record that lies — and those positions are less written than the one you were reaching for.
entries.example: The strongest Indigenous-authored work in the genre exists because the writers had standing the outside market had denied them for a century. A writer without that standing still has the whole of the settler side of the frontier, which the genre has barely examined from the inside.
entries.application: If you decide not to write it, write down what drew you and look for the version you can hold. The redirection almost always produces a better book than the original idea.

entries.category: The Star Persona as Political Product
entries.name: The Persona Is the Text
entries.description: In this genre the leading figure arrives carrying meaning the story did not create and cannot fully control.
entries.principle: The western is organised around continuing star personas to an unusual degree, because its B-unit economics and its series formats rewarded a recognisable figure over a distinctive script. The consequence for craft is that a persona is a set of prior commitments the audience brings into the room — about competence, about violence, about what kind of authority is legitimate — and a story either uses them, tests them, or is quietly overruled by them.
entries.example: The film that made Wayne a star, Ford's Stagecoach (1939), introduces him with a camera move that announces significance before the character has done anything. Siegel's The Shootist (1976) is constructed entirely out of what the audience already believes about the man in it.
entries.application: Write down what your audience believes about the figure at the centre before you write their first scene. In prose the equivalent is the type — the hired gun, the marshal, the drifter — and the same rule applies.

entries.category: The Star Persona as Political Product
entries.name: Wayne, and the Politics Sold With the Product
entries.description: The genre's central persona carried an explicit politics, and the record is on the page rather than inferred.
entries.principle: John Wayne's screen figure and his public political positions were marketed together and were understood by contemporary audiences as the same product, which makes him the clearest case of the genre's persona-as-argument. The craft point is not biographical: it is that a persona with stated politics changes what a film can mean, so a director working with one is either endorsing, complicating or fighting it, and the audience is scoring that in real time.
entries.example: Ford's The Searchers (1956) builds a character out of Wayne's established authority and makes that authority inseparable from racial hatred, which is a use of the persona rather than a departure from it. Wayne's 1971 Playboy interview stated positions on race and Native American dispossession that are part of the public record and that many viewers now read the films through.
entries.application: If you are working with or against a loaded persona, decide which and make the decision legible. The library's rule holds here: state the record at the level it supports, mark disputes as disputes, and adjudicate nothing.

entries.category: The Star Persona as Political Product
entries.name: Eastwood, and the Persona That Turns on Itself
entries.description: The most sustained example in the genre of a star dismantling the figure he built.
entries.principle: A persona accumulated over decades is a resource that can be spent, and spending it is one of the most powerful moves available in a genre this conventional. The technique requires the earlier version to be present in the audience's memory in detail, which is why it cannot be borrowed — the writer has to have built the thing being taken apart, or be working with someone who did.
entries.example: Eastwood's figure was assembled across Leone's trilogy from 1964 and hardened through the 1970s, and Unforgiven (1992) recovers it in order to itemise what it costs, ending on a man who is neither redeemed nor punished. The film's dedication to Sergio Leone and Don Siegel names the two directors who built the persona it is spending.
entries.application: In prose, the equivalent is a series character. If you are writing one, decide early whether the later books will charge for the earlier ones — it is the strongest structural card the form has and it can only be played once.

entries.category: The Star Persona as Political Product
entries.name: Autry, Rogers and the Persona as Merchandise
entries.description: The singing-cowboy figure was a licensing business with films attached, and that explains its content.
entries.principle: The B-western star persona was built to sell records, radio hours, comic books, lunch boxes and endorsements to a family audience, and the content followed the licence: a hero who does not drink, does not shoot first, does not kiss, and whose moral code is publishable. This is the clearest case in the genre of commercial structure determining moral structure, and it is why the second mode looks the way it does.
entries.example: Autry's Republic pictures from 1935 ran alongside a recording and radio career, and by the late 1940s he was publishing a cowboy code through his Melody Ranch radio show that was aimed squarely at children — the code postdates the films and codifies what they were already selling. Roy Rogers inherited and industrialised the model, and Hopalong Cassidy was rebuilt for the screen from 1935 as a family brand against Mulford's harder original.
entries.application: When you write in the second mode, work out who the licence is for. A hero constrained by a merchandising audience is a real and interesting constraint — it is where the genre's most rigid ethical codes come from.

entries.category: The Star Persona as Political Product
entries.name: Mitić, and the Persona as State Policy
entries.description: The Eastern Bloc built its own western star, and his meaning was set by a ministry rather than a market.
entries.principle: DEFA was a state studio, so the Indianerfilme's anti-colonial politics were policy rather than a film-maker's argument, and the persona at the centre of them was assembled to carry that policy — dignified, articulate, defending a homeland against American expansion. It is the cleanest available demonstration that the western's iconography is politically portable, and that a persona means what its production system needs it to mean.
entries.example: Gojko Mitić played the Indigenous lead across most of the DEFA cycle from Die Söhne der großen Bärin (1966) and became a national figure in the German Democratic Republic. The films' anti-colonial argument and the casting of a Serbian actor in those roles are both true, and the card states both.
entries.application: Ask what your production system needs your central figure to mean. Personas are not only commercial artefacts, and a story that assumes its hero's meaning is neutral has usually inherited someone else's politics.

entries.category: The Star Persona as Political Product
entries.name: Writing For or Against a Persona
entries.description: The practical technique, for screenwriters casting into a persona and novelists writing a type.
entries.principle: Working with a persona is a matter of managing expectation debt. Writing for it means giving the audience the anticipated competence and then charging interest — the figure does what they came for, and the story extracts a price. Writing against it means establishing the expectation and then withholding it, which requires the withholding to arrive early enough to be read as intent rather than as failure.
entries.example: Hawks's Rio Bravo (1959) writes for the persona and spends the film qualifying it with dependence on other people. Peckinpah's Ride the High Country (1962) casts two ageing western stars and makes their age the subject, so the persona and the character arrive together.
entries.application: Establish the expectation in the first act whichever way you are going. A subversion that arrives in Act Three reads as a writer changing their mind.

entries.category: Quoting, Adapting and the Contemporary Western
entries.name: In This Genre the Original Is Usually the Story
entries.description: A large share of the canon began as short fiction, and the adaptation is better known than the source.
entries.principle: The western's relationship to the short story is unlike any other genre's: several of its defining films are adaptations of stories of a few thousand words, and the compression of the original is often what makes the film work. For a writer this is a structural lesson — these premises are strong enough to carry a feature precisely because they were built to carry twenty pages — and for a reference work it is a discipline: card the original as the original.
entries.example: Johnson's The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1949) is the source Ford filmed in 1962, and her A Man Called Horse (1950) and The Hanging Tree preceded their films the same way; all three first appeared in magazines and were collected in Indian Country (1953). Leonard's Three-Ten to Yuma appeared in Dime Western Magazine in March 1953 and has been filmed twice, in 1957 and 2007, both times under the punctuated title and both times adding most of their running time.
entries.application: If your premise fits in twenty pages, write it in twenty pages first. The genre's history says the compression survives expansion and the reverse is much rarer.

entries.category: Quoting, Adapting and the Contemporary Western
entries.name: What Survives Adaptation and What Does Not
entries.description: The genre's adaptations lose the same things every time, and knowing which lets you protect them.
entries.principle: Moving between prose and screen in this genre reliably preserves landscape, action and iconography and reliably loses interior justification, vernacular narration and moral ambiguity — because the first three are photographable and the last three live in sentences. The consequence is that adapted westerns tend to arrive more certain than their sources, and a writer adapting has to decide deliberately how to carry the doubt across.
entries.example: Portis's True Grit (1968) is narrated by Mattie in old age, and both films must find a substitute for a voice that is the book's whole method. Le May's The Searchers (1954) states motives that Ford's film withholds, which is why the film is the more argued-about work.
entries.application: Name the thing your source does that a camera cannot do, and design its replacement before you start. If you cannot name it, you are adapting the plot rather than the book.

entries.category: Quoting, Adapting and the Contemporary Western
entries.name: Quotation, Homage and the Reader Who Knows
entries.description: The genre is unusually quotable, and a quotation is an argument about the thing quoted.
entries.principle: Because the western's inventory is small and fixed, a single shot, line or gesture can invoke a whole prior work, and the invocation always carries a position — agreement, correction or affection. The craft requirement is that the quotation must also work for a reader who does not recognise it. A scene whose only function is recognition is a favour to the initiated and a dead spot for everyone else.
entries.example: Leone's C'era una volta il West (1968) quotes Ford's iconography extensively and uses it to argue the opposite case. Tarantino's Django Unchained (2012) casts Franco Nero opposite the character named after his, which is legible as a joke to anyone and as an argument to those who know Corbucci's Django (1966).
entries.application: Test every quotation by deleting the reference and asking whether the scene still does its job. If it does not, the scene is an in-joke wearing a plot.

entries.category: Quoting, Adapting and the Contemporary Western
entries.name: Parody Requires the Form Reproduced Competently
entries.description: The technical demand of comic westerns, which is why so few of them work.
entries.principle: Parody depends on the borrowed form being reproduced accurately enough to be recognised before it is altered, which means the parodist must be able to build a functional western first. This is the rule the comedy pack states and it bites hardest in this genre, because the western's conventions are so rigid that a sloppy reproduction reads as incompetence rather than as comedy. The corollary is that the best parodies double as demonstrations of the form.
entries.example: Brooks's Blazing Saddles (1974), carded in the comedy pack, stages its set pieces straight before breaking them, and its target is the industry as much as the genre. Lipský's Limonádový Joe (1964) does the same job from inside the Eastern Bloc on the singing-cowboy form specifically.
entries.application: Write the straight version of the scene, make sure it works, then break it. A parody that skips the first step is a sketch.

entries.category: Quoting, Adapting and the Contemporary Western
entries.name: The Remake and the Rights Chain
entries.description: The genre's borrowings have a legal history, and knowing it prevents a common class of error.
entries.principle: The western's international traffic ran on licences, options and, in one famous case, litigation, and the popular accounts of who remade what are frequently wrong about whether permission existed. This matters for a reference work because "remake", "adaptation", "unlicensed transposition" and "homage" are four different claims, and it matters for a working writer because the same distinctions govern what they may do.
entries.example: Sturges's The Magnificent Seven (1960) reached the screen through a rights chain rather than a studio licence — Lou Morheim acquired the remake rights cheaply — sources give figures an order of magnitude apart and the pack does not pick one — and they passed to Yul Brynner, and Anthony Quinn sued over the arrangement and lost. Leone's Per un pugno di dollari (1964) took Kurosawa's Yojimbo (1961) without permission and Toho's suit settled, with fifteen per cent of worldwide receipts the best-attested term.
entries.application: Use the correct word. If you cannot establish that permission existed, write that the film transposes the earlier one rather than that it remakes it.

entries.category: Quoting, Adapting and the Contemporary Western
entries.name: Writing in the Second Mode on Purpose
entries.description: Using the genre's furniture for a story about something else, without pretending otherwise.
entries.principle: A great deal of good work uses the hat, the standoff, the frontier town and the drifter as a vocabulary for stories that contest no ground at all, and the pack treats this as a mode rather than a failure. What breaks is inconsistency: a story that borrows the iconography for two acts and then reaches for the moral weight of a settlement argument it never set up has cashed a cheque it did not write.
entries.example: Whedon's Firefly (2002) runs the whole vocabulary on a spaceship and is consistent about it. Nightow's Trigun (1995) does the same in manga. Crichton's Westworld (1973) makes the detachment its actual subject by building a literal simulation of the genre.
entries.application: Decide your mode in the outline and hold it. If you want the weight, you have to do the work of establishing a claim to ground, and then you are not in the second mode any more.

entries.category: The Contemporary Western on the Page and Screen
entries.name: The Anachronism Engine
entries.description: What actually powers a neo-western, and the reason so many of them stall.
entries.principle: A western set in the present runs on a specific mismatch: a frontier moral vocabulary — self-reliance, personal jurisdiction, violence as settlement — meeting a landscape of banks, leases, agencies and cameras that does not recognise it. The engine is genuine incompatibility, not nostalgia. A neo-western in which the old code merely feels sad has no motor; one in which it produces a consequence the modern world then processes does.
entries.example: McCarthy's No Country for Old Men (2005) sets a code against an economy that does not negotiate and lets the economy win without a confrontation. Mackenzie's Hell or High Water (2016) makes the bank the land-grabber, which restores the range war with modern instruments.
entries.application: Find the exact point where your character's code produces an outcome the present cannot absorb. That collision is the story; everything else is setting.

entries.category: The Contemporary Western on the Page and Screen
entries.name: The Prestige Television West
entries.description: The form's current centre of gravity, and what long-form does to the genre's structures.
entries.principle: Serialised television has become the western's most active form, and length changes the genre's mechanics in specific ways: the walk-down loses its finality, the ride-out is deferred indefinitely, and the community — normally a backdrop — becomes the protagonist because it is the only thing that persists. The trade is that the genre's compression, its greatest asset in prose and film, has to be rebuilt at the level of the season.
entries.example: Milch's Deadwood (2004) makes the camp itself the lead and the institutions the plot. Sheridan's Yellowstone (2018) restores the cattle empire as a going concern with a modern legal war around it, and Harjo's Reservation Dogs (2021) uses the form's patience for a community portrait the film-length western has no room for.
entries.application: If you are writing long-form, decide what persists between seasons and make that the subject. A serialised western organised around a single man's arc will run out of arc.

entries.category: The Contemporary Western on the Page and Screen
entries.name: The Market a Western Writer Actually Faces
entries.description: The commercial floor of the genre, stated plainly, because most craft advice pretends it does not exist.
entries.principle: The western's trade publishing has been thin for decades while its readership has not disappeared, and the practical result is a market with three distinct floors: the long-running series paperback lines with fixed specifications, a substantial independent and digital market where the genre performs far better than its trade reputation suggests, and a screen pipeline that is currently narrow and concentrated. Knowing which of the three you are writing for determines length, content and pace before any craft question arises.
entries.example: Western Fictioneers was founded in 2010 as a working-writer body for exactly this field and gives the Peacemaker Awards. The Spur Awards date from 1953 — the year Western Writers of America was founded and the publication year of the first honoured works — with the first Spurs presented at WWA's inaugural convention in Denver in 1954 in five categories; they now include categories that did not exist a generation ago, which is a readable map of where the market moved.
entries.application: Read a current series line's specification and a current award category list before you plan a book. Together they tell you what is being bought.

entries.category: The Contemporary Western on the Page and Screen
entries.name: The Western After the Counter-Western
entries.description: Where the form actually is now, and what a writer entering it is entering.
entries.principle: The genre's centre has moved: the most vital current work is being made by the people the classical form wrote out, and it is not confined to correction — it uses the machinery, keeps the pleasures and changes what the country is for. A writer coming to the western now is joining a conversation already in progress rather than reviving a dead form, and the useful question is what this body of work has made available that was not available before.
entries.example: Harjo's Reservation Dogs (2021) and Kunuk's Atanarjuat (2001) work from inside communities the genre used as scenery. Samuel's The Harder They Fall (2021) assembles documented Black figures into a genre picture on purpose. Trachtenberg's Prey (2022) puts the captivity narrative's machinery in the hands of the people it was written against.
entries.application: Read the counter-western before you write the western. It is where the form's live problems are being solved, and a writer who has not read it will spend a year rediscovering answers that already exist.

entries.name: The Claim Audit
entries.description: Run at outline stage, before any scene is drafted: does every party to your central conflict hold a claim you can state in their own words?
items: Who holds the contested ground at the story's opening, and how did they come to hold it?
What is each claimant's warrant — purchase, treaty, conquest, labour, prior occupancy, or nothing but arrival?
Could each claimant state their entitlement in one sentence, in the first person, without irony?
Does any party's warrant come out as an admission of guilt? If so you have found a verdict, not a warrant.
Are both sides lawful, or is one simply criminal? If the latter, check whether you are writing a crime story.
Who adjudicates, and by what authority — a court, a gun, a mob, a company, a cavalry troop, a bank?
Is there a physical instrument recording the claim, and can the plot survive it burning?
If nobody contests the claim, what is testing it instead, and is there a clock on it?

entries.name: The Collapse Test
entries.description: Run once the premise is fixed and again on the finished draft: is this a western, and does the pack's contract apply to it?
items: Remove the contested claim to ground and the force that settles it. Does the story collapse?
If it stands, does it stand inside the western's iconographic system, or in a documented lineage of exchange with it?
If you are relying on lineage, can you name the exchange — what was taken from whom, and when?
Is the force in your story only violence, or does it include the court, the company, the market and the weather?
Which mode are you in: contesting a claim, or circulating the iconography? Both are legitimate; confusing them is not.
If the work belongs to another pack's contract — crime, romance, literary, historical, horror — have you handed it across and kept only the western residual?

entries.name: The Empty-Country Check
entries.description: Run before drafting any scene of arrival, claim or settlement: who was already here, and does the prose know it?
items: Is the land described as waiting, or as held — and if held, by whom?
Are the people already present named as a people, or rendered as terrain, weather or threat?
If a treaty, a purchase, a removal or a war stands behind this ground, does the story know which one?
Does the narrator use the availability of the country as an unexamined premise?
Would the scene work identically with a different nation substituted? If so, you have written a composite.
Does the story ask the reader to feel the thrill of arrival, or to notice what arrival costs — and does it know which it is doing?

entries.name: The Living-Culture Screen
entries.description: Run before drafting, not after, whenever a named Indigenous nation, language, ceremony or belief appears. Any single no is a stop, not a note.
items: Is the nation named specifically, with the name it uses for itself?
Have you read what that community has published about outside use, before reading the standard ethnography?
Is the material you are using something the community holds should not be discussed with outsiders?
Does your plot require restricted material — ceremony, song, sacred narrative, medicine practice — to function?
Do the characters from that community have interests, relationships and internal disagreements that predate your plot?
Is there a scene between two of them with no settler present and no reference to the main story?
Would this treatment of a tradition you belong to read as respectful?
Do you have a consultant with standing in the community, engaged early enough to change the plot, credited and paid?
Why this material, and why you? If you cannot answer the second half, that is an answer.

entries.name: The Violence Ledger
entries.description: Run on the outline, listing every act of violence in the story: what does each one buy, and from whom?
items: For each killing, what is purchased — a claim, an office, a debt, a question of who may stay?
Which of them have a blank beside them? Those are either doing work you have not identified or should not be there.
How close does the reader stand to each one, and is the proximity a choice?
Is the reader enjoying any of them in a way the story does not know about?
Does any act of violence settle nothing, and if the story is in that mode, have you audited for a payoff you did not intend to give?
Have you drafted the scene after the climactic violence? If the story has nothing to say afterwards, the violence was the point.

entries.name: The Who-Pays Pass
entries.description: Run on a complete draft: for every cost the story imposes, is the person who bears it on the page?
items: Name the person who bears the consequence of each act of violence. Are they in a scene?
Who pays for the settlement the story endorses — the dispossessed, the labourers, the women who bury the dead, the town that has to live with it?
If the only people affected by a killing are the shooter and the shot, has the story understated its own subject?
Does any character absorb a cost off the page and return unchanged?
Is a wound healing across a scene transition, and what week of story did that throw away?
Does the ending distribute the costs it created, or leave them where the reader will not look?

entries.name: The Who-Is-Absent Pass
entries.description: Run on a complete draft, with the cast list in front of you: who is missing from a country that actually contained them?
items: Who is in this landscape historically who is not in your draft — Black, Mexican, Chinese, Indigenous, and the women of all of them?
What are the women in your story doing when they are not being looked at? Does the domestic and productive economy exist on the page as work?
Is any group present only as an obstacle, a service or a lesson?
Does the story contain a person of colour with an interest of their own rather than a corrective walk-on?
If your cast is homogeneous, is that a fact about the setting you can defend, or a default you inherited?
Does the narration's vocabulary for people differ from what those people call themselves?

entries.name: The Legal-Title Pass
entries.description: Run whenever ownership, boundary or jurisdiction is at stake: do you know what the instruments actually were?
items: What kind of claim is it — homestead entry, patent, purchase, grant, lease, allotment, treaty right, prior occupancy?
Has it been proved up, recorded, contested or merely asserted?
Whose water is it, and under which doctrine — prior appropriation or riparian right?
Is the range open or fenced, and who paid for the wire?
Which office has jurisdiction here: town marshal, county sheriff, deputy US marshal, tribal authority, the army?
Could the character you have given authority to actually make this arrest, in this place, over this person?
Is there a railroad grant, a company holding or an absentee owner behind any of it?

entries.name: The Period-Materials Pass
entries.description: Run on the drafted scenes, weapon by weapon and object by object: would a reader who knows the material catch you?
items: How many rounds does each weapon hold as it is actually carried, and have you tracked them?
How long does a reload take, and does any scene depend on it not taking that long?
Does a pistol out-shoot a rifle anywhere in your draft?
Is black powder smoke doing what it did — marking every position after the first shot?
What did each object cost, and could this character afford it?
What is everyone eating, and where did it come from?
Does any wound heal faster than the period allows, and who was obliged to stay while it did not?

entries.name: The Horse-and-Distance Pass
entries.description: Run with a map and a calendar: does your story move at the speed the country allows?
items: How far is it between each pair of locations, and how long does that take at the pace being ridden?
Is anyone arriving in time who could not have?
What does each animal eat and drink, and where does that come from on this route?
How many remounts does the party have, and how does that change the arithmetic?
Where is the water in the season the story is set in?
Does the weather function as a deadline, or only as atmosphere?
Could a reader draw a rough map from the text?

entries.name: The Language Pass
entries.description: Run at outline stage and again on the draft: what language is each scene actually in, and who is permitted to understand it?
items: Mark every scene with the language being spoken before you write it.
Where a language other than English is spoken, what does the reader get — translation, subtitle, or exclusion?
Do you have a fluent speaker as consultant, credited and paid, for any language you do not speak?
Are register, dialect and period right, and are gender, kinship and formality markings intact?
Are you writing the period's idiom or the genre's screen convention, and are you consistent?
Have you decided once, and held, how to handle profanity — period-accurate, modern, or elided?
Is any dialect rendered in phonetic spelling, and would the voice survive with the spelling removed?

entries.name: The Landscape-and-Score Pass
entries.description: Run on the drafted scenes: is the country a party to the dispute, or is it scenery?
items: Does the terrain change a character's decision at least once per act?
Name one thing in each landscape paragraph that only someone who worked that ground would know.
Cut every adjective that could apply to any wide country anywhere. What is left?
Is the season doing structural work, or only mood?
What is the reader hearing? Decide which scoring convention they have arrived with and whether you are using or fighting it.
If a song appears, is it narrating — a ballad, a corrido, a cantador's account — and does the story agree with what it claims?

entries.name: The Which-Mode Pass
entries.description: Run at outline stage and again at the end of the first draft: are you in the same mode you started in?
items: Are you contesting a claim to ground, or circulating the iconography?
If the second, does the story anywhere reach for moral weight it has not set up?
If you are revising the form, is the classical machinery still operational, or have you dismantled the structure as well as the argument?
If you are writing an anti-western, does the story flinch into a satisfying climax?
If you are writing elegy, check the forgiveness: mourning a world excuses you from asking who was in it.
Is there a set piece in the outline you cannot justify twice?

entries.name: The Adaptation and Quotation Pass
entries.description: Run when working from a source or quoting a prior work: what survives, what is lost, and who is the reference for?
items: What does the source do that a camera cannot, and what have you designed to replace it?
Has interior justification, vernacular narration or moral ambiguity gone missing in the move?
Is the adapted version more certain than its source, and did you mean it to be?
For each quotation, delete the reference. Does the scene still do its job?
If you are parodying, have you built the straight version first and confirmed it works?
Is your word for the borrowing correct — remake, adaptation, transposition, homage — and can you establish that permission existed?

entries.name: The International-Sources Pass
entries.description: Run whenever the story draws on a tradition outside the Anglophone American West.
items: Have you verified the material in its own-language sources, or only in English writing about it?
Are you using the original title and year alongside the release title?
Which Ostern do you mean — the DEFA Indianerfilme or the Soviet form, which are different objects?
If you are transplanting a structure, have you left behind the legal and social order the audience will read wrongly?
Are the tradition's own politics intact, or have you kept the iconography and dropped the argument?
For the Mexican, Brazilian, Australian and Indian traditions: is the antagonist the one that tradition actually has?

entries.name: The Received-Wisdom Pass
entries.description: Run last, on the finished draft, with a pen: which of these claims did you check, and which did the genre hand you?
items: List every factual assertion the draft makes in passing rather than in argument. Those are the dangerous ones.
Which superlatives are in the text — the first, the only, the largest, the most? Can each be sourced?
Is any claim about what a creator intended or said resting on a commonplace rather than a citable instance?
Is any award named by a category the awarding body never used, or dated by the wrong one of its three years?
Is a hypothesis presented as a fact, or a disputed reading presented as settled?
Where two sources disagree and the item is small, have you stated the disagreement rather than picking a side?
Is anyone written in the present tense whose living status you have not checked this month?

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: The Man Whose Skills Unfit Him for the Society He Secures
entries.description: The competence that saves the community is the same competence that bars its holder from living in it.

examples.text: Ford builds Ethan out of exactly the capability the genre admires and then makes it inseparable from his hatred, so the door closing on him is a judgement rather than a mood.
Schaefer puts the whole proposition in a child's sightline, which forces the reader to want the thing the book is arguing against.
Schaefer returns to the same figure two decades later with the skills obsolete rather than dangerous, which is the elegiac variant of the same trope.
Four capable men are reintegrated without cost, which delivers the pleasure of the trope and none of its argument.

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: The Fastest Gun and the Challenger
entries.description: Reputation as a queue of young men, each arriving to take the title by killing its holder.

examples.text: Henry King makes the reputation itself the antagonist and gives the challenger no motive beyond the standing he would inherit.
Swarthout puts a dying man in a town where the queue is still forming, so the plot is a race between two ways of being killed.
Corbucci removes the ritual entirely and lets the challenger simply shoot, which is the trope refused rather than inverted.

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: The Reformed Shootist and the Past That Arrives
entries.description: A man who has put the work down, and the errand that makes him pick it up.

examples.text: Eastwood makes the return physically difficult — a man who cannot mount, cannot shoot, cannot hold his drink — so the recovery of competence is itself the horror.
The constable's transformation is played as a revelation of what he already was rather than as a relapse.
The past arrives as a tournament bracket, which converts a moral problem into a structure.

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: The Hired Gun
entries.description: Violence bought as a service, and what the purchase says about the buyer.

examples.text: Wilson arrives as a specialist retained by capital, and the film is careful that he is competent rather than wicked.
Hall's town hires its own law and discovers it has bought a man rather than an office.
Kurosawa's ronin sells himself to both sides at once, which exposes the transaction the western usually dignifies.

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: The Professional's Code
entries.description: A group whose loyalty runs sideways to each other rather than upward to a society.

examples.text: Hawks makes competence the entire moral content and lets the town be irrelevant to it.
Peckinpah keeps the code and removes everything it might have served, so the group's loyalty becomes the only remaining value.
Sippy hires two petty criminals and lets the code form between them under obligation rather than arriving intact.

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: Reputation as a Liability
entries.description: A name that precedes its owner and makes ordinary life impossible.

examples.work: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford
examples.text: Hansen treats celebrity as the actual subject and the killing as a career move within it.

examples.work: Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid
examples.text: Goldman's script makes the pursuit impersonal and inexorable precisely because the names are worth chasing.
The reputation is asserted through three hours of incident without ever costing the man anything, which leaves the trope as biography.

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: The Kid
entries.description: The young man learning the trade, and the question of whether the teacher should teach it.

examples.text: Hawks makes the succession a rebellion and lets the older man be wrong without being weak.
McCarthy gives the apprenticeship no moral content at all, which is the trope stripped to its mechanism.
The apprenticeship is a friendship group, so nothing is transmitted and nothing is at stake.

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: The Man Who Will Not Draw
entries.description: Refusal as a move, and the pressure the genre applies to anyone who declines the ritual.

examples.text: Clark's narrator declines to act and the book makes the refusal into the indictment rather than the excuse.
Grant writes a gunfighter into a Quaker household and makes the refusal a sustained argument rather than a single gesture.
Wyler's newcomer declines every public challenge and settles one privately where nobody can see it, which costs him the town's respect and the film's argument depends on that.

entries.category: The Gunfighter and the Man of Violence
entries.name: The Ageing Gunfighter
entries.description: The body failing at the trade, and a world that no longer requires it.

examples.text: Peckinpah casts two ageing stars and makes the casting the argument.
McMurtry gives two old rangers a job that no longer needs doing and eight hundred pages to discover it.
Siegel builds a valediction out of what the audience already believes about the man in the role.

entries.name: The Fence
entries.description: Enclosure as the moment the country stops being common, rendered as a single physical object.

examples.text: Richter writes enclosure as an argument between a cattleman and a plough that neither party can win, and lets the grass itself deliver the verdict.
Sheridan makes the boundary line the show's permanent subject, with every season turning on who may cross, buy or condemn a piece of it.
Costner sets free grazing against a fenced town and manufactures the clarity his material does not contain.

entries.name: The Water Right
entries.description: The claim that outranks title, and the one most often decided by force.

examples.text: Wyler makes a river the actual prize and lets two ranching families ruin themselves over access to it.
Anderson moves the same fight to oil and water and shows the buyer acquiring both by acquiring the people.
Kelton removes the antagonist and lets the absence of water do the work a rival claimant usually does.

entries.name: The Homestead Proved Up
entries.description: The claim earned by residence and labour, and the years of work the story compresses.

examples.text: Cather writes the proving as agricultural knowledge accumulating, which is the least romantic and most convincing version.
Barry lets a homestead be assembled by people with no legal standing to hold it and makes the fragility the point.
The land run is staged as a sporting event, which removes both the labour and the dispossession.

entries.name: The Cattle Baron's Reach
entries.description: An empire assembled from claims, and the point at which scale becomes its own warrant.

examples.text: Borden Chase's story ran in the Saturday Evening Post in 1946 as Blazing Guns on the Chisholm Trail and reached book form under this title two years later; the founding gesture is a man deciding the land is his and defending the decision.
Sheridan restores the cattle empire as a present-day going concern with modern instruments and the same argument.
Ferber tracks the empire across generations and lets the second generation inherit the question rather than the answer.

entries.name: The Railroad Coming Through
entries.description: The corporation that redraws every claim in the country without firing a shot.

examples.text: Leone makes the railway the actual protagonist and the gunmen its contractors.
Brooks builds a whole comedy on a rail route and a land grab, which only works because the audience knows the plot cold.
Mackenzie substitutes a bank for the railroad and the grievance transfers without adjustment.

entries.name: The Land Office and the Forged Paper
entries.description: The clerk, the ledger and the document that decides who owns a valley.

examples.text: Milch makes the absence of any recognised title the engine of a season and the arrival of the paperwork a hostile act.
Ferber opens on a land run and spends the book on what the filings became.
The water rights plot is legible enough for children, which is a genuine achievement and a thin version of the trope.

entries.name: The Squatter and the Deed
entries.description: Occupancy against paper, and the sympathy the genre usually assigns to the wrong one.

examples.text: Schaefer gives the homesteaders patents and the cattleman prior use, which is why the conflict cannot be settled by argument.
Thornton shows the same collision in Australia with the paperwork stripped away and the outcome unchanged.
deWitt lets a chemical claim-jumping scheme stand in for the whole apparatus of title.

entries.name: The Sale Under Duress
entries.description: A transaction that is legally valid and morally void, which the genre uses to indict the law itself.

examples.text: The immigrants' holdings are acquired by making residence impossible rather than by purchase.
Grann documents guardianship and marriage used as instruments of transfer, which is the trope's real historical form.
Mendonça Filho and Dornelles stage the same acquisition as a foreign hunting party and let the village answer it.

entries.name: The Land That Beat Them
entries.description: A claim defeated by the country rather than by a claimant.

examples.text: Williams strands a hunting party in a winter that has no interest in their venture and lets the enterprise simply fail.
Punke makes the country the only real antagonist and the man's survival a matter of arithmetic.
Reichardt shoots in a nearly square frame so the horizon is withheld from the audience as it is from the party.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Marshal Who Cannot Compel the Town
entries.description: An office with real limits, and a community that declines to stand behind it.

examples.text: Zinnemann makes the town's refusal the entire plot and gives the refusers reasons rather than cowardice alone.
Dmytryk sets an elected office against a hired one and lets the town discover it prefers the hired one.
Frank puts the office in a town that has no men in it and makes the limits demographic rather than moral.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Posse
entries.description: Deputised violence, and the moment it stops being deputised.

examples.text: Wellman shows the legal fiction collapsing in real time and gives the men who object no power to stop it.
Portis assembles a posse of three with three incompatible warrants and lets the incompatibility drive the plot.

The earliest broadcasts carry no origin at all and the ambushed company of commissioned Texas Rangers is a later accretion assembled across the serials; either way the effect is to replace a lawful body with a masked individual, which removes the trope's whole legal problem.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Lynching
entries.description: The community executing without a court, and the genre's most direct examination of what law is for.

examples.text: Clark makes the whole book an aftermath and refuses the reader any figure who could have prevented it.
Samuel restages the trope with the racial history the studio era removed from it.
Tarantino plays the mob as farce and then lets the farce kill people, which is a legitimate and heavily argued choice.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Circuit Judge
entries.description: Law arriving periodically, in a person, on a schedule the country does not respect.

examples.text: Hathaway puts Parker's court, its gallows and its deputies on screen before any of the riding, so the federal machinery is established as the thing the plot then leaves behind.
The series builds a deputy US marshal's authority out of distance, paperwork and a judge who is rarely present.

examples.work: The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean
examples.text: Huston plays the self-appointed bench entirely as eccentricity, which converts a jurisdictional problem into a character part.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Jurisdiction That Ends at the River
entries.description: A boundary that stops the law and does not stop anyone else.

examples.text: Villeneuve makes the crossing itself the horror and jurisdiction the thing being deliberately evaded.
McCarthy sends his riders south and lets Mexico have a legal system that beats them.
Sen puts an Aboriginal detective between two jurisdictions and makes neither of them his.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Corrupt Office
entries.description: The badge held by the wrong man, and the difficulty of removing it lawfully.

examples.text: Leone gives the town two criminal powers and no legitimate one, which is the cycle's founding position.
Yost inherits Leonard's premise that the marshal and the criminal are from the same place and hold the same manners.
Mann makes the local legal apparatus the instrument of dispossession rather than its opponent.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Trial That Cannot Reach the Powerful
entries.description: A courtroom that works exactly as designed and still cannot touch the man who ordered it.

examples.text: Thornton stages a trial in the open air that acquits and still kills its defendant.
Kent shows an officer whose crimes are administrative facts nobody will record.
Weiden builds a present-day novel on the jurisdictional gap that makes some crimes on tribal land effectively unprosecutable.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Vigilance Committee
entries.description: Organised extra-legal authority that keeps minutes, and the respectability that makes it worse.

examples.text: The Stock Growers' Association votes, files and hires, which is the trope in its documented form.

Wister has his hero take part in a hanging and then gives Judge Henry a full chapter to argue that frontier lynching is the people resuming a power they had only lent to the courts, which is the trope stated by a believer rather than examined by a critic.
The committee is a costume for a feud, so the institutional question never arises.

entries.category: Law, Its Absence and Its Arrival
entries.name: The Law That Arrives With the Railroad
entries.description: Order delivered by a corporation, on its own schedule and in its own interest.

examples.work: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
examples.text: Ford stages statehood as a convention and lets the audience watch the legend being adopted as policy.
The closing frontier is rendered as the arrival of agencies, timetables and files rather than of sheriffs.
Ford makes federal order and federal cruelty the same delivery, arriving on the same infrastructure.

entries.name: The Captive Who Does Not Want to Return
entries.description: The rescue that is also an abduction, and the oldest plot in the genre's inheritance.

examples.text: Johnson reverses the direction of travel and makes belonging a thing acquired by obligation rather than by birth.
Berger's narrator crosses in both directions repeatedly until the question of which side he is on stops being answerable.
Trachtenberg puts the machinery of the captivity plot in the hands of the people it was written against.

entries.name: The Scout Who Belongs to Neither Side
entries.description: The interpreter and guide whose usefulness depends on a divided loyalty nobody trusts.

examples.text: Aldrich gives the Apache scout a professional rationale the film respects and the officers do not.
Guthrie makes his trapper fluent enough to see exactly what he is helping to destroy.

Costner makes translation the mechanism of every negotiation in the film and gives the work to a woman who was herself taken as a child, so the go-between belongs fully to neither side by history rather than by choice.

entries.name: The Treaty Signed and Broken
entries.description: A legal instrument the story can name, and the breaking of it as documented policy rather than villainy.

examples.text: Daves makes the negotiation and signing of an agreement the film's actual climax, and its breaking the epilogue.

examples.work: Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee
examples.text: Brown organises a whole history around the sequence of instruments and their violation.
Weiden shows the present-day legal residue of those instruments as a working constraint on a crime plot.

entries.name: The Removal
entries.description: Forced relocation as an administrative act, carried out by clerks as much as by cavalry.

examples.text: The march is rendered as an order being followed, which is what makes the film's sympathies land.
Cozzens keeps the military and civilian decision-making in the same frame so the policy is legible.
Nelson stages the atrocity as spectacle after ninety minutes of romance, which lets the audience enjoy the film and be appalled at it separately.

entries.name: The Sympathetic Chief
entries.description: The 1950s studio cycle's answer to its own record, and the specific way it still fails.

examples.text: Daves builds a whole film on negotiation rather than pursuit, and casts a white star as Cochise, which is the cycle's characteristic combination.
DEFA gives the Indigenous lead the film's moral authority and casts a Serbian actor in the part, which is the same combination arrived at from the opposite politics.

The released ending lets Massai live and the pursuit simply break off, which returns the authority the story spent two hours removing — and it was imposed by United Artists over the ending Aldrich shot and Lancaster wanted, in which Massai is shot in the back as in Wellman's source novel. The instructive failure is a studio's, not a director's.

entries.name: The Massacre Rendered as Policy
entries.description: A documented mass killing staged so that it reads as a decision rather than as an action sequence.

examples.text: Penn reaches the Washita through a film that has been alternating registers throughout, so the sequence arrives as rupture rather than as climax.
Gwynne keeps the reprisals in both directions on the page, which is what makes the account usable rather than exculpatory.
Kent refuses the revenge structure her material invites and leaves the killings unresolved and administrative.

entries.name: The Trading Post and the Terms of Exchange
entries.description: Contact as commerce, where the rate of exchange is the relationship.

examples.text: Guthrie is precise about what is traded and at what rate, which is where the novel's moral information lives.
Noda builds a whole adventure on Ainu subsistence knowledge and the value of what is being extracted from it.
Pollack lets a withdrawal from society be sustained entirely by an exchange economy his protagonist barely understands.

entries.name: The Boarding School
entries.description: Assimilation as an institution, and the genre's most under-used piece of documented history.

examples.text: Eyre's characters live downstream of the institutions without the film ever having to explain them.
Harjo and Waititi let the historical residue sit inside a comedy without turning the comedy into a lesson.
Mourning Dove writes a protagonist formed by that schooling and belonging comfortably nowhere as a result.

entries.name: The Nation That Is Still Here
entries.description: The correction to the vanishing premise: a present-tense community with institutions, politics and a future.

examples.text: Kunuk works entirely in Inuktitut and inside a community's own narrative tradition, with no settler frame at all.
Jones writes contemporary Blackfeet life as ordinary and lets the horror come from an obligation inside it.
The series is about leaving and staying, which is a set of problems only a continuing community can have.

entries.name: The Horse as Property, Partner and Casualty
entries.description: The genre's defining animal, and the three incompatible things a story usually asks it to be.

examples.text: Adams treats the string as equipment with names, which is the working relationship rather than the sentimental one.
McCarthy makes horsemanship the only competence his protagonist has and the only thing anyone respects him for.

A horse was driven off a cliff and drowned for a single shot, and the outcry led directly to the American Humane Association's film unit the following year; the industry's animal-welfare regime begins with a western.

entries.name: The Six-Gun and What It Cannot Do
entries.description: The genre's central object, and the gap between what it does on screen and what it did.

examples.text: Siegel opens on a demonstration of marksmanship and spends the rest of the film establishing what it cannot buy.
The game's dead-eye mechanic is the screen convention made explicit as a rule system, which is a useful way to see it.

The rapid lever work is real and mechanical — a set screw in the enlarged loop trips the trigger as the lever closes — but the titles fire twelve rounds from a seven-round magazine, which is the clean example of iconography overriding mechanism.

entries.name: The Hat, the Coat and the Silhouette
entries.description: Costume doing characterisation before a word is spoken, and the shorthand it has become.

examples.work: Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo
examples.text: Leone assigns the three men fixed silhouettes and lets the audience track a three-way plot at distance.
Morris reduces the entire genre to a set of silhouettes and demonstrates how few lines the recognition actually needs.
Nightow rebuilds the same silhouette vocabulary off Earth, which shows it travelling intact.

entries.name: The Badge
entries.description: A piece of metal standing in for an institution that may not exist.

examples.text: Hawks makes the badge a workload rather than an authority, distributed among people who are not equipped for it.
The series gives its protagonist a card instead of a badge and makes the substitution the premise.
The badge is federal, the country is not, and the distance between those two facts is the show.

entries.name: The Rope
entries.description: The one object that is a tool, a weapon and an execution, depending on who is holding it.

examples.text: Wellman keeps the rope in shot as equipment throughout, so the execution is continuous with the work.
Adams writes roping as a skill with a failure rate, which is rarer on the page than it should be.
Samuel uses the object's double meaning deliberately in a film about who the genre lynched.

entries.name: The Threshold — Doors, Porches and Who May Come In
entries.description: The genre stages its social order at doorways, and the saloon door is only the most quoted of them.

examples.text: Ford opens and closes on a doorway and makes the frame itself the statement about who belongs inside.
Ray builds an entire film around who is permitted to stand in a saloon and on what terms.
Jenkins makes the question of which doors a Black cavalry sergeant may enter the constant condition of the story.

entries.name: The Table — Cards, Whiskey and the Sitting Down
entries.description: The genre's negotiation space, where information is exchanged and status is settled without a shot.

examples.text: Milch runs most of his politics across tables and makes the seating itself the argument.
Altman puts a business partnership together over a table and lets the arithmetic be audible.

examples.work: Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo
examples.text: Leone stages a three-handed standoff as a card table with no cards, which is why it reads as a game.

entries.name: Boot Hill and the Burial
entries.description: Who gets buried where, by whom, and what the ground says about the town.

examples.text: McMurtry makes an entire return journey out of a promise about where a body will lie.
Peckinpah leaves his dead unburied and lets the scavengers arrive, which is the refusal of the trope.
Charlier and Giraud give the genre's ritual furniture a documentary density that the American comics of the period did not attempt.

entries.name: Main Street as a Stage
entries.description: A single thoroughfare designed by the genre for viewing, and the spectators who make it a court.

examples.text: Daves builds a whole final act out of one walk down one street in front of a town that will not intervene.
Hall keeps the town watching from windows and makes the audience the third party to every confrontation.
The street is a set for a set piece, and the town's opinion of what happens on it never affects anything.

entries.name: The Preacher and the Schoolteacher
entries.description: The two civilising figures the genre imports, and the work it makes them stand for.

examples.text: Cather makes education a material process with costs, rather than an emblem of arriving civilisation.
Ford loads a coach with the town's respectable opinion and lets the journey dismantle it.
The preacher is a gunfighter in a collar, which uses the figure's authority and none of its obligations.

entries.name: The Doctor Who Cannot Do Enough
entries.description: Medicine at the limit of the period, and the scene where competence runs out.

examples.text: Ford's drunk physician is redeemed by a delivery, and the pairing of a discredited doctor with a moment of undeniable competence became the standard shape.
