Barry writes wounds and disease at the period's actual mortality and lets characters simply die of them.
The series' physician is the one recurring figure allowed to be sceptical about the violence, and the show uses him as its conscience for twenty years.

entries.name: The Newspaper and the Printed Legend
entries.description: The press as the machine that converts an event into a fact, and the genre's own account of how it lies.

examples.work: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
examples.text: Johnson's story is the source, and the mechanism is simpler and colder than the film's.
Ferber puts a frontier newspaper at the centre and lets the paper make the town's history as it goes.

examples.work: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford
examples.text: Hansen treats print celebrity as an industry with its own incentives, which is why the killing is a career move.

entries.name: The Company Store and the Debt
entries.description: Economic capture as the real instrument of control, and the town that is owned rather than governed.

examples.text: Altman makes the arrival of a mining company a takeover bid with a violent enforcement clause.
McCunn writes a woman who is herself the property being traded and works out from there.

examples.work: How Much of These Hills Is Gold
examples.text: Zhang builds a family's whole trajectory on extractive labour and the debts it leaves.

entries.name: The Brothel as an Institution
entries.description: The female workplace the genre most often puts on screen, and the difference between using it and writing it.

examples.text: Eastwood gives the women an economic grievance, a collective decision and the money to act on it, which is what makes the plot move.
McMurtry writes a madam as a proprietor with accounts, staff and standing, which is the institution rather than the atmosphere.
The institution is set dressing, present in every frame and consequential in none.

entries.name: The Town Meeting
entries.description: The community deciding in public, and the genre's clearest available test of what it actually believes.

examples.text: The church scene gives every faction a reasonable argument and lets the reasonable arguments produce abandonment.
Sturges makes the town's collective decision one it took years earlier and has been maintaining by silence ever since.
The village's collective deliberation is the plot's engine and the reason its answer works.

entries.name: The Town That Empties
entries.description: Depopulation as an ending — the boom over, the herd gone, the railway routed elsewhere.

examples.text: McMurtry writes the closing of a Texas town as an ordinary economic fact and gets the whole genre's elegy out of it.
Williams lets the market for hides collapse offstage and destroy everyone who staked on it.
Sturges arrives in a town whose emptiness is a cover-up rather than a decline.

entries.category: The Trail, the Journey and the Country
entries.name: The Drive
entries.description: A herd moved a thousand miles by a dozen men, and the logistics that generate the genre's best ensembles.

examples.text: The miniseries gives the drive the duration it needs, so the route's monotony and attrition register as they do not in a feature.
Hawks turns the drive into a succession crisis and lets the route itself apply the pressure.
The series makes the drive an engine for episodic incident and demonstrates how much plot the format will carry.

entries.category: The Trail, the Journey and the Country
entries.name: The River Crossing
entries.description: The obstacle that kills without an antagonist, and the genre's most reliable attrition scene.

examples.text: The crossing is the story's most remembered sequence precisely because the danger is not an antagonist and nobody could have prevented it.

Borden Chase's Saturday Evening Post serial of 1946, Blazing Guns on the Chisholm Trail, reached book form under this title two years later, and it establishes the crossing as the drive's recurring test of authority.
Ford films the crossing as ordinary labour distributed across a whole company, with the danger arriving from the ground rather than from anyone's decision.

entries.category: The Trail, the Journey and the Country
entries.name: The Stampede
entries.description: The herd as a physical system that can fail catastrophically, and the one western set piece with no human antagonist at all.

examples.text: Rydell puts inexperienced boys on a drive so that every failure of stock handling is legible to an audience that knows nothing about cattle.
The series ran the scene often enough to establish the convention and to exhaust it.
The stampede is a comic set piece with no consequence, which shows how completely the iconography survives detached from the risk.

entries.category: The Trail, the Journey and the Country
entries.name: The Wagon Train
entries.description: A society in motion, governed by agreement rather than office, deciding its own route.

examples.text: Guthrie's company elects, disputes and reverses itself, which is the trope's political version.
Ford builds a whole film out of a company's internal composition and the strangers it takes on.
Parkman's account, serialised in The Knickerbocker from 1847 and published under this title in 1849, supplies a great deal of the convention's furniture, and its condescension came with it.

entries.category: The Trail, the Journey and the Country
entries.name: The Pass Before the Snow
entries.description: A deadline set by the season, and the decision to push on that the reader can see coming.

examples.text: The calendar is explicit and the party's arithmetic is on the page, so the pressure is structural rather than atmospheric.
Punke makes the season the whole antagonist and the body's repair schedule the clock.
Manfred puts a man on a schedule set entirely by cold and injury, with no company to argue with about it.

entries.category: The Trail, the Journey and the Country
entries.name: The Water That Is Not There
entries.description: Thirst as a plot mechanism, and the map that turns out to be wrong.

examples.text: Kelton runs a whole novel on an absence and never supplies a villain to blame it on.
Ford strands three men in a desert with an infant and lets the arithmetic of water govern every decision to the end.
Corbucci relocates the same scarcity to snow and starvation, which shows the mechanism is not about deserts.

entries.category: The Trail, the Journey and the Country
entries.name: The Guide Who May Be Wrong
entries.description: Authority resting entirely on claimed knowledge, and the moment the claim becomes untestable.

examples.text: Reichardt gives the party no way to check the guide and makes that epistemic problem the film.
Parkman records his own dependence on guides whose competence he cannot assess and whose motives he consistently misreads, which is the trope before it was a trope.
Cooper puts the knowledge with a prisoner and makes the escort's dependence on him the arc.

entries.category: The Trail, the Journey and the Country
entries.name: The Arrival That Is Not Worth It
entries.description: The destination reached, and the discovery that the journey was the only thing with meaning in it.

examples.text: Anderson's prospector acquires everything he set out for and has nobody left to hold it with.
deWitt's brothers reach the thing they were sent for and find it destroys the people who have it.

examples.work: The Treasure of the Sierra Madre
examples.text: Huston lets the gold be recovered and then blown back across the country by the wind, which is the trope's most literal statement.

entries.name: The Woman Who Runs the Place
entries.description: Proprietorship in a genre that assumes it away, and the authority that comes with a ledger.

examples.text: Ray builds the whole film around two women with property and lets the men be their instruments.
Turner's diarist runs an Arizona ranch through widowhood, drought and remarriage, and the form records the management rather than describing it.
Frank's town is run by women because the men are dead, which is a premise rather than an argument and still changes every scene.

entries.name: The Mail-Order Bride and the Marriage of Convenience
entries.description: Marriage as a contract for labour and land, which is the romance engine the genre reaches for first.

examples.text: McCunn writes the transaction without romance and lets the woman negotiate from inside it.
Wellman ships a hundred and forty women west to marry men they have not met, and the film is far better on the journey than on anything that follows it.
Jones films the arrangement as an exchange of labour and land and then withdraws from its consequences at the point they become hardest.

entries.name: The Widow and the Land
entries.description: Inheritance without standing, and the pressure applied to a woman who will not sell.

examples.text: Stevens keeps Marian's authority over the homestead visible even as the film's attention goes elsewhere.
Swarthout builds a journey out of what the frontier did to women it had no institutions for.
Pearce's housekeeper files her own adjacent claim before she marries her employer, so the land she ends up holding is hers and not inherited.

entries.name: The Child Who Sees
entries.description: A young witness whose incomprehension is the story's method of judgement.

examples.text: Jiles gives her child witness no language the adults share, so everything is judged by what she does rather than what she says.
Portis reverses it: the child understands perfectly and the adults do not.
Wilder's child narration records the removal of a family from land they had no right to settle, and does not know it is doing so.

entries.name: The Sod House and the Winter
entries.description: Shelter as an achievement, and the season that tests it once a year.

examples.text: Cather writes the dugout and the first winter as material facts and lets the prose do nothing to soften them.
Cather makes the accumulation of a house over years the actual plot.
Turner uses a diary form so that the labour is recorded rather than described.

entries.name: The Daughter Who Rides
entries.description: The girl or woman who takes the genre's central competences, and what the story charges her for it.

examples.text: Hathaway lets Mattie hire, negotiate and ride, and the film's comedy comes from the men adjusting.
Greenwald takes the documented case of a woman living as a man and makes the disguise a working condition rather than a twist.

examples.work: The Drover's Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson
examples.text: Purcell rewrites a national short story so the woman holds the rifle and the claim.

entries.name: The Family Split by the Line
entries.description: Kinship crossing the frontier the story is about, so the conflict runs through a household.

examples.text: Berger gives his narrator two families and no way to be loyal to both.
Welch writes a family whose losses run along the line the reservation drew, and refuses to explain any of it to an outside reader.
Eyre's plot is a journey to collect a father's ashes and a negotiation over who is entitled to grieve him.

entries.name: The Long Pursuit
entries.description: Years of tracking as a structure, and the way the duration changes the pursuer.

examples.text: Le May states the motives the film withholds and the pursuit reads differently for it.
McCarthy runs a pursuit with no moral arc attached to it at all, which is the trope stripped to motion.
Leone withholds the reason for the pursuit until the last minutes and makes the withholding the film's structure.

entries.name: The Grievance That Cannot Be Stated
entries.description: A wrong the character will not name, and the pressure that creates in every scene around it.

examples.text: Mann puts the wrong and the bounty in the same man so the motive can never be cleanly declared.
Savage builds a rancher's whole performance of hardness around something he cannot say.
Proulx uses the genre's inherited reticence as the actual mechanism of the loss.

entries.name: The Man Who Gives It Up
entries.description: Revenge abandoned, and whether the story treats that as maturity or as defeat.

examples.text: The renunciation costs the money as well as the satisfaction, which is what makes it credible.
Leonard's protagonist declines the expected escalation repeatedly and pays for each refusal.
Grey's gunman completes one killing and only then puts the work down, and the book is honest that what follows is a withdrawal from the world rather than a return to it.

entries.name: The Wrong Target
entries.description: Vengeance discharged on someone who did not do it, and the genre's most efficient indictment of the practice.

examples.text: Aldrich shows reprisal falling on people chosen for availability rather than for guilt, and the officers knowing it.
Young builds the manhunt on a single mistranslation of the word for horse, so an entire state's force is directed at a man who did nothing the law says he did.
Tarantino's plantation sequence is exact about who is killed and who merely watches, which is a moral claim.

entries.name: The Reckoning That Costs the Avenger Everything
entries.description: Revenge achieved, and the discovery that achieving it was the last thing the character could do.

examples.text: Ritt's protagonist dies for passengers who spent the film despising him, and the film declines to make them worthy of it.
Corbucci maims his avenger before the final reckoning, so the victory is executed by a man who can no longer hold a gun properly.
Sherin films Leonard's 1970 novel to an ending that grants the constable the standoff and withholds any suggestion that it restored anything.

entries.name: The Feud
entries.description: Reciprocal violence with no origin anyone can locate, running on obligation rather than grievance.

examples.text: Sippy makes the feud asymmetric — a maimed policeman and a bandit — so the obligation is legible on both sides.
Yost inherits Leonard's Kentucky and makes the feud a matter of families who share manners and history.

examples.work: With His Pistol in His Hand
examples.text: Paredes reconstructs how a border killing became a ballad and a standing grievance on one side and a police record on the other.

entries.name: The Legend Printed Instead of the Fact
entries.description: The genre's own account of how it manufactures history, and the idea it is quoted for most often.

examples.work: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
examples.text: Ford stages the whole mechanism — the truth available, the newspaper declining it, the town preferring the senator — and refuses to editorialise.

examples.work: Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson
examples.text: Altman shows the legend being assembled as a payroll, with its subjects present and drawing wages for it.
Gwynne tracks how the Parker captivity became a national story and what the story required leaving out.

entries.name: The Wild West Show
entries.description: The frontier performing itself for money while it is still happening, which is one of the places the genre's iconography was assembled.

examples.work: Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson
examples.text: Altman makes the show's manufacture of history the entire subject and casts the manufacture as the villain.
McMurtry follows figures who have become their own exhibits and are being paid for it.

Mourning Dove's protagonist enters both the Ladies' Race and the Squaw Race at a fair, wins both, and is refused both purses, which is the same machinery of staged authenticity operating at a local scale.

entries.name: The Dime Novelist in the Story
entries.description: A character whose job is turning the events of the plot into the version the reader already knows.

examples.work: Deadwood Dick, the Prince of the Road
examples.text: Wheeler wrote the West into being at speed for a mass market, and real men afterwards claimed the name he had invented, which is the manufacture running in both directions.
Penn's frame is an interview with a historian, so the whole film is a contested testimony.
Porter's film is the moment the manufacture moved from print to screen, and its bandits are already conventions rather than people.

entries.name: The Old West as an Attraction
entries.description: The frontier as heritage, reenactment and theme park, and the present-tense politics of that.

examples.text: Crichton builds a literal simulation and makes the detachment of the iconography from any argument the actual premise.
The game sells the closing of the frontier as a recreational experience, which is a version of the same transaction and knows it.
McMurtry writes a town whose only remaining relation to the myth is a cinema that is shutting.

entries.name: The Genre Quoted Inside Another Genre
entries.description: Western furniture appearing in stories that contest no ground, and what the borrowing is for.

examples.text: Nightow runs the full silhouette vocabulary off Earth and uses it to signal a moral register rather than a setting.
Whedon transplants the whole idiom to a spaceship and keeps the frontier's social texture without any of its land claims.
Brooks reproduces the form accurately enough to break it, which is the requirement parody actually imposes.

entries.name: The Iconography, and Where Each Piece Came From
entries.description: The genre's visual vocabulary is a small, dateable set of borrowings, and knowing their sources is what lets a writer use them deliberately.
entries.principle: The hat, the boot, the saddle, the revolver, the badge, the batwing door and the wide street are not a record of the frontier but a selection from it, standardised by illustrators, showmen and costume departments between roughly 1880 and 1940 and largely fixed thereafter. Every element carries an argument: the silhouette says competence, the badge says an institution exists, the street says the encounter will be public and witnessed. A writer who treats the vocabulary as neutral description inherits all of those arguments without choosing any of them.
entries.example: *Deadwood Dick, the Prince of the Road* fixes the outfit for a mass readership in 1877, decades before most of what it depicts. *Stagecoach* consolidates the screen version so completely that later films quote it rather than the period. *Rango* reassembles the whole set for children and demonstrates how few elements the recognition actually requires.
entries.application: Take each visible element in your opening scene and name what it is asserting. Anything you cannot justify twice is furniture, and furniture is fine — provided you know that is what it is.

entries.name: The Dime Novel as a Factory
entries.description: The genre's conventions were manufactured at industrial speed for a mass market before they were anything else.
entries.principle: Beadle's list from 1860 and the story papers that followed produced western fiction on a schedule, in fixed lengths, with a required quota of incident, and those constraints did more to fix the form than any single author's intentions. The consequence is that the western's conventions are commercial artefacts with dates, not deposits left by history — and that they ran in both directions, with real men afterwards adopting the names and the outfits the fiction had invented.
entries.example: *Deadwood Dick, the Prince of the Road* is the clearest case: Edward L. Wheeler invented the figure in 1877 and Nat Love, Richard Clarke and others subsequently claimed the name. *Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson* dramatises the same manufacture with its subjects present and on the payroll.
entries.application: When you reach for a convention, ask what it was invented to sell. The answer usually tells you what it is still doing in your scene.

entries.name: The Wild West Show as a Second Factory
entries.description: The frontier performing itself for paying audiences while the events were still in living memory, with the participants playing themselves.
entries.principle: The touring show turned recent history into a repeatable programme with a running order — the attack on the settler's cabin, the pony express, the buffalo hunt, Custer's last stand — and it employed the people it depicted, including Lakota performers and, briefly, Sitting Bull. That combination is what makes it a factory rather than a memorial: the participants were paid to reproduce a version of events shaped for an audience, and the version travelled further than the events.
entries.example: *Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson* makes the manufacture its whole subject and treats the payroll as the point. *Cogewea, the Half-Blood* shows the same machinery at local scale, in a fair whose races are segregated and whose prizes are withheld.
entries.application: If your story is set after about 1883, the show exists inside its world and your characters have opinions about it. That is usually a more interesting fact than anything you would invent.

entries.name: The Star Persona as the Myth's Delivery System
entries.description: The genre's arguments reached audiences attached to particular faces, and the faces carried commitments the individual films did not make.
entries.principle: Because the western ran on continuing personas — B-unit series stars, then studio-era leads, then a handful of figures whose politics were marketed alongside their films — the myth was transmitted as a set of prior beliefs about specific men rather than as a set of propositions. A film could then confirm, qualify or attack those beliefs, and audiences scored it against what they already held. This is why casting is an argument in this genre in a way it is not in most others.
entries.example: *The Searchers* builds a character out of an established authority and makes that authority inseparable from racial hatred. *The Shootist* is assembled almost entirely from what an audience already believed about the man in it, and works only on that basis.
entries.application: Identify the persona your protagonist is standing in the shadow of, even in prose. If you do not name it, your reader will supply one, and it will be the classical default.

entries.name: Photography, Painting and the Composed West
entries.description: The look of the frontier reaches us through pictures that were composed, staged and sometimes faked, and the composition carried the argument.
entries.principle: Survey photography, studio portraiture of Indigenous subjects, and the painting of Remington, Russell and their successors supplied the genre with its light, its horizon line and its idea of what a significant moment looks like. Much of it was arranged: subjects were posed in borrowed regalia, landscapes were selected for emptiness, and the frame excluded railways, fences and towns that were already there. The western inherited the exclusions along with the compositions.
entries.example: *Stagecoach* and the films that follow it use a landscape chosen for the absence of what was actually in it, and the choice reads as documentary because the painting tradition had already made it look like truth.
entries.application: Ask what is outside your frame. In this genre the most consequential decision is usually what a description leaves out rather than what it includes.

entries.name: The Myth Was Assembled While the Events Were Still Happening
entries.description: There is no period at which the frontier existed and the story of it did not; the two ran concurrently and interfered with each other.
entries.principle: The dime novels, the shows, the newspapers and the memoirs were all in production while the events they described were continuing, and participants read them, corrected them, sued over them and shaped their own conduct to them. That concurrency is a craft resource: a character in 1878 has already read about people like themselves, and can be flattered, embarrassed or misled by the version in circulation.
entries.example: *Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson* is built on exactly this — figures performing an account of events they took part in. *The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford* shows a killer negotiating with the legend while its subject is still alive to object to it.
entries.application: Let your characters have read the magazines. A frontier populated by people who know how they are being written about is more interesting and more accurate than one that does not.

entries.name: The Furniture Detached From the Argument
entries.description: The iconography travels perfectly well without the settlement claim attached, and that is a mode rather than a mistake.
entries.principle: Because the vocabulary is a fixed and legible set, it can be lifted whole into stories that contest no ground at all — space, fantasy, comedy, children's fiction — and it will still carry its associations of competence, isolation and public reckoning. This is the pack's second mode, and it is where the genre's actual output by volume mostly sits. The reason to card it here rather than dismiss it is that iconography is most visible when detached, so these works are the best available evidence of what the furniture means.
entries.example: *Firefly* runs the whole vocabulary on a spaceship. *Trigun* does it in manga. *Westworld* makes the detachment its literal premise by building a simulation of the genre and charging admission.
entries.application: Decide whether your story is contesting anything. If it is not, commit to the second mode — the failure is reaching for the moral weight of a claim you never established.

entries.name: The Myth in the Present Tense
entries.description: Rodeo, reenactment, heritage tourism and western wear keep the myth in production now, which a contemporary story has to write around.
entries.principle: The frontier myth is not a historical residue but a live industry with a calendar, a costume, a competitive circuit and a retail market, and it is currently the main way most people encounter the genre's vocabulary. A neo-western is therefore not importing an old idiom into a modern setting; it is depicting people who are already using that idiom on purpose, for reasons of identity and commerce.
entries.example: *Yellowstone* is set inside the working version of this and treats the persona as a thing its characters maintain deliberately. *The Last Picture Show* writes the moment a town's last relation to the myth closes down. *Red Dead Redemption 2* sells the closing of the frontier as a recreational experience, which is the same transaction at one further remove.
entries.application: In a contemporary setting, ask which of your characters are performing the myth and which are living downstream of it. The two groups behave differently and rarely understand each other.

entries.name: Cowboy as a Political Posture
entries.description: The figure has been an active political vocabulary in American public life for a century, and a story set now cannot use it neutrally.
entries.principle: The cowboy has been deployed as a claim about self-reliance, about the legitimacy of unilateral action, and about who counts as native to a place, by politicians, advertisers and movements across the whole political spectrum. Philip Deloria's work on playing Indian describes the adjacent move — assuming an identity in order to claim a country — and the two operate together. A writer using the figure today is entering an argument already in progress.
entries.example: *Yellowstone* stages the posture as an inheritance being defended. *Bacurau* shows the same iconography arriving from outside as a colonial imposition, which is what makes its answer legible.
entries.application: Ask what your use of the figure is claiming, because it is claiming something. Neutrality is not one of the available positions.

entries.name: The Empty Country
entries.description: The first and most consequential of the myth's claims: that the land was available.
entries.principle: The classical western's plots require ground that can be entered, held and improved without displacing anyone with a prior interest, and the genre secures this by description rather than by argument — the country is rendered as waiting, and the absence of prior claimants is never stated because it is never raised. This is a rhetorical operation, and it is the one every subsequent claim rests on. Remove it and the settlement argument has to be made rather than assumed.
entries.example: *The Virginian* renders Wyoming as available and never puts the question. *Little Big Man* puts a named people into the same country and the availability evaporates without a word of argument. *Meek's Cutoff* shows a party who cannot read the country at all, which is the same premise inverted.
entries.application: Write the sentence that states who was there. If your draft cannot accommodate that sentence anywhere, the emptiness is doing structural work and you should know it.

entries.name: Necessary Violence
entries.description: The claim that the killing was regrettable and unavoidable, which converts an act into a cost.
entries.principle: The myth does not celebrate violence; it presents violence as a price paid reluctantly by people who would have preferred another route, and that reluctance is what makes it acceptable. The move is doing two things at once — it licenses the act and it credits the actor with moral seriousness for regretting it. The revisionist tradition attacks the second half more often than the first, which is why revisionist westerns are frequently more violent rather than less.
entries.example: *Shane* stages the reluctance explicitly and lets a child watch it. *Unforgiven* recovers the whole apparatus in order to itemise what it costs and to deny the actor the credit. *The Wild Bunch* removes the necessity and leaves the act.
entries.application: Ask who in your story benefits from the violence being described as unavoidable. Reluctance is a claim, and claims have beneficiaries.

entries.name: The Law That Follows
entries.description: The claim that violence is a temporary stage which institutions succeed and validate.
entries.principle: The myth's third claim is chronological: gunfighting is what happens before courts, and courts are what the gunfighting was for. This retrospectively converts private killing into a founding act, and it is why the classical western can be simultaneously about lawlessness and about order. Two things break it — showing the law arriving badly or in someone's interest, and showing that it never arrives at all.
entries.example: *The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance* stages the succession as a convention and shows the institution adopting a lie as policy. *Deadwood* shows institutions arriving as a hostile takeover. *Warlock* shows a town that hires its law privately because the public version has not turned up.
entries.application: Decide what your story thinks the violence was for. If the answer is nothing, you are writing against this claim and the structure will fight you.

entries.name: The Vanishing Indian
entries.description: The claim that Indigenous peoples were disappearing of their own accord, which relieves the story of the need to explain where they went.
entries.principle: This is the myth's most durable and least examined claim: the elegiac register in which Indigenous nations are always already receding makes dispossession into weather. It licenses sympathy without responsibility, which is why it survives in works that consider themselves corrective — a film can mourn a people and still not name who removed them. The correction is not more sympathy but a present tense.
entries.example: *Cheyenne Autumn* sympathises at length and keeps the disappearance in the passive voice. *Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner* and *Reservation Dogs* refuse the premise simply by being set now, with institutions, politics and futures.
entries.application: Check whether any Indigenous character in your story is doing something other than declining. If not, you have written the claim rather than a people.

entries.name: Regeneration Through Violence
entries.description: Richard Slotkin's account of the underlying structure: the nation renews itself through violence at its edge.
entries.principle: Slotkin's argument, developed across three volumes from 1973, is that American national identity is organised around a repeating story in which contact with the wilderness and violence against its inhabitants produces renewal — and that the western is that story's most efficient vehicle. It is a literary-historical thesis rather than a psychological finding, and the pack marks it as one. Its practical value to a writer is that it identifies why the genre's endings feel earned even when its plots do not justify them.
entries.example: *Regeneration Through Violence* is the study itself. *Blood Meridian* can be read as the thesis run without the renewal, which is why it reads as an attack on the whole structure rather than on any particular film.
entries.application: Ask what your ending renews. If violence in your story produces a settled community, a marriage or a restored inheritance, you are inside this structure and should decide whether you mean to be.

entries.name: The Self-Made Claim
entries.description: The claim that entitlement is produced by labour and courage rather than by capital, inheritance or policy.
entries.principle: The myth insists that what a man holds he made, and it systematically obscures the federal survey, the army, the railroad grant, the eastern bank and the immigrant labour that produced the conditions for holding it. This is not incidental: the whole moral appeal of the homestead and the ranch depends on the claim being personally earned. The most efficient revision is simply to show the paperwork and the payroll.
entries.example: *Giant* tracks an empire across generations and lets the second generation inherit rather than earn. *Heaven's Gate* puts the capital and the hired guns on screen together. *There Will Be Blood* makes acquisition itself the protagonist's craft.
entries.application: Name the outside money and the public policy behind your protagonist's holding. If neither exists in your story, check whether that is a fact about the setting or an inherited claim.

entries.name: The Moral Structure the Western Asserts
entries.description: What the classical form says is good, stated plainly enough to be reproduced, quoted or attacked.
entries.principle: The classical western holds that competence is a virtue, that a man's word binds him, that violence in defence of the defenceless is honourable, that the community's judgement is worth something but does not override an individual conscience, and that the person who does the necessary killing forfeits the settled life it makes possible. Those five propositions are the moral structure — and stating them explicitly is what allows the form to be parodied, since a parodist must reproduce a structure competently before altering it, and the comedy pack's hand-off names this card as the source.
entries.example: *Shane* asserts all five without argument. *Rio Bravo* asserts them and then makes competence a shared burden rather than a solitary gift, which is the most-copied variation on them. *Blazing Saddles* reproduces them accurately enough to break, which is why the parody works on people who have never seen a western.
entries.application: Check your story against the five. Agreeing with all of them is a choice; disagreeing with one is a plot; disagreeing with all of them requires you to supply something else, and most failed westerns fail here.

entries.name: The Frontier Thesis and What It Licensed
entries.description: Turner's 1893 argument, its enormous influence, and the work it did for the myth.
entries.principle: Frederick Jackson Turner's thesis held that the frontier — and specifically its closing, which he dated to the 1890 census — was the formative force in American character and democracy. Whatever its merits as history, it supplied the genre with a licence: a scholarly account in which the frontier is a process rather than a place taken from people, and in which its closing is a loss to be mourned rather than a conquest to be reckoned with. Much of the genre's elegiac register descends from it.
entries.example: *The Frontier in American History* collects the argument. *The Wild Bunch* and *Ride the High Country* are unthinkable without the closing it dates and dramatises.
entries.application: If your story mourns the closing of the frontier, work out who is doing the mourning and what they lost. The elegy is inherited and it comes with a position attached.

entries.name: The New Western History's Replacement Vocabulary
entries.description: The scholarly correction that retired the word frontier as an analytic term, and what it offers a writer instead.
entries.principle: From the 1980s a body of work — Patricia Nelson Limerick's especially — argued that frontier is a process word that only functions from the settler's side, and replaced it with conquest, place, continuity and, later, settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event. The substitution is useful to a novelist as well as a historian: continuity says the story does not end in 1890, place says the land has a history before the plot arrives, and structure says dispossession is a system rather than a series of incidents.
entries.example: *The Legacy of Conquest* is the argument. *Winter Counts* and *Reservation Dogs* are what continuity looks like in fiction — a present tense in which the consequences are still administrative rather than elegiac.
entries.application: This pack uses frontier throughout because the object of study is a myth that is called the frontier myth. Every time you use it as though it described a real thing rather than a claim about one, you have adopted a position.

entries.name: The Claims Are Load-Bearing Together
entries.description: The myth's propositions support one another, so removing one obliges the story to reinforce or abandon the rest.
entries.principle: Emptiness licenses necessity, necessity licenses the law that follows, the law that follows validates the violence retrospectively, and the vanishing premise removes the party who would object to all of it. Pull out one and the others sag. This is why partial revisions so often feel incoherent: a film that denies the empty country while keeping necessary violence has to find some other warrant for the killing, and if it does not, the killing is simply murder the story still expects the audience to enjoy.
entries.example: *Dances With Wolves* denies the vanishing premise and the emptiness while retaining the elegiac register, which is precisely the seam its critics work. *Blood Meridian* removes all of them at once and supplies nothing in their place, which is why it is exhausting rather than merely bleak.
entries.application: List which of the five claims your story keeps. A story that keeps none needs a different engine, and you should know what it is before Act Two.

entries.name: Revision Is Not the Anti-Western
entries.description: Two operations that are routinely treated as one, and the structural difference between them.
entries.principle: Revision reverses the moral polarity of the form while leaving its machinery fully operational — the ride-in, the escalation, the walk-down all still work, and still deliver. The anti-western withholds the machinery's satisfactions structurally, so there is no functioning climax to reverse. The distinction matters because the two fail in opposite directions: a revision that dismantles the structure has nothing left to disappoint the audience with, and an anti-western that relents into a satisfying climax has become a revision with an unearned ending.
entries.example: *Unforgiven* restores every element of the ritual in order to charge for it, which is revision. *McCabe & Mrs. Miller* declines to stage its killing for pleasure at all, which is not.
entries.application: Decide which you are writing before Chapter One, and audit the climax against the decision. The failure is almost always at the ending rather than the premise.

entries.name: Ford Was Revising Ford
entries.description: The correction is internal to the tradition and much earlier than the standard account allows.
entries.principle: The received chronology has a classical period followed by a revisionist reaction beginning in the 1960s, and it is wrong in a way that matters: the genre's most authoritative classical film-maker was building critiques into his own work from the late 1940s and continued for two decades. Treating revision as an external arrival makes the classical form more naive than it was and the revision more original than it was, and it obscures the fact that the machinery was designed by people who could see what it was doing.
entries.example: *Fort Apache* ends by having its survivors adopt a version of events they know to be false, in 1948. *The Searchers* makes admired competence inseparable from hatred in 1956. *Cheyenne Autumn* is a late and explicit attempt at restitution by the same hand.
entries.application: Do not write your revision as though the form has never been examined. The best objections to the western are already inside it, and repeating them as discoveries reads as a failure to have watched anything.

entries.name: Reversing the Polarity, Keeping the Machinery
entries.description: The core revisionist move, and why it still satisfies as a western.
entries.principle: The technique is to leave the form's engineering untouched and change who the violence serves and what it purchases. Because the audience's expectations are structural rather than moral, the machinery keeps delivering — tension, escalation, a public reckoning — while the conclusion arrives in the wrong direction. This is why revisionist westerns remain popular entertainments rather than becoming essays, and it is the single most reliable technique in the mode.
entries.example: *The Wild Bunch* keeps the professional ethic entirely intact and removes everything it might have served. *Django Unchained* runs the rescue and the reckoning at full classical strength and puts them at the disposal of the person the classical form would have made the object.
entries.application: Keep your set pieces. If you find yourself cutting the walk-down to avoid endorsing it, you have lost the instrument you needed to make the argument.

entries.name: The Elegy as a Revision That Forgives
entries.description: The mode that accepts the revisionist account of the cost and declines to prosecute.
entries.principle: Elegy agrees that the settlement was violent and unjust and then makes obsolescence rather than guilt its subject, so the emotional payload is loss instead of indictment. The structural marker is that the antagonist is time — fences, railways, actuarial age — and the protagonist's skills are correct and no longer wanted. Its power is real and its characteristic risk is precise: mourning a world excuses the story from asking who else was in it.
entries.example: *Ride the High Country* is the mode in miniature. *Lonesome Dove* spends eight hundred pages earning it. *The Shootist* puts a disease where the closing frontier goes.
entries.application: If you are writing elegy, name one person in the story who is glad the world is ending. If nobody is, the mourning has no opposition and the mode will slide into nostalgia.

entries.name: The Parody as a Revision That Cannot Forgive
entries.description: Comic treatment as a form of critique, and the technical demand it makes.
entries.principle: Parody attacks the form by reproducing it accurately and then breaking it, which means the parodist must first build a functioning western — the conventions are rigid enough that a loose reproduction reads as incompetence rather than as comedy. Where elegy forgives, parody declines to, because the mechanism of the joke is the exposure of a convention as a convention. This is the operation the comedy pack's hand-off card depends on, and it needs the moral-structure card to work from.
entries.example: *Blazing Saddles* stages its set pieces straight before breaking them and targets the industry as much as the genre. *Limonádový Joe* performs the same operation on the singing-cowboy form from inside the Eastern Bloc.
entries.application: Write the straight version, confirm it works, then break it. A parody that skips the first step is a sketch, and the genre's conventions will not carry it.

entries.name: The Sympathetic-Indian Studio Cycle
entries.description: The 1950s attempt at correction from inside the studio system, and the specific way it fails.
entries.principle: A run of films from around 1950 reversed the genre's sympathies deliberately, giving Indigenous characters grievances, negotiating positions and moral authority — while casting white actors in the parts, routing the story through a white intermediary, and resolving it through that intermediary's conscience. The result is a cycle that is genuinely trying and structurally incapable of succeeding, and it is the clearest available demonstration that sympathy is not the variable that matters.
entries.example: *Broken Arrow* makes negotiation rather than pursuit the whole plot and casts a white star as Cochise. *Devil's Doorway* makes the legal apparatus the instrument of dispossession and does the same. *Apache* goes further and had its ending replaced by the studio so its protagonist survives.
entries.application: If a story's Indigenous characters need a settler to carry their argument to the audience, the structure is doing the work the sympathy was meant to undo. This is the term the pack uses instead of the retired label Indian Western.

entries.name: Revision by Casting
entries.description: The cheapest and most decisive revision available, and the one the genre took longest to make.
entries.principle: Who is on screen determines what a scene can mean, independently of the script, and in a genre whose central figures were racially fixed by convention the substitution is itself the argument. It operates in both directions: casting Indigenous actors in Indigenous parts changes the film's relation to its material, and casting a European actor as an Indigenous lead changes it too, whatever the politics of the screenplay.
entries.example: *Prey* puts a Comanche protagonist at the centre of a captivity-adjacent structure and the plot's meaning inverts without a line of argument. *Die Söhne der großen Bärin* delivers explicitly anti-colonial content with a Serbian actor in the lead, which is the same lever pulled the other way.
entries.application: Cast before you revise. In screen work the decision precedes the script's arguments, and in prose the equivalent is deciding whose consciousness the reader is inside.

entries.name: Revision by Withholding the Payoff
entries.description: Building the machinery to full readiness and then declining to fire it.
entries.principle: The form's satisfactions are so reliably anticipated that withholding one is a legible statement rather than an absence — the audience knows exactly what did not happen. It is a more precise instrument than inversion because it does not have to supply an alternative, and it is harder to sustain, because the pressure to relent increases with every scene that builds.
entries.example: *Il grande silenzio* constructs an entire film toward a walk-down and refuses the outcome the form demands. *The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford* withholds the confrontation and spends its length on the anticipation and the aftermath instead.
entries.application: If you withhold, withhold once and late. Two withheld payoffs read as a story that does not know how to end, and the audience stops anticipating, which removes the instrument.

entries.name: Revision by Duration
entries.description: Length as an argument — the genre's compressions are where its evasions live.
entries.principle: Much of what the classical western asserts survives only because the form is short: a journey that takes ninety minutes cannot show the tedium and attrition that would make its cost legible, and a town settled in the third act cannot show what settling one actually involved. Extending the duration is therefore a revision in itself, and it requires no explicit critique — the material simply stops fitting the shape.
entries.example: *Lonesome Dove* gives the drive the length it needs and the venture turns out not to have been worth it. *Deadwood* makes a camp's institutional formation the plot because there is time for institutions. *Meek's Cutoff* refuses to compress a crossing and the refusal is the whole film.
entries.application: Ask which of your compressions are hiding something. The scene you are cutting for pace is often the one carrying the cost.

entries.name: When Revision Becomes Its Own Cliché
entries.description: The reversal is now the default, and a default cannot revise anything.
entries.principle: Since roughly 1990 the grim, muddy, morally compromised western has been the expected form rather than the surprising one, which means its moves no longer carry the charge they were built to carry — a dirty saloon, a corrupt marshal and a joyless killing now signal seriousness in the way clean shirts and a decisive walk-down once signalled adventure. A writer who reaches for the revisionist register as a default has adopted a convention while believing they are examining one.
entries.example: *Hostiles* reproduces the register faithfully — the mud, the exhaustion, the compromised officer — and its critics divide precisely over whether the reproduction is doing any work. *Bacurau* escapes the trap by importing the machinery into a place with a live political grievance, so the grimness is earning something.
entries.application: Ask what your revision is revising. If the answer is a version of the genre nobody has made for sixty years, you are arguing with a straw man in a costume.

entries.name: The Revision That Restores What It Attacks
entries.description: The commonest failure mode: a critique whose structure returns the authority its content removes.
entries.principle: A story can reverse every stated sympathy and still hand the moral centre back to the party it set out to displace, usually through structure — the outsider who learns, the settler whose conscience organises the material, the ending in which the dispossessed are saved by someone from the dispossessing side. The content and the architecture are making opposite claims, and architecture wins.
entries.example: *Dances With Wolves* denies both the empty country and the vanishing premise and retains an elegiac frame in which a settler's transformation is the story's arc, which is exactly the seam its critics work. *Apache* has its protagonist spared at the end, and the sparing is done by the pursuing authority.
entries.application: Delete your protagonist from the outline and ask whether the story still has a shape. If it collapses, the structure has made them the subject regardless of what the dialogue says.

entries.name: Revising From Inside the Community
entries.description: The form worked by the people it was built to write out, which is where the genre's live problems are being solved.
entries.principle: The most consequential current revision is not a technique but a position: writers and film-makers from the communities the classical form used as scenery are working the same machinery from the other side, and the results are not corrections appended to the genre but functioning westerns with different assumptions about who the country is for. What distinguishes them technically is specificity — a named nation with its own protocols and internal disagreements in place of a composite — and a present tense.
entries.example: *Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner* works entirely in Inuktitut with no settler frame at all. *The Only Good Indians* builds a horror novel on a specific broken hunting obligation. *Sweet Country* and *The Drover's Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson* do the equivalent work on the Australian frontier.
entries.application: Read this body of work before you write your revision. Most of the objections a settler writer arrives at have already been made better, and the interesting problems are further on.

entries.name: Who Adjudicates
entries.description: Every contested claim in the genre is settled by somebody, and identifying who is the first analytic move.
entries.principle: Legitimacy in the western is conferred by a small set of adjudicators — a court, a gun, a mob, a company, a cavalry troop, a bank, and occasionally the land itself — and each carries a different account of where authority comes from. The genre's arguments are usually about which adjudicator should have decided rather than about who was right, and stories that do not know which one is operating produce endings that feel arbitrary.
entries.example: In *Warlock* three armed men hold three different sources of authority and the town cannot choose between them. In *High Noon* the community is the adjudicator and it declines the role.
entries.application: Name the adjudicator for each dispute in your outline. If the same one settles everything, your story has one institution and probably one theme.

entries.name: The Walk-Down as a Court
entries.description: The formal duel is a judicial procedure in disguise, and reading it that way is what makes it breakable.
entries.principle: The walk-down has all the features of a trial: the parties consent, the time and place are agreed, witnesses attend, the verdict is delivered publicly and the community accepts the result as settling the matter. That is why it satisfies — it is not a fight but a judgement — and it is why the revisionist attack on it consists of removing procedural elements: the shot from cover, the shot in the back, the man who will not consent to appear.
entries.example: *The Virginian* establishes the form as a settlement the town endorses. *Unforgiven* restores every procedural element and then narrates what the procedure is actually for.
entries.application: Decide what verdict your walk-down delivers and who accepts it. A confrontation the town does not care about is a fight, and fights are much less interesting than trials.

entries.name: The Posse's Legal Fiction
entries.description: Deputisation as a real legal instrument, and the point at which the instrument stops covering what is being done.
entries.principle: The posse is authority lent temporarily to private men, and the whole of its dramatic value lies in the gap between what the lending authorises and what the men do. Because the fiction is genuinely legal at the outset, the collapse can be gradual and deniable, and each participant can locate the moment of illegitimacy slightly later than the last. That is the mechanism, and it is why the posse produces the genre's best group-culpability writing.
entries.example: *The Ox-Bow Incident* shows the fiction dissolving in real time while every man present continues to describe himself as acting under it.
entries.application: Establish who deputised your posse and under what authority, then track the exact scene at which that authority stops covering them. If nobody in the group notices, you have written a mob from the start.

entries.name: The Mob Claiming to Be the People
entries.description: Extra-legal violence justified as popular sovereignty, and the argument it actually makes.
entries.principle: The genre's lynchings are rarely presented as lawlessness by their participants; they are presented as the community reclaiming a power it had only delegated to distant courts. That argument has a genuine nineteenth-century pedigree and it is what makes the trope dangerous rather than merely brutal — it is a constitutional claim, and stories that treat it as simple savagery misunderstand why anyone went along with it.
entries.example: *The Virginian* has Judge Henry make the argument explicitly and at length, in a novel that endorses it. *Heaven's Gate* shows the same claim made by an association with minutes, membership and a payroll.
entries.application: Let someone in your mob make the argument properly. A lynching nobody defends is a scene; a lynching defended in terms the reader can feel the pull of is a chapter.

entries.name: The Company as an Instrument
entries.description: Corporate power as an adjudicator with no face, and the genre's difficulty in dramatising it.
entries.principle: Railroads, mining concerns, cattle associations and banks settle more claims in the western's world than gunmen do, and they present a craft problem: they have no body to confront and no conscience to appeal to, so the form's usual climax is unavailable. The two solutions are to personify — a hired enforcer, a company man — which risks converting a structural problem into a villain, or to let the institution win, which is honest and hard to make satisfying.
entries.example: *C'era una volta il West* makes the railway the actual protagonist and the gunmen its contractors. *McCabe & Mrs. Miller* lets the corporation win and gives the audience no confrontation that would have changed it.
entries.application: Decide early whether your institution gets a face. If it does, keep the face subordinate — the moment killing him solves the problem, the story has said the problem was a man.

entries.name: The Cavalry as an Instrument
entries.description: State force with a stated policy, and the difference between depicting soldiers and depicting a campaign.
entries.principle: The cavalry western is the only part of the genre where the violence has an explicit authorising policy with a name, a budget and an archive, which removes every ambiguity the form usually relies on. A story can attend to the men — competence, boredom, fear, command — or to what the men were sent to do, and doing only the first produces work in which policy is invisible while its execution is admired.
entries.example: *Fort Apache* builds the institution lovingly and indicts its commander. *Ulzana's Raid* rebuilds the same machinery to argue the opposite case with the same professional respect.
entries.application: Put the policy on the page once, in a document or an order. It costs a paragraph and it stops the campaign reading as weather.

entries.name: Consent Manufactured After the Fact
entries.description: The device by which an act becomes legitimate retrospectively, through acceptance rather than authorisation.
entries.principle: A great deal of the genre's legitimacy is produced backwards: the killing is done, the town accepts the result, and the acceptance is what converts it into justice. This is why the community's reaction shot matters more than the shooting, and why a story that shows the town refusing to ratify an outcome has attacked the whole apparatus without staging any argument at all.
entries.example: *The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance* shows a whole political career built on a ratification that everyone eventually knows to be false. *Sweet Country* delivers a formally correct verdict that the settlement then declines to let stand.
entries.application: Write the ratification scene. If your story has none, the reader will supply consent by default, and you will have endorsed the outcome without noticing.

entries.name: The Record That Ratifies the Outcome
entries.description: The newspaper, the ledger and the report as the last step in legitimation, and the genre's own account of how they lie.
entries.principle: An act becomes settled when it is written down, and the western is unusually self-aware about this: the press, the court reporter and the company's books convert a contested event into a fact that later characters inherit. The distinction from Historical's archive material is that this pack is not asking how a record survives or how to read it, but what the act of recording does to the legitimacy of what it records.
entries.example: *The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance* stages the decision to print the legend as an editorial choice made in the room. *Cimarron* puts a frontier newspaper at the centre and lets it make the town's history as it goes.
entries.application: Decide who writes your story's events down and what they leave out. In this genre the record is a participant, not a frame.

entries.name: The Witness Who Is Not Called
entries.description: Legitimacy secured by the absence of the party with the strongest objection.
entries.principle: The genre's adjudications are almost always conducted among the people with standing to be heard, and the party whose claim is most directly at stake is structurally absent — not silenced dramatically, simply never in the room. This is the machinery's quietest operation and its most efficient, because it requires no argument and produces no scene a reader can object to.
entries.example: *The Ox-Bow Incident* is a rare case where the absence is made the subject, through a letter read aloud after the fact.
entries.application: For each adjudication in your story, list who is not present. If the missing party is the one with the strongest claim, you have found either your story's subject or its blind spot.

entries.name: Possession Becoming Title
entries.description: Time as a legitimating instrument — holding ground long enough to be held to own it.
entries.principle: The most durable claim in the genre is simply duration: a family that has worked a place for three generations is treated by the story, and usually by the law, as owning it regardless of how the first generation acquired it. This is the mechanism by which the whole settlement argument is eventually retired, and it is what makes the neo-western possible, because by the twentieth century the contested acquisition is far enough back to be inheritance.
entries.example: *Giant* runs the conversion across generations and lets the heirs receive a question rather than an answer. *Yellowstone* stages the same inheritance as something to be defended with modern instruments.
entries.application: Work out how many generations your story is from the original acquisition. The answer determines whether your characters can plausibly not know, and that is usually the most interesting thing about them.

entries.name: Treaty
entries.description: The instrument that made Indigenous nations sovereign counterparties, and the date the United States stopped using it.
entries.principle: Treaties are agreements between sovereigns, which is why they were the instrument used with Indigenous nations for most of a century and why they carry obligations that survive their breach. Congress ended treaty-making with tribes in the Indian Appropriations Act of 1871 and thereafter used agreements, statutes and executive orders, which changed the legal character of every subsequent transaction. A story set before or after that line is working with different instruments, and the difference is not decorative.
entries.example: A plot turning on a broken agreement in 1867 and one turning on an executive-order reservation in 1885 have different remedies, different signatories and different archives behind them.
entries.application: Find the actual instrument governing your ground and its year. The genre's stock phrase about broken treaties conceals half a dozen distinct legal acts, and knowing which one you have changes who can object and how.

entries.name: Allotment
entries.description: The policy that broke communal title into individual parcels and transferred the remainder, and the mechanism most western fiction omits entirely.
entries.principle: The General Allotment Act of 1887 divided reservation land into individual holdings, held in trust for a period, and declared the remainder surplus for sale to settlers — so the largest transfer of Indigenous land after the wars was administrative rather than military. Later amendments accelerated the alienation of allotted parcels, and the policy was not ended until 1934. This is the instrument behind the checkerboarded jurisdictions that still govern crime, taxation and water on many reservations today.
entries.example: A present-day story in which some ground on a reservation is under tribal authority and adjacent ground is not is describing the residue of this Act rather than an oddity.
entries.application: If your story touches reservation land in any period after 1887, establish its allotment status. It determines who polices it, who may sell it and who may be prosecuted for what happens on it.

entries.name: The Homestead Entry
entries.description: The claim the genre's sympathies rest on, and the paperwork it actually required.
entries.principle: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered a quarter section to a claimant who filed, resided, improved and stayed for five years, at which point a patent issued; a commutation clause allowed purchase after six months at a fixed price per acre. Every element is dramatic: the filing has a date, residence can be challenged, improvements can be inspected, and the five years are a clock the story can run. Most westerns give the homesteader the moral position without any of the machinery that produced it.
entries.example: *Shane* gives its homesteaders patents and its cattleman prior use, which is why the conflict cannot be settled by argument and has to be settled by a specialist.
entries.application: Give your homesteaders a filing date and a proving-up deadline. It converts a sympathy into a plot.

entries.name: The Patent and Proving Up
entries.description: The moment a claim becomes property, and the vulnerability of everything before it.
entries.principle: Until the patent issues, a homestead entry is a conditional interest that can be contested, abandoned or lost, and the contest is conducted through the land office rather than through a court — which means a rival with better paperwork, a bribed clerk or a well-timed affidavit can defeat a family that has done the work. The genre's fence-and-gunfight version of the range war is downstream of a documentary war that is usually more decisive.
entries.example: *Deadwood* makes the absence of any recognised title the engine of a season, and the arrival of the machinery a hostile act rather than a relief.
entries.application: Put one contest in the land office. It is the cheapest way to show that the violence in your story is a response to a losing legal position.

entries.name: Water: Prior Appropriation and Riparian Right
entries.description: Two incompatible doctrines, one of which governs almost everywhere the genre is set.
entries.principle: Riparian right attaches water to the land it touches and is the eastern inheritance; prior appropriation gives it to whoever first put it to beneficial use, regardless of where they are, and became the rule across the arid West. The consequence is that in most western settings water is a separate, senior and transferable property from land, and a man can own a valley and not own the river in it. This single fact generates more plausible conflict than any number of rustlers.
entries.example: *The Big Country* makes a river the actual prize and lets two families ruin themselves over access. *There Will Be Blood* shows the same senior right being acquired quietly along with the people who hold it.
entries.application: Decide who holds the senior water right on your ground and in what year they perfected it. Then let your antagonist buy it rather than fight for it.

entries.name: Open Range and Its Fencing
entries.description: The custom that made the cattle economy possible, and the invention that ended it.
entries.principle: Open range is not an absence of law but a customary regime in which stock graze the public domain and the burden of fencing falls on the cultivator rather than the herder — which is why herd laws reversing that burden were fought so bitterly. Cheap barbed wire from the mid-1870s made enclosure economically possible for the first time, and the resulting conflicts are about who bears a cost rather than about who is lawless.
entries.example: *The Sea of Grass* writes the collision as an argument between a cattleman and a plough that neither can win. *Heaven's Gate* shows the enclosure being enforced with hired men and a membership list.
entries.application: Establish which fencing regime governs your county and in what year it changed. The range war becomes legible the moment the reader knows who is legally obliged to build the fence.

entries.name: The Railroad Grant
entries.description: The largest single transfer of land in the genre's period, made by statute to corporations, in a pattern that still shapes the map.
entries.principle: The Pacific Railway Acts granted alternate sections along the right of way, producing a checkerboard in which railroad land and public land alternate square by square for miles on either side. The company then sold it, which made railroads the West's largest land dealers as well as its carriers, and gave them an interest in who settled where. A story that treats the railroad only as transport has missed the larger transaction.
entries.example: *C'era una volta il West* makes the railway the actual protagonist and everyone else its contractors, which is closer to the record than most American treatments.
entries.application: If a line runs through your setting, work out who owns the alternate sections and what they are asking for them. It is usually a better antagonist than a gunman.

entries.name: The Reservation Boundary
entries.description: A line with legal force that most westerns draw as though it were geography.
entries.principle: A reservation boundary is created by a specific instrument, has been moved by later instruments more often than not, and governs jurisdiction rather than merely occupancy — which is why crimes, taxes, water and policing change character at the line. Its history is usually one of successive reductions, and the reductions have dates and documents. Treating it as a static edge of a map removes the entire legal drama available at it.
entries.example: *Winter Counts* builds a present-day novel on the jurisdictional gap that makes some offences on tribal land effectively unprosecutable, which is this boundary doing its actual work.
entries.application: Find the instrument that drew your boundary and the ones that moved it. Then decide which side of it your crime happens on, because that decides who can investigate.

entries.name: Mineral Claim and the Mining District
entries.description: A parallel property system with its own law, invented by the miners themselves and later ratified by Congress.
entries.principle: Mining camps wrote their own codes — how a claim is located and marked, how much work must be done annually to hold it, how disputes are heard — and these local codes were largely confirmed by the General Mining Act of 1872. The result is a regime in which possession depends on continuous labour rather than on a deed, disputes are heard by a body of interested neighbours, and a claim can be lost by going away. That is an unusually good engine for a story.
entries.example: *McCabe & Mrs. Miller* sets a business against a company in a camp where nothing is titled and everything is held. *Thousand Pieces of Gold* works the same setting from the position of a person who is herself treated as property in it.
entries.application: Give your camp a written code and let a character quote it. The system's amateurism is its dramatic gift — the rules are known, local and arguable.

entries.name: What a Claim Actually Was
entries.description: The summary card: the difference between the genre's shorthand and the instruments underneath it.
entries.principle: The western says a man owns a valley. Underneath that sentence sit a homestead entry with a filing date, a patent that may not have issued, a senior water right perfected in a different year by a different person, a grazing custom, a mineral claim held by annual labour, a railroad section in the middle of it, and a treaty or executive order that governed all of it before any of them existed. Knowing which of these your character holds is the difference between a dispute and a brawl.
entries.example: The strongest range-war fiction is legible precisely because the writer knew which instrument each side held, whatever the reader is told.
entries.application: Write the stack for your central ground: instrument, date, holder, and what is unresolved. It takes twenty minutes and it supplies the plot.

entries.name: Specificity Over the Composite
entries.description: The genre's default Indigenous figure has no referent, and the correction is precision rather than sympathy.
entries.principle: The classical western's composite assembles Plains dress, Southwest landscape and invented ceremony into a figure that corresponds to no nation, and no amount of respect improves it, because the fault is referential rather than tonal. Nations differ in language, kinship, subsistence, governance, religion and their relations with one another and with the United States, and those differences generate plot that the composite cannot. Historical's archive cards ask how a record survives and how to read it; this card asks something prior — whether the subject of your sentence exists.
entries.example: *The Only Good Indians* runs its whole causal engine on a specific Blackfeet hunting obligation, which a composite could not have supplied. *Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner* is legible only because everything in it is particular to one people and one place.
entries.application: Write the nation's name at the top of the outline. If the story works identically with another nation substituted, you have written the composite and no revision of the prose will fix it.

entries.name: What the Record Supports, and at What Confidence
entries.description: State claims about a culture at the confidence the evidence actually carries, and say when that is low.
entries.principle: Much of what the genre asserts about Indigenous practice rests on nineteenth-century observation by hostile or untrained witnesses, on a small number of much-quoted monographs, and on later popularisation that hardened conjecture into fact. The craft rule is to state the confidence level in the card or the scene: what is documented, what is inferred, what is contested among the people concerned. Historical's cards cover how to read a source; this one is about the obligation to declare uncertainty when writing about people who can read what you wrote.
entries.example: *Navaho Witchcraft* is a standard outside source whose own conditions of collection are disputed, and a writer who does not know that will state its contents as settled.
entries.application: Mark every claim about practice as documented, inferred or contested before you dramatise it. Then write the scene so an inferred claim does not have to be true for the scene to work.

entries.name: The Appropriation History Is Part of the Material
entries.description: Where a genre has a record of taking, the record travels with the subject and belongs in the work.
entries.principle: A writer approaching Indigenous material in this genre is not approaching it first: there is a documented history of extraction, invention and profit that the audience may know and the community certainly does. Naming that history is a craft act rather than an apology — it tells the reader which tradition your treatment belongs to, and it forecloses the reading in which you did not know. This is what Historical's card on what is owed to a living tradition points at from the archive's side; here it is a question about the genre's own conduct.
entries.example: *A Man Called Horse* is the genre's most-copied instance of the borrowed-ceremony device, and the sun-dance sequence it is remembered for is an assembly rather than a record. The screen zombie's derivation from a functioning religion is the library's standing case in Horror; the western's equivalents are the invented ceremony and the ancient burial ground, both now generic devices with traceable origins.
entries.application: Say, somewhere in the work or its apparatus, what tradition of treatment you are writing in and against. A note is cheap; the alternative is being placed in a tradition you did not choose.

entries.name: Objections From Within the Culture
entries.description: Communities have said, in writing and often specifically, what outsiders may use; those statements are findable and they are not unanimous.
entries.principle: The relevant objections are usually documented — tribal resolutions, statements from cultural offices, published protocols, individual writers on the record — and they are frequently more specific than an outsider expects, permitting some uses and refusing others. They are also not unanimous, and a writer who finds one statement has found one position rather than the community's. Historical's card asks who may speak a tradition; this one asks what has actually been said about your particular use, and requires you to have looked.
entries.example: The public record on Diné witchcraft material contains both scholarly circulation and sustained objection to that circulation, and a writer who has read only the first will not know the second exists. *Skinwalkers* is the case where an outside novelist worked with sustained consultation and was recognised for it by the nation concerned, which is what the other side of that record looks like.
entries.application: Search for what has been said about outside use of your specific material before you search for the material itself. Record what you find, including disagreement, and do not present one voice as the community.

entries.name: Redface, and the DEFA Problem
entries.description: Casting and voice as the site where a work's politics and its practice can point in opposite directions.
entries.principle: The genre's history contains a large body of work in which Indigenous characters are played by non-Indigenous actors, including work whose explicit content is anti-colonial — which is the hardest case, because it cannot be dismissed as indifference. The rule is to hold both facts at once: the argument the work makes and the practice by which it made it, without letting either cancel the other. This is a claim about production rather than about sources, which is what distinguishes it from anything in the archive collection.
entries.example: *Die Söhne der großen Bärin* opens a state-backed cycle with genuinely anti-colonial content and a Serbian actor in the Indigenous lead across most of it. *Broken Arrow* does the same thing from the opposite politics and the opposite production system.
entries.application: If you are writing about these works, write both halves in the same paragraph. If you are making one, notice that the casting will be read as the more reliable statement.

entries.name: The Disputed Identity Claim
entries.description: Live disputes about a creator's ancestry, handled as disputes with their disputants named and nothing adjudicated.
entries.principle: The field contains a number of contested claims to Indigenous identity, at various evidentiary temperatures, and the library's rule holds: state the dispute, name who is disputing and on what basis, give the range of positions, and adjudicate nothing. What makes this different from an ordinary contested biography is that the standing of the claim bears directly on how the work is read, so the dispute cannot simply be omitted as gossip.
