entries.example: *The Education of Little Tree* is the settled end of the range — published in 1976 as a Cherokee memoir by a man who had been an Alabama Klan organiser and a speechwriter for George Wallace, which is established rather than disputed. At the other end sit claims challenged by tribal organisations, claims defended by their subjects, and claims where the documentary evidence has moved more than once, including in 2024.
entries.application: Give both sides a source. A contested card with only one side sourced does not ship, and that rule protects the subject as often as it protects the reader.

entries.name: The Finding the Subject Accepted
entries.description: A third category the library did not previously have: an identity claim investigated, found unsupported, and acknowledged by the person who made it.
entries.principle: Between a live dispute and an established fabrication there is a case the library had no shape for — a formal finding of no ancestry that the subject publicly accepts. It is not a dispute, because nobody is contesting it; it is not a fabrication in the Forrest Carter sense, because there is no evidence of deliberate imposture and the subject has not defended the claim. The card states the finding, states the acceptance, and stops, and the pack treats it as its own category rather than forcing it into one of the other two.
entries.example: In 2025 the Tribal Alliance Against Frauds found no Indigenous ancestry for the author of *Green Grass, Running Water*, and he publicly accepted the finding. That obliges every pack in this library which cards him as Indigenous to be corrected, which is why the category matters beyond the individual case.
entries.application: If your source describes someone as Indigenous, check whether that description has been examined recently. The category is new and the record is moving.

entries.name: Consultation Is Not Permission
entries.description: What consultation actually requires, and the three ways the industry's version of it falls short.
entries.principle: Consultation means a named person with standing, engaged early enough to change the story, credited and paid at a professional rate. The three common substitutes are a late read for reassurance, an individual treated as authorised to speak for a nation, and a credit without authority. And consultation, even done properly, does not confer permission: a consultant can tell you what is accurate without telling you that it is yours to write. Historical's card asks who may speak a tradition; this one asks what a working relationship with a community obliges you to do.
entries.example: *Dance Hall of the Dead* belongs to a body of work built on sustained consultation over decades, for which the Navajo Nation named its author a Special Friend of the Dineh in 1987 — the standard, and rare precisely because it took decades. *Prey* is the screen equivalent, with a Comanche and Blackfeet producer credited on the production rather than consulted on a finished script.
entries.application: Ask whether your consultant can change the plot. If not, do not describe the work as consulted — and do not treat a yes on accuracy as a yes on entitlement.

entries.name: Restricted Material
entries.description: Some knowledge is held under protocols that determine who may know it, and publication does not release it.
entries.principle: Ceremony, song, sacred narrative, medicine practice and certain names are governed by rules about who may hold and transmit them, and those rules do not lapse because an outsider printed the material in 1904. The craft consequence is practical: a plot that requires restricted material to function needs redesigning, and redesigning it is ordinary work. The substitution that almost always improves the story is obligation for ceremony, because an obligation has two parties and a ritual has an audience.
entries.example: *Winter Counts* builds a crime plot on jurisdiction and obligation rather than on ceremony, and *The Only Good Indians* runs its whole causal engine on a broken hunting duty — which is both safer and more dramatic than anything a ritual would have supplied.
entries.application: If your climax needs a ceremony, replace it with an obligation and see what improves. This is the point at which the ethical constraint and the craft advice are the same advice.

entries.name: The Card as a Craft Warning
entries.description: The test this whole section is written to satisfy, stated as a test.
entries.principle: A reference entry about a living culture should leave its reader better informed about why the standard genre treatment fails, and worse equipped to repeat it. That is the opposite of a stat-block: the material is not being supplied for use, it is being supplied so the writer understands the terms on which it might be used, or declines. A card that reads as a menu has failed the test regardless of how respectful its language is.
entries.example: *Bone Tomahawk* is the case the test is for: a technically accomplished film whose antagonists are constructed so as to be deniable, and which a reader of a merely respectful card would be no better equipped to think about. The library's Horror pack sets this standard in its folklore collection, and the question is the same — does the reader finish better armed to write the cliché, or less willing to?
entries.application: Read your own draft card back and ask what it enables. If it hands a writer a usable device with a caution attached, rewrite it until the caution is the device.

entries.name: What the Italian Cycle Keeps and Drops
entries.description: The clearest natural experiment in the genre: the same iconography with the settlement argument removed.
entries.principle: The Italian cycle retains the hats, the standoffs, the desert town and the professional gunman, and drops the claim to ground, the civic justification and the law that follows — substituting money as the object and leaving the violence with nothing to purchase. That combination is what produces the cycle's characteristic nihilism, and it is also what makes it useful analytically: it shows exactly how much of the western's moral weight was carried by the argument rather than by the furniture.
entries.example: *Django* substitutes a coffin of gold for any claim to ground. *Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo* makes the Civil War a removable backdrop to a treasure hunt.
entries.application: If your story's violence has no civic result, you are working inside this cycle whether or not you meant to be, and the audience will supply its conventions.

entries.name: The Ostern's Relocation of the Argument
entries.description: Two Eastern Bloc traditions, routinely merged, in which the contested authority is revolutionary rather than juridical.
entries.principle: The East German Indianerfilme relocate sympathy to the Indigenous side and deliver anti-colonial content as state policy; the Soviet Ostern proper mostly leaves North America entirely and puts the form in the Russian Civil War and Central Asia, where what is contested is which order will govern rather than who holds a valley. Both keep the genre's machinery and replace its politics, and merging them — as most Anglophone accounts do — loses the more interesting of the two.
entries.example: *Die Söhne der großen Bärin* opens the DEFA cycle as an answer to the West German Karl May films. *Beloye solntse pustyni* moves the whole apparatus to the Caspian and makes revolutionary authority the thing in dispute.
entries.application: Say which Ostern you mean. And notice what the Soviet line demonstrates: the western's structure survives the removal of America entirely.

entries.name: The Nordestern's Inversion of the Antagonist
entries.description: The Brazilian tradition in which the threat is the landowner and the drought, and the bandit is resistance.
entries.principle: The nordestern keeps the horse, the rifle, the hard sun and the walk down a dirt street, and inverts the antagonist: the danger is the latifundio, the colonel and the weather rather than an Indigenous nation or an outlaw. The consequence is that banditry reads as a political response rather than as criminality, and the ballad-singing narrator functions as a rival historical record rather than as atmosphere. It is the single strongest demonstration that the genre's iconography is politically detachable.
entries.example: *Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol* hands the narration to a cantador so the film is structured as a ballad being sung. *Bacurau* restages the whole tradition against a foreign hunting party and lets the village answer.
entries.application: Ask who owns the land before you decide who fires first. A story in this tradition that makes the bandit merely criminal has adopted the landowner's account.

entries.name: The Two-Way Traffic With Japanese Cinema
entries.description: An exchange documented on both sides, in which neither tradition is the other's source.
entries.principle: The relevant Japanese material is not period drama in general but the chanbara and the wandering-gambler film, whose masterless swordsman occupies the western's drifter position: skill without a place, arriving where he is needed and unable to remain. The traffic runs both ways and is documented — one crossing produced a licensing chain, another produced litigation — and treating either side as merely derivative misdescribes a genuine conversation.
entries.example: *Shichinin no samurai* became *The Magnificent Seven* through a rights chain, and *Yojimbo* went the other way into the Italian cycle through a suit that Toho won. *Sukiyaki Western Django* closes the loop by making the borrowing its subject.
entries.application: Borrow the structure, not the costume. What transfers is the masterless professional and the town that needs him; what does not is a legal and social order your reader will read wrongly.

entries.name: The Australian Western's Own Dispossession
entries.description: A second settler frontier that reached the form independently, and where the counter-tradition is strongest.
entries.principle: Australia has its own bushranger legend, its own pastoral economy and its own dispossession, arrived at without borrowing the American vocabulary, so the iconography differs while the claim is identical — which makes it the best available control on what is specific to the American myth and what belongs to settlement itself. Its centre of gravity has moved decisively toward Indigenous authorship, so the counter-western there is not marginal but central.
entries.example: *Sweet Country* and *The Drover's Wife: The Legend of Molly Johnson* work the same country from Indigenous positions. *The Proposition* imports the American revisionist grammar deliberately and says so.
entries.application: Do not transplant American furniture into this setting. The legal instruments, the economy and the terms of dispossession all differ, and the differences are the material.

entries.name: The Northern's Inversion: Law Arrives First
entries.description: The Canadian tradition whose organising premise removes the American form's central condition.
entries.principle: The Northern was for decades a rival label rather than a subgenre, and it runs on the premise that the mounted police reached the west ahead of large-scale settlement, so the story cannot turn on the absence of law. What replaces it is a frontier of extraction and endurance where the antagonist is climate and distance and the moral question is obedience rather than jurisdiction. Historians qualify the premise heavily; the tradition runs on it regardless, which is itself the useful fact.
entries.example: *The Grey Fox* imports an American train robber into a country that is already administered, and the whole film runs on his discovery that there is nowhere in it to be an outlaw. The Yukon endurance fiction fixes the climate frontier for a mass audience alongside it.
entries.application: If you set a western in Canada, establish what the law already is before Chapter One. Writing it as an American west with snow is the tradition's characteristic misuse.

entries.name: The Dacoit Film's Synthesis
entries.description: India's own frontier form, and the 1970s film that absorbed the American and Italian westerns without becoming either.
entries.principle: The dacoit film has its own banditry, landscape and social grievance, and its characteristic structure is a village under predation hiring outsiders — so the settlement argument arrives as a question about protection and vengeance rather than about title. When it absorbed the American and Italian cycles it kept its own moral economy, which is why the result is a synthesis rather than an adaptation.
entries.example: *Sholay* carries its acquisitions on the surface — the hired-defenders structure, the Italian cycle's iconography and scoring, set-pieces answering Leone — and remains a dacoit film in its obligations and its ending.
entries.application: Treat the borrowing as a two-way claim. A tradition that takes what it needs and keeps its own ending has not been colonised by the form; it has used it.

entries.name: The Production System That Made Export Possible
entries.description: The infrastructure behind the myth's travel: locations, co-production money, post-synchronisation and Anglicised names.
entries.principle: The international western exists because of a specific industrial arrangement — Spanish and Italian locations standing in for the American southwest, co-production treaties routing money across three or four countries, international casts speaking their own languages on set and dubbed entirely afterwards, and directors and composers billed under Anglicised pseudonyms so the product would read as American. That system explains the cycle's reliance on faces, gesture and music, and it means no version of many of these films is the original.
entries.example: *Per un pugno di dollari* exists in versions that differ in dialogue and running time with no authoritative cut, and was released with its director and composer billed under Anglicised names — both direct consequences of the production system rather than accidents of distribution.
entries.application: If you are quoting this style, notice you are quoting a sound produced by dubbing. On the page the equivalent is dialogue with no regional texture at all, which can be an effect and is usually an accident.

entries.name: The Myth as an Export Commodity
entries.description: What travelled, what did not, and what that tells you about which parts of the myth are load-bearing.
entries.principle: Exported, the western reliably keeps its iconography, its professional protagonist and its public reckoning, and reliably loses its specific historical claim — the American settlement argument does not survive translation because the audience has no stake in it. What arrives in its place is whatever the receiving tradition has instead: revolution, banditry against landowners, colonial dispossession, or nothing at all. That pattern is the strongest available evidence about which elements of the myth are structural and which are local.
entries.example: The Italian cycle drops the claim and substitutes money; the nordestern substitutes the landowner; the Ostern substitutes revolutionary authority; *Sholay* substitutes obligation to a village.
entries.application: When you borrow from another tradition, work out what it put in the place of the American claim. Copying the surface without the substitute produces a western about nothing, which is the second mode arrived at by accident.

entries.category: Guns, and What They Actually Did
entries.name: The Single-Action Revolver Holds Five
entries.description: The genre's central object, carried safely, holds five rounds and not six.
entries.principle: The Colt Single Action Army of 1873 and its contemporaries have no transfer bar and no hammer block, so a blow on the hammer can fire a chambered round. Anyone who carried one daily carried it with the hammer down on an empty chamber, which means five. The exception is a man who has just loaded in expectation of trouble, and that exception is itself a scene: loading the sixth chamber is a decision the reader can watch him make.
entries.example: The B-unit tradition's bottomless revolver is the single most recognisable marker of the second mode, and it is a marker precisely because everyone who has handled the weapon knows the count.
entries.application: Track ammunition in your outline the way you track time of day. A man who is empty has a problem the reader can count, which is worth more than any amount of described marksmanship.

entries.category: Guns, and What They Actually Did
entries.name: The Reload Is Slow, and That Is the Scene
entries.description: Reloading a period revolver takes far longer than the genre allows, and the delay is a gift rather than a constraint.
entries.principle: A cartridge revolver is reloaded one round at a time through a loading gate, with the ejector rod clearing each spent case first — a deliberate operation measured in tens of seconds under no pressure and considerably longer under any. Before metallic cartridges it is worse: a cap-and-ball revolver is a five-minute proposition, which is why men who expected trouble carried two guns or spare loaded cylinders rather than reloading in a fight.
entries.example: Stories that give a character an unbroken volley have removed the only natural pause a gunfight contains, which is why so many of them have to invent one.
entries.application: Put the reload in the scene. It is the western's equivalent of the empty magazine and it produces the same thing — a forced choice under a clock.

entries.category: Guns, and What They Actually Did
entries.name: What a Pistol Could Actually Reach
entries.description: The effective range of a revolver is short enough to change the geography of every confrontation.
entries.principle: A period revolver in trained hands is reliable at conversational distance and increasingly a matter of luck beyond it; a rifle out-ranges it by an order of magnitude. That gap governs the shape of western violence: pistol work is close, sudden and usually indoors or in a street, while anything at distance is rifle work, which means ambush, cover and patience rather than confrontation. A story that lets pistols reach across a valley has erased the distinction the genre's set pieces are built on.
entries.example: The walk-down exists as a form precisely because the weapons involved require the parties to come within a few dozen paces of one another, in the open, in front of witnesses.
entries.application: Decide the weapon before you decide the distance, and let the weapon set the staging. Most implausible western action is a range error rather than a marksmanship error.

entries.category: Guns, and What They Actually Did
entries.name: The Repeater, the Single-Shot and Who Had Which
entries.description: Rifle technology moved fast in this period and was distributed unevenly, often to the disadvantage of the side with the budget.
entries.principle: Lever-action repeaters were commercially available from the 1860s and were bought by anyone who could afford them, while the United States Army issued a single-shot breechloader for decades on grounds of ammunition economy and long-range accuracy. The result is a recurring and well-documented situation in which private citizens, ranch hands and Indigenous fighters carried faster weapons than the soldiers opposing them. The buffalo rifle is a third category again — heavy, slow, and lethal at a distance neither of the others could reach.
entries.example: The genre routinely arms everyone identically, which flattens the most interesting asymmetry available in a period firefight.
entries.application: Give each side a specific weapon and let the difference set the tactics. Rate of fire against range is a better engine than courage against cowardice.

entries.category: Guns, and What They Actually Did
entries.name: Black Powder Marks Your Position
entries.description: Until the 1890s every shot produced a cloud, and the cloud is a plot device.
entries.principle: Black powder produces dense white smoke and heavy fouling, so a concealed shooter is concealed exactly once, a sustained exchange fills a street or a room with smoke that obscures everyone, and a weapon fired repeatedly becomes progressively harder to work. Smokeless powder arrives commercially at the end of the century, which means most of the genre's period is fought under the older condition and the transition itself is dateable.
entries.example: The clean, clear-aired gunfight is a convention of the smokeless era projected backwards, and it removes both the concealment problem and the fouling one.
entries.application: Fire the first shot and then ask what everyone can see. In an enclosed fight the answer after three or four rounds is very little, and that is usually more interesting than accuracy.

entries.category: Horses, Distance and What a Day Costs
entries.name: What a Horse Costs to Keep
entries.description: The animal is a continuous expense and a continuous constraint, not a vehicle that waits outside.
entries.principle: A working horse needs grazing time or carried feed, substantial daily water, rest, shoeing and attention to its back and feet, and the requirement does not pause because the plot is urgent. Grain lets an animal work harder than grass alone, which is why forage is a logistical problem rather than a background fact. War's combat cards on fodder and march rates cover the column's version of this; the western's version is the single rider and the small party, where there is nobody to carry the feed.
entries.example: A story in which horses are picketed overnight without water or grazing and ridden hard the next morning has spent an animal it does not know it has lost.
entries.application: Give every animal in your story a feed and water plan for each day it works. The plan will constrain your route, and the constraint is the plot.

entries.category: Horses, Distance and What a Day Costs
entries.name: A Day's Ride Is Shorter Than You Think
entries.description: The genre's most common technical error is a factor of two or three on distance.
entries.principle: A horse moving at a working pace covers ground at a rate closer to a fast walk sustained than to a gallop, and a day's travel for a rider who intends to ride again tomorrow is measured in the low tens of miles rather than the high ones. Pushing beyond that is possible once, at a cost, and the cost is the animal. This single figure governs who can arrive in time, how far help is, how long a body lies undiscovered, and whether a threat two days out is credible.
entries.example: The chase that covers a hundred miles between dawn and dusk is the genre's standing impossibility, and it is invisible only because everyone repeats it.
entries.application: Draw the map, put times on the routes, and only then write the pursuit. The working-day figure is the most useful number in this collection.

entries.category: Horses, Distance and What a Day Costs
entries.name: The String, the Remuda and Why Riders Change Horses
entries.description: Working outfits solved the endurance problem by carrying spare animals, which is why a drive moves a herd of horses too.
entries.principle: A cowhand on a drive did not have a horse; he had a string of them, and changed mounts through the day according to the work — one for night herding, one for cutting, one for rough country. The remuda is therefore a second herd requiring its own handler, and the whole arrangement exists because no single animal can do a day's work. Cavalry, stage lines and express riders solved the same problem with relays and remounts.
entries.example: A lone rider with one horse is the genre's most-used figure and its least representative, and stories that put him on a long journey usually have to break the animal's biology to get him there.
entries.application: Decide whether your character can change horses. If they cannot, their range is a day's ride and their plot has to fit inside it.

entries.category: Horses, Distance and What a Day Costs
entries.name: The Horse as Property, and Horse Theft as a Capital Matter
entries.description: Taking a man's horse in this country was understood as endangering his life, and the law and the custom reflected that.
entries.principle: In an environment where distance is lethal, an animal is not merely valuable but load-bearing for survival, and horse theft accordingly attracted penalties and extra-legal responses out of proportion to the property value. That reasoning is worth knowing precisely because it is the same reasoning the vigilance committees used about everything else: the argument is always that ordinary remedies are too slow for a country this size.
entries.example: The genre's summary hangings for horse theft are not an invention, and the argument advanced for them is the one Judge Henry makes at length in *The Virginian*.
entries.application: If your story turns on a stolen horse, let a character make the survival argument out loud. It converts a property crime into an attempted killing, which is how the period understood it.

entries.category: Horses, Distance and What a Day Costs
entries.name: Cavalry Horse Management, and Where War Owns It
entries.description: The column's version of the same physics, which the War pack already holds.
entries.principle: Mounted troops move at the rate of their slowest element and their range is set by forage rather than by the men, which the war-military pack covers in its cards on the horse-drawn army running on fodder and on march rates being set by the road. Western does not restate them. What this pack adds is the campaign's asymmetry: a cavalry column tied to grain, wagons and a supply line, pursuing parties who could change mounts, live off the country and disperse, which is why the pursuit narratives in this genre so often end in exhaustion rather than in contact.
entries.example: The recurring pattern of Indian Wars campaigning is a column that cannot catch what it is chasing and a winter camp that cannot move, and both facts are logistical rather than tactical.
entries.application: If you are writing a campaign, work out the forage before the tactics — and cite War's cards rather than rewriting them, because that pack owns the column.

entries.category: The Cattle Economy: Money, Labour and the Drive
entries.name: What a Drive Cost and What It Earned
entries.description: The arithmetic that made the great drives worth doing, and the reason they stopped.
entries.principle: The drives existed because cattle were worth several times more at a railhead than in south Texas, and the margin covered a crew, a cook, a horse herd and months of risk. The numbers matter to a story because they determine everything else: the size of the herd sets the size of the crew, the crew's wages set the outfit's tolerance for delay, and the price at the far end is set by a market the characters cannot see and will not learn about until they arrive.
entries.example: *Butcher's Crossing* takes the same structure into hides and lets the market collapse while the party is out of contact, which is the honest version of the risk every drive carried.
entries.application: Fix your prices at both ends and your crew's wages before you write the route. The margin is the story's tolerance for everything that goes wrong.

entries.category: The Cattle Economy: Money, Labour and the Drive
entries.name: The Crew, and Who Was Actually In It
entries.description: The working outfit was more mixed than the genre shows, and the most-cited figures come with a caveat attached.
entries.principle: The most frequently quoted estimates put roughly a quarter of the hands on the great drives as Black and a further eighth as Mexican, with Richard Slatta noting that these are the highest figures on offer and rest on thin documentation. The safe statement is the negative one: no serious estimate supports an all-white outfit, the vaquero tradition is the source of the equipment and much of the vocabulary, and the classical western's crews are a selection rather than a record.
entries.example: *Night Song* and *The Harder They Fall* work from the documented presence rather than from the convention, and neither has to invent anyone to do it.
entries.application: Build your outfit from the labour market rather than from the films. And when you use a figure, use it with its caveat — the estimates are contested and a card that states one flatly will be wrong in one direction or the other.

entries.category: The Cattle Economy: Money, Labour and the Drive
entries.name: The Chuckwagon, the Cook and the Order of the Day
entries.description: A drive is a moving camp with a fixed routine, and the routine is where the ensemble writing lives.
entries.principle: The outfit runs on a schedule — night guard in shifts, breakfast before light, the herd strung out and moving by dawn, a nooning, a bedground chosen for water and grass before dark — and the cook, who drives the wagon, arrives ahead and outranks almost everyone in practice. That structure supplies a working day the reader can learn, which is what makes the interruptions legible.
entries.example: *The Log of a Cowboy* is the procedural baseline and is unliterary on purpose; its authority is entirely in the order of the day.
entries.application: Establish the routine in the first fifty pages so the reader knows what normal looks like. Every disaster in this material is a deviation from a schedule, and a reader who does not know the schedule cannot feel it.

entries.category: The Cattle Economy: Money, Labour and the Drive
entries.name: Trails, Railheads and Why the Map Moved
entries.description: The routes were commercial infrastructure that shifted year by year as railways, quarantines and settlement changed the arithmetic.
entries.principle: A trail exists because a railhead exists, and railheads moved west and north as track was laid and as Kansas counties enacted quarantine laws against Texas fever that pushed the herds further from settlement each season. So the route is dated: a drive in one year and a drive five years later go to different towns by different ground for reasons that are legal and epidemiological rather than geographical.
entries.example: The shift from one shipping point to the next is the reason a boom town in this material has a lifespan measured in a handful of seasons.
entries.application: Fix your year first, then your railhead, then your route. Getting this wrong is the error a reader who knows the material will catch on the first page.

entries.category: The Cattle Economy: Money, Labour and the Drive
entries.name: How the Drives Ended
entries.description: The open-range cattle economy did not decline gradually; it was closed by wire, law, weather and track within about a decade.
entries.principle: Four things ended it more or less together: barbed wire made enclosure cheap, quarantine laws closed routes, railways reached the producing country so the cattle no longer had to walk, and a catastrophic winter in the mid-1880s destroyed herds that had been stocked far beyond what the range could carry. The elegiac register of the late western is not a mood; it is a response to a documented economic collapse with a date.
entries.example: *Lonesome Dove* is set precisely in the closing window and spends its length discovering that the venture was already obsolete.
entries.application: If your story mourns the passing of this world, know which of the four causes you are mourning. They have different villains and different politics.

entries.name: Barbed Wire and the Cost of Enclosure
entries.description: A cheap manufactured good that reorganised property across half a continent inside twenty years.
entries.principle: Before cheap wire, fencing a large holding in a country without timber was economically impossible, which is why open range was a custom rather than a choice. Once wire was mass-produced the calculation reversed, and the resulting conflicts — including organised fence-cutting campaigns serious enough to require legislative response — are about who bears a cost rather than about lawlessness. The wire also closed trails, cut stock off from water, and did both without anyone having to confront anyone.
entries.example: *The Sea of Grass* writes the collision as an argument between two legitimate uses that the country itself eventually settles.
entries.application: Date your fence. Wire before it was cheap is a rich man's statement; wire after it was cheap is ordinary practice, and the difference tells the reader what kind of antagonist they have.

entries.name: Water Development: Wells, Windmills and Tanks
entries.description: Most of the range was unusable until someone lifted water to it, and the lifting is capital.
entries.principle: Grass without accessible water carries no stock, so the effective map of a ranching country is a map of its water, and developing water — drilling, pumping, tanking, piping — requires money that a homesteader does not have and a company does. This is the quiet mechanism by which large holdings assembled themselves out of small ones without a shot: control the water and the surrounding land has no value to anyone else.
entries.example: *The Big Country* makes a river the actual prize, and the reason the families cannot simply go elsewhere is that elsewhere has no water.
entries.application: Put the water on your map before the boundaries. Then work out who paid to develop it, because that is who really holds the country.

entries.name: Stocking Rates and the Die-Up
entries.description: Grass is a finite annual crop, and the industry's founding disaster was arithmetic rather than weather.
entries.principle: A given range supports a given number of animals in a given year, and the open-range boom of the 1880s was financed on the assumption that it supported more. Overstocked country produced animals in poor condition going into winter, and a severe winter then killed them at a scale that broke companies and ended careers. The weather is the proximate cause and the stocking rate is the actual one, which is the distinction most fiction on the subject misses.
entries.example: The winter that ended the boom is the event the entire elegiac western is written after, and it is the closest thing the genre has to a dateable catastrophe.
entries.application: Decide how many animals your range carries and let a character be wrong about it. Ruin by optimism is a better story than ruin by blizzard.

entries.name: Grazing the Public Domain
entries.description: For most of the genre's period the biggest ranches ran their stock on land nobody owned, which is what made the empires possible and unstable.
entries.principle: An outfit that ran thousands of animals typically owned only the deeded ground around its water and used the surrounding public domain by custom and by force, which meant its holding was enormous, unrecorded and legally indefensible against anyone who filed on the right quarter section. That combination explains both the scale of the cattle empires and their vulnerability to a single homesteader with a patent and a stubborn streak.
entries.example: *Shane*'s cattleman has the better custom and the worse paperwork, which is the whole shape of the range-war plot.
entries.application: Separate what your rancher owns from what he uses. The gap between the two is where every threat in the story comes from.

entries.category: Law, Jurisdiction and Who Could Arrest Whom
entries.name: Four Offices, Four Jurisdictions
entries.description: Town marshal, county sheriff, deputy US marshal and constable are different jobs with different powers, and the genre collapses them.
entries.principle: A town marshal is hired by a council and his authority stops at the town limits. A county sheriff is elected, serves civil process and runs the jail across a much larger area. A deputy United States marshal is appointed federally, works enormous districts and enforces federal law rather than local ordinance. A constable is a minor township officer. They are not ranks in one hierarchy, and a character who moves between them is changing employers, territory and legal powers rather than being promoted.
entries.example: *Warlock* puts an elected office, a hired town office and a federal one in the same street and gets an entire novel out of the incompatibility.
entries.application: Pick the office before you write the badge. The question of whether your protagonist can lawfully make this arrest, here, over this person, is usually more interesting than whether he can win the fight.

entries.category: Law, Jurisdiction and Who Could Arrest Whom
entries.name: Paid by the Fee, Not by the Month
entries.description: Federal lawmen were compensated by mileage and service fees rather than salary for most of the period, which shaped who they arrested and how far they travelled.
entries.principle: A deputy marshal earning fees for serving process, mileage for travel and a share on certain arrests has an economic interest in which warrants he takes, how far he rides and how many prisoners he brings back alive — and no interest at all in cases that will not pay. This is not corruption but a structure, and it produces exactly the incentives it looks like it produces. Salaries came late.
entries.example: A deputy working the Indian Territory out of a federal court was covering an area larger than several states on a fee schedule, with a wagon, a cook and a guard, and the economics of that trip determine everything about who he arrests.
entries.application: Work out what your lawman is paid for. The fee structure is a plot generator and it costs nothing to establish.

entries.category: Law, Jurisdiction and Who Could Arrest Whom
entries.name: Federal, Territorial and Tribal Jurisdiction
entries.description: Who may prosecute a crime in Indian Country has depended on the identity of the parties and the nature of the offence, and it changed by statute during the genre's period.
entries.principle: Jurisdiction has turned on whether the accused and the victim are Indigenous, whether the offence is on tribal land, and whether the offence appears on a federal list — a structure established in the 1880s after a Supreme Court decision found that federal courts lacked authority over an offence between two tribal members, and modified repeatedly since. The practical consequence in fiction and in life is gaps: categories of offence that in practice nobody prosecutes.
entries.example: *Winter Counts* builds a present-day crime novel on precisely that gap, which is not a historical curiosity but a current condition.
entries.application: Establish who your victim and your accused are, and where the offence happened, before you decide who investigates. In this material those three facts determine the entire remainder of the plot.

entries.category: Law, Jurisdiction and Who Could Arrest Whom
entries.name: What a Trial Actually Looked Like
entries.description: Courts existed, functioned and were slow, distant and formal, which is the opposite of the genre's usual assumption.
entries.principle: The frontier had grand juries, indictments, defence counsel, appeals and a documentary record, and the reason so much of the genre's violence happens outside them is distance and delay rather than absence. A federal district might cover a territory the size of a country with one judge, so the gap between an offence and a trial is measured in months and hundreds of miles — which is the actual argument the vigilance committees made, and it was not a stupid one.
entries.example: *True Grit* opens with the machinery working — a court, a hanging, deputies with warrants — and the plot consists of leaving it behind.
entries.application: Establish that the court exists and then make it far away. That is both accurate and a better engine than pretending there is no law at all.

entries.category: Bodies: Wounds, Medicine, Food and Weather
entries.name: The Gunshot Wound Before Antisepsis
entries.description: Surviving being shot is a matter of weeks with a fever in the middle, and the timetable restructures your plot.
entries.principle: Antiseptic practice was published in the late 1860s and adopted slowly and unevenly, so for much of the genre's period the danger is infection rather than the wound. A limb hit may be survivable and may cost the limb; an abdominal wound is usually fatal and slowly; and everything in between involves days of fever during which the patient is helpless and someone must stay. That obligation to stay is the most useful thing this collection can give a writer.
entries.example: The shoulder wound healed across a scene transition is the genre's standing evasion, and it throws away a week of story and a change in the power relations of the cast.
entries.application: Give every significant wound a duration in days, then ask who is obliged to remain. The answer is usually your two-hander.

entries.category: Bodies: Wounds, Medicine, Food and Weather
entries.name: What People Ate, and What It Cost Them
entries.description: The working diet was narrow, heavy and repetitive, and its deficiencies show up in bodies.
entries.principle: Trail and camp food is built around what keeps and travels — salt pork, beans, flour, dried fruit, coffee — with fresh meat when something is killed and vegetables rarely. The consequences are real and dateable: scurvy on long expeditions, dental disease, and a general narrowness that makes any variation a genuine event. Food is also money, and an outfit's provisioning is one of the clearest ways to show what it can afford.
entries.example: The cook's authority on a drive derives directly from this, which is why he outranks men who are nominally senior to him.
entries.application: Write one meal properly and let the rest be shorthand. Readers calibrate a whole economy from a single accurate description of what is in the pot.

entries.category: Bodies: Wounds, Medicine, Food and Weather
entries.name: Cold, Heat and the Water Requirement
entries.description: The environment kills on a schedule that a writer can and should know.
entries.principle: A person working in heat needs water measured in gallons a day and degrades quickly without it; cold kills faster than most fiction allows, especially when wet and windy; and both conditions impair judgement well before they impair the body, which is the dramatically useful part. Weather in this genre should function as a clock rather than as atmosphere, and the clock has real numbers behind it.
entries.example: *Meek's Cutoff* runs its entire plot on the water requirement and makes the party's degrading judgement the actual subject.
entries.application: Give your characters a water plan and then break it. Poor decisions made by dehydrated people are more interesting and more accurate than poor decisions made by stupid ones.

entries.category: Bodies: Wounds, Medicine, Food and Weather
entries.name: Disease Killed More People Than Anyone Shot
entries.description: The genre's ratio of violent to non-violent death is inverted relative to the record.
entries.principle: Cholera, dysentery, typhoid, tuberculosis and childbirth killed overwhelmingly more people on the trails and in the settlements than gunfire did, and the epidemic diseases introduced into Indigenous nations killed on a scale that no armed conflict in the period approaches. A story does not have to be about this to be shaped by it: it determines who is missing from a family, why a wagon company is short-handed, and what everyone is afraid of.
entries.example: *Days Without End* lets characters simply die of disease at the period's actual rates, which is rarer on the page than it should be.
entries.application: Kill someone of something other than violence. It costs a paragraph and it recalibrates the reader's sense of the whole world.

entries.category: How the West Was Made: Production, Location and the Tie-In Economy
entries.name: The B-Unit Economy
entries.description: Most westerns ever made were made cheaply and fast, and the economics explain the content.
entries.principle: The series western was shot in about a week on standing sets and familiar locations, built around a contracted star with a fixed screen personality, and padded with stock footage and musical numbers because both were cheaper than coverage. Every convention people mock in these films — the interchangeable plots, the recycled chases, the hero who never changes — is a production decision rather than a failure of imagination, and the whole apparatus existed to fill a programme slot at a price.
entries.example: The persona is the text in these films and the plot is the delivery mechanism, which is why the strongest of them are the ones that use the constraint rather than fighting it.
entries.application: If you write in this mode, treat the specification as the form. And if you write about the genre, remember that this is the output your generalisations have to survive.

entries.category: How the West Was Made: Production, Location and the Tie-In Economy
entries.name: The Tie-In Economy
entries.description: The singing cowboy existed because of records, radio and merchandise, and the merchandise came first more often than not.
entries.principle: The B-western star was a licensing business with films attached — songs sold records, radio hours sold the persona, and the persona sold hats, guns, lunch boxes and comic books to children — and by the television era the merchandising revenues on a successful western property could exceed the production revenues outright. The content followed the licence: a hero aimed at a family audience does not drink, does not shoot first, and operates under a published code, because a code is a brand specification.
entries.example: The televised revival of a 1930s screen property at the end of the 1940s set off a merchandising boom that is the clearest single demonstration of which end of the business was the tail.
entries.application: Ask who your hero's moral code is for. The genre's most rigid ethics come from its most commercial corner, and that is an interesting fact rather than an embarrassing one.

entries.category: How the West Was Made: Production, Location and the Tie-In Economy
entries.name: Location, the Code and the Wire
entries.description: Three production facts that shaped what the genre could show: where it was filmed, what it was forbidden, and how the horses were fallen.
entries.principle: The western's landscape is a small number of repeatedly used locations, several of them on Indigenous land whose residents were employed as extras and as labour, so the genre's most famous scenery is also a working relationship with the people it usually erased. The Production Code shaped the violence and the miscegenation plots directly. And the falling-horse effects that make the cavalry charges legible were produced by trip wires that killed animals, until the outcry over a western in 1939 produced the industry's animal-welfare regime the following year.
entries.example: The reckoning began with a horse driven off a cliff and drowned for a single shot, and the American Humane Association's film unit followed almost immediately.
entries.application: Know how the effect you are describing was achieved. In a genre this dependent on animals and locations, the production history is part of the material rather than trivia about it.

entries.category: Before the Genre — Captivity, the Dime Novel and the Frontier Thesis
entries.name: Before the Genre: The Captivity Narrative
entries.description: The oldest layer of the inheritance, a century and a half before anything called a western.
entries.principle: The captivity narrative is the earliest sustained American popular form about contact, and it establishes almost everything the western later inherits: the frontier as a moral boundary, the taken woman or child as the thing at stake, the returned captive as a problem, and a theological frame in which suffering at the hands of another people is meaningful. It also establishes the genre's characteristic evidentiary problem, since the narratives were edited, ghost-written and published to argument.
entries.example: Rowlandson's account of 1682 is the founding text and was among the most widely read books in colonial America.
entries.application: If your story has a captivity in it, you are working in a tradition with a documented editorial history. Read what the form was for before deciding what yours is for.

entries.category: Before the Genre — Captivity, the Dime Novel and the Frontier Thesis
entries.name: Cooper and the First Frontier Romance
entries.description: The moment the frontier became a subject for fiction rather than testimony, and the shape it took.
entries.principle: Cooper's Leatherstocking sequence, published across the 1820s and 1830s, converts the captivity material into romance and invents the genre's central figure a full lifetime before the events most westerns depict: a white man competent in Indigenous skills, loyal to a vanishing order, and unable to live in the settlement he protects. The vanishing premise, the noble and ignoble pairing, and the scout who belongs to neither side all arrive fully formed here.
entries.example: The Last of the Mohicans is the template, and the historical pack cards it because its primary contract is a claim about the past.
entries.application: When you reach for the scout or the vanishing premise you are reaching for 1826 rather than 1876. Knowing the date makes the convention easier to use deliberately.

entries.category: Before the Genre — Captivity, the Dime Novel and the Frontier Thesis
entries.name: Beadle, the Story Papers and Industrial Manufacture
entries.description: From 1860 the western is a mass-produced commodity, and the production conditions fix the form.
entries.principle: Beadle's dime novels and the story papers that followed produced western fiction on a schedule at a fixed price, and the constraints — length, incident quota, series continuity, a recognisable hero — did more to standardise the genre's conventions than any author's intention. The traffic ran both ways: real figures were written into fiction while alive, and men afterwards adopted names and outfits the fiction had invented.
entries.example: Deadwood Dick, the Prince of the Road appears in 1877 and is claimed afterwards by several men who had not existed as Deadwood Dick before he was printed.
entries.application: Treat the conventions as commercial artefacts with dates. Almost every one was invented to solve a production problem.

entries.category: Before the Genre — Captivity, the Dime Novel and the Frontier Thesis
entries.name: Turner, 1893
entries.description: A scholarly thesis that gave the myth its intellectual licence and its elegiac register.
entries.principle: Frederick Jackson Turner argued that the frontier had formed American character and democracy and that its closing, which he dated from the 1890 census, ended a formative era. Whatever its standing as history — and it has been comprehensively contested — it supplied the genre with a frame in which the frontier is a process rather than a place taken from people, and its closing a loss rather than a completion. The elegiac tradition runs on it.
entries.example: The Frontier in American History collects the argument, and the late western's sense that something has just ended is downstream of it.
entries.application: The mourning in your story has a source. Knowing it is a thesis rather than a fact lets you decide whether your characters share it.

entries.category: The Wild West Show and the Silent West
entries.name: The Wild West Show, 1883 to 1913
entries.description: Thirty years in which the frontier toured as a live programme, with its participants performing themselves.
entries.principle: The touring show turned recent events into a repeatable running order and employed the people it depicted, including Lakota performers and, for one season, Sitting Bull. It travelled to Europe repeatedly, which is how the iconography reached the audiences that later produced the Italian cycle and the Karl May tradition. It is the most important vector by which the myth became international, and it did so before cinema existed.
entries.example: Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson is the reckoning with it, made ninety years later.
entries.application: If your story is set after 1883 the show exists in its world. Your characters have seen the posters and have an opinion about the version being sold.

entries.category: The Wild West Show and the Silent West
entries.name: The First Screen Westerns
entries.description: The genre is present at the beginning of narrative cinema and supplies it with an early repeatable formula.
entries.principle: The western arrives on screen within a decade of cinema itself, and it does so with its conventions already manufactured by print and by the touring show — so the earliest films are not inventing a form but photographing one. The first screen western star emerges within a few years, and the pattern of a continuing persona built across many short films is established immediately, which is the pattern the whole B-unit tradition later runs on.
entries.example: The Great Train Robbery in 1903 is the commonly cited landmark, and its bandits are conventions rather than people from the first frame.
entries.application: Very little about the screen western's conventions originates on screen. If you are looking for where one came from, look at print first.

entries.category: The Wild West Show and the Silent West
entries.name: Hart, Mix and the Two Silent Traditions
entries.description: Two incompatible versions of the form established in the 1910s and 1920s, and the genre has alternated between them ever since.
entries.principle: The silent era produced a realist strain built on weathered authenticity, moral seriousness and physical plausibility, and a showman's strain built on costume, stunt work, speed and spectacle. Both were commercially successful, and the tension between them — the dirty west against the bright west — is the oldest live argument in the genre and is still running.
entries.example: The realist strain's elaborate period detail and the showman's rhinestone-and-trick-riding version are both fully formed before sound arrives.
entries.application: Decide which tradition you are in. Most disagreements about whether a western is any good turn out to be disagreements about which of these two it should have been.

entries.category: The Wild West Show and the Silent West
entries.name: The Sound Epics and the Retreat into the B-Unit
entries.description: The genre attempted prestige at the arrival of sound, did not recover its costs, and spent a decade as programme filler.
entries.principle: A run of large-budget westerns at the turn of the 1930s failed commercially, and the A-western largely disappeared for most of that decade while the form survived as low-budget series product. This is the origin of a split the genre never lost: a prestige tradition that appears in bursts and a continuous commercial tradition underneath it that never stops.
entries.example: Cimarron takes the Academy's top award for 1930/31 and is followed not by a prestige cycle but by a decade of B-units.
entries.application: The genre's history is not a rise and fall but two traditions running at different rates. Which one you are working in sets your length, your budget and your audience.

entries.category: The B-Unit, the Serial and the Radio West
entries.name: Republic, the Series Star and the Singing Cowboy
entries.description: The 1930s industrial model that produced most of the westerns ever made.
entries.principle: From the mid-1930s a small group of studios produced series westerns built around contracted stars with fixed personalities, shot in about a week, and increasingly organised around music because songs sold records and radio time. The singing cowboy is not a curiosity but the industry's most profitable configuration, and the family audience it was built for is what fixed the moral code these films run on.
entries.example: The Republic model from 1935 pairs a recording and radio career with a film series in which the persona is the product.
entries.application: This is the volume. If your account of the genre does not accommodate the singing cowboy, it is an account of a fraction of it.

entries.category: The B-Unit, the Serial and the Radio West
entries.name: The Serial and the Juvenile West
entries.description: Weekly episodic westerns aimed squarely at children, and the conventions they hardened.
entries.principle: The chapter serial delivered the genre's furniture to a juvenile audience on a weekly cliffhanger structure, which selected hard for legibility: unambiguous hats, unambiguous morality, unlimited ammunition and a hero who cannot be hurt. Many of the conventions later mocked as western clichés are serial conventions specifically, engineered for a nine-year-old arriving mid-run.
entries.example: The masked-hero formula and the bottomless revolver both belong to this tradition rather than to the feature western.
entries.application: Before you mock a convention, work out which audience it was engineered for. Most of them are solutions to a real problem.

entries.category: The B-Unit, the Serial and the Radio West
entries.name: The Radio West
entries.description: Two decades in which the western's most-heard versions had no pictures, and where television's grammar was written.
entries.principle: Network radio carried the genre from the early 1930s, and by the early 1950s it had produced an adult, sound-designed, morally serious western aimed at grown-ups — before television attempted one. The landscape was built entirely in sound effects, the violence was ugly and its aftermath was played, and the property that resulted transferred to television and ran there for two decades.
entries.example: The radio series that began in 1952 and was marketed as an adult western is the direct source of the longest-running western in American television history.
entries.application: Radio is where the television western's grammar comes from. If you are writing about the 1950s screen western, some of the invention happened earlier and in another medium.

entries.category: The B-Unit, the Serial and the Radio West
entries.name: The 1939 Revival
entries.description: A single year in which the A-western returned, and the template it set for two decades.
entries.principle: After a decade in the B-units, a cluster of major-studio westerns appeared in 1939 and re-established the form as prestige product. The template they set — an ensemble in transit, a town under pressure, a landscape shot as an actor, a star persona with moral weight — governs the studio-era western until the early 1960s.
entries.example: Stagecoach is the year's most consequential release and consolidates the screen version so completely that later films quote it rather than the period.
entries.application: When people say the classical western they usually mean the two decades this year opens. Knowing that dates the thing you are revising.

entries.category: The Studio Peak and the Adult Western
entries.name: The Post-War Turn Inward
entries.description: From about 1950 the form relocates its conflict inside the protagonist, and the industry gives the shift a name.
entries.principle: The post-war westerns took the classical machinery and made the gunman's psychology the subject: reputation as a trap, competence as a compulsion, violence as a symptom. Bazin named the tendency the sur-western in 1955 and meant it as a complaint — a western embarrassed by being one — and the complaint is worth keeping as a test even though the films are frequently excellent.
entries.example: The 1950 releases that make reputation itself the antagonist open the cycle, and the 1952 marshal picture is its most argued case.
entries.application: This is the first of the genre's two great self-examinations, and it happens inside the studio system rather than against it.

entries.category: The Studio Peak and the Adult Western
entries.name: The Cavalry Cycle and the Sympathetic-Indian Cycle
entries.description: Two overlapping 1950s cycles that took the genre's central subject seriously and could not get past their own casting.
entries.principle: The cavalry films built the institution with affection and, at their best, indicted its commanders; the sympathetic-Indian films reversed the genre's sympathies, gave Indigenous characters negotiating positions and moral authority, and routed all of it through white actors and a white intermediary's conscience. Both cycles demonstrate that sympathy is not the variable that matters, and both are why this pack retires the label Indian Western.
entries.example: The 1950 releases that make negotiation rather than pursuit the plot are the cycle's opening, and their casting is the cycle's limit.
entries.application: The 1950s tried, within the constraints it accepted. Knowing what it could not do is more useful than knowing that it failed.

entries.category: The Studio Peak and the Adult Western
entries.name: Television Saturation, 1955 to 1962
entries.description: The period when the western was much of what American television was, and what that did to the form.
entries.principle: At the end of the 1950s the western occupied a share of American prime time no genre has held before or since, with dozens of concurrent network series, and the effect was twofold: it exhausted the conventions at enormous speed, and it moved the audience's baseline from the cinema to the living room. The feature western's subsequent turn toward revision is partly a response to a form whose classical version was on television nightly and free.
entries.example: The longest-running of these series began in 1955, ran twenty seasons, and had begun on radio three years earlier.
entries.application: The revisionist western is arguing with television as much as with the studio films, which is why its targets sometimes look like straw men to people who only know the features.

entries.category: The Studio Peak and the Adult Western
entries.name: The Peak and Its End
entries.description: The classical form's last coherent years, and the works that closed them from inside.
entries.principle: By the early 1960s the studio western had produced its own valedictions — films about ageing men, obsolete skills and legends known to be false — so the elegiac register that dominates the rest of the genre's history is established before the revisionist wave arrives. The end of the classical period is internal rather than external, which is the same point the specialist makes about revision generally.
entries.example: The two 1962 releases that treat obsolescence and the printed legend respectively are the classical form examining its own closure.
entries.application: Do not date the genre's self-criticism to 1969. The classical form had already written its own ending twice by 1962.

entries.category: Revision, the Italian Cycle and Collapse
entries.name: The Italian Cycle, 1964 to 1975
entries.description: A decade in which many of the most commercially significant westerns were made in Europe by people with no stake in the American argument.
entries.principle: Beginning in 1964 an Italian-led production system made several hundred westerns using Spanish locations, international casts, co-production financing and post-synchronised sound, keeping the American form's iconography while discarding its settlement argument. Its influence on the American genre is direct and acknowledged, and its economics — cheap, fast, exportable — are why it could take risks the studios could not.
entries.example: The 1964 release that transposed a Japanese film without permission opens the cycle and ends in a suit the Japanese studio won.
entries.application: The cycle is not a parody of the American western and not a tribute to it. It is what the form looks like to people who never believed the contract.

entries.category: Revision, the Italian Cycle and Collapse
entries.name: The American Revision, 1962 to 1976
entries.description: Fifteen years in which the American western reversed its own polarity, in public, with the same machinery.
entries.principle: The revisionist wave kept the form's engineering and changed who the violence served: massacres staged as policy, cavalry campaigns indicted, outlaws given grievances, settlement presented as commerce with an enforcement clause. It coincides with a war, with the Indigenous rights movement, and with a collapse in the studio system's authority, and it is best understood as the genre catching up with criticism it had already made of itself.
entries.example: The 1969 release that stages the largest battle in the genre to purchase nothing at all is the wave's central text.
entries.application: Revision is a fifteen-year period with a politics, not a permanent mode. Writing as though it were the genre's natural state misdates the whole field.

entries.category: Revision, the Italian Cycle and Collapse
entries.name: The Collapse
entries.description: The western effectively stops being a commercial form for roughly a decade, and the reasons are industrial as much as cultural.
entries.principle: By the late 1970s the genre had exhausted its television audience, alienated part of its film audience with the revision, and lost its economic logic as the studios reorganised around wide releases and event pictures. A single catastrophic production at the turn of the 1980s became the marker for the collapse and is still cited as its cause, which overstates one film's role in a decline already well advanced.
entries.example: The 1980 production whose failure is treated as the genre's death certificate was closer to a late symptom than a cause.
entries.application: Be careful with the standard story here. The received account attributes an industry-wide change to one film, which is exactly the kind of received wisdom this pack exists to check.

entries.name: The Revival, 1985 to 1995
entries.description: The genre returns as prestige material, and returns in the revisionist register by default.
entries.principle: A decade of high-profile westerns re-established the form commercially and critically, and they arrived already revisionist — muddier, more compromised, more attentive to the cost — because that was now the register in which the genre could be taken seriously. The consequence is that the reversal became the default within a single cycle, which is why the revisionist move stopped carrying a charge.
entries.example: The 1990 and 1992 releases that took the Academy's top award between them are the revival's landmarks and its two arguments — the sympathetic epic and the indictment.
entries.application: After 1992 the grim western is the expected one. If your story is revising, work out what it is revising, because the classical version has not been the default for a long time.

entries.name: Long-Form Television
entries.description: The genre's current centre of gravity, and the structural change that came with it.
entries.principle: From the late 1980s the most ambitious westerns have increasingly been made at length for television, and the form's mechanics change accordingly: the walk-down loses its finality, the ride-out is deferred indefinitely, and the community becomes the protagonist because it is the only element that persists across a season. The compression that is the western's greatest asset in prose and film has to be rebuilt at the level of the arc.
entries.example: The 1989 miniseries adaptation of a Pulitzer-winning novel demonstrated the audience existed, and the 2004 camp series demonstrated what the length was actually for.
entries.application: If you are writing long-form, decide what persists between seasons. A serialised western organised around one man's arc will run out of arc.

entries.name: The Neo-Western
entries.description: The form moves into the present and finds the same claims with modern instruments.
entries.principle: The neo-western keeps the contested claim to ground and the force that settles it and relocates them to a landscape with banks, leases, agencies and highways — which produces the mode's characteristic engine, a frontier moral vocabulary meeting a system that does not recognise it. It is the descendant of the elegiac western rather than a separate invention, and it is currently the genre's most commercially reliable form.
entries.example: The 2007 adaptation that hands the country to an economy which does not negotiate is the mode's central text; the 2016 bank picture restores the range war with modern instruments.
entries.application: The anachronism is the engine. Nostalgia alone will not power a neo-western, and most of the ones that stall have mistaken the second for the first.

entries.name: The Counter-Western
entries.description: Much of the most vital current work is being made by the people the classical form wrote out, and it is not confined to correction.
entries.principle: Since roughly 2000 the genre's live problems have increasingly been worked by Indigenous, Black and non-American film-makers and writers using the form's machinery from the other side, with specificity in place of the composite and a present tense in place of the vanishing premise. This is not a corrective appendix to the genre but a body of functioning westerns with different assumptions about who the country is for.
entries.example: The 2001 Inuktitut feature, the 2021 comedy series and the 2022 Comanche-language release are three different solutions to the same inherited problem.
entries.application: Read this work before you write your revision. The interesting problems in the genre are further on than most newcomers assume.

entries.name: Where the Form Is Now
entries.description: A genre with a narrow screen pipeline, a substantial independent prose market and an unusually healthy critical conversation.
entries.principle: The current position is uneven: theatrical westerns are made in small numbers and concentrated in a few hands, long-form television is the most active screen venue, trade prose publishing is thin while independent and digital publishing in the genre is substantial, and the critical and scholarly conversation is livelier than at any point since the 1970s. A writer entering the field now faces three distinct markets with three different specifications.
entries.example: The working-writer bodies and their awards — one founded in 1953, one in 2010 — map where the prose market actually is rather than where its reputation puts it.
entries.application: Find out which of the three markets you are writing for before you plan a book. They want different lengths, different content and different pace.

entries.name: Regeneration Through Violence
entries.description: Slotkin's account of the structure underneath the genre, and what kind of claim it is.
entries.principle: Richard Slotkin argued across three volumes from 1973 that American national identity is organised around a repeating story in which contact with the wilderness and violence against its inhabitants produces renewal, and that the western is that story's most efficient vehicle. It explains why the genre's endings feel earned even when its plots do not justify them. It is a literary-historical and cultural-historical argument built from readings of texts, not a psychological finding, and it is marked as such here rather than dressed in the vocabulary of evidence (robustness: literary-historical argument, not an empirical claim).
entries.example: Blood Meridian can be read as the thesis run with the renewal removed, which is why it registers as an attack on the whole structure rather than on any particular film.
entries.application: Ask what your ending renews. If violence in your story produces a settled community, a marriage or a restored inheritance, you are inside this structure and should decide whether you mean to be.

entries.name: Violence Framed as Defensive
entries.description: How a story's framing changes what an audience will accept, and how far the evidence for that actually goes.
entries.principle: People judge the same act very differently depending on whether it is presented as initiated or as retaliatory, and narrative framing is unusually good at supplying the second reading — which is the mechanism the western's necessary-violence claim runs on. The broad finding that framing and prior justification shift moral judgement is well supported; the stronger claims sometimes made about media violence causing real-world aggression are contested and the effect sizes are disputed, so the pack states the first and declines the second (robustness: framing effects robust; media-effects claims contested).
entries.example: The genre reliably shows the antagonist striking first, and the reliability is the tell: it is a structural requirement rather than a plot preference.
entries.application: Notice how often your story arranges for the other side to move first. If it always does, the arrangement is doing moral work you have not argued for.

entries.name: Retributive Justice and Its Appeal
entries.description: Why the reckoning satisfies, and why the satisfaction is durable even in readers who disapprove of it.
entries.principle: The desire to see a wrongdoer suffer proportionately is a well-attested feature of human moral judgement across cultures and appears early in development, and it operates somewhat independently of beliefs about deterrence — people endorse punishment that they do not expect to prevent anything. That is why the walk-down works on audiences who oppose capital punishment, and why the revisionist withholding of it registers as a genuine deprivation rather than as a mere surprise (robustness: robust).
entries.example: Unforgiven is built on the gap between the appetite and the endorsement: it delivers the reckoning and refuses to let the audience feel clean about having wanted it.
entries.application: You can withhold the reckoning, but you cannot pretend the appetite is not there. A story that assumes the reader does not want it will misjudge every scene leading up to it.

entries.category: Belonging, Exile and the Unfit Man
entries.name: The Competent Outsider
entries.description: Why the figure who does not belong is the genre's most durable protagonist.
entries.principle: The outsider with a needed skill is a structurally efficient protagonist: he can be admired without being accountable, he supplies the community's lack, and his position lets the audience hold the society at a critical distance while still wanting it to survive. The pull is a matter of narrative economy and identification rather than a documented psychological need for such figures, and the pack does not claim more than that (robustness: craft observation, not an empirical claim).
entries.example: Shane runs the whole configuration through a child's admiration, which is the most efficient version of it ever built.
entries.application: Ask what your outsider is exempt from. The exemptions are the source of the appeal, and they are also where the story's evasions accumulate.

entries.category: Belonging, Exile and the Unfit Man
entries.name: Tompkins and the Flight from the Sentimental
entries.description: The argument that the western is defined by what it is refusing, and what follows for its treatment of women.
entries.principle: Jane Tompkins argued that the western is constitutively a reaction against the nineteenth-century sentimental novel and against the domestic and religious authority associated with women — which is why its heroes are inarticulate, its interiors are absent, its violence is physical rather than moral, and its women are obstacles or prizes. It is a literary-historical thesis rather than a psychological account of readers, and it is the most productive single idea in the pack's Trope collection (robustness: literary-historical argument, not an empirical claim).
entries.example: The genre's characteristic reticence and its aversion to interiority are, on this reading, the same gesture rather than two conventions.
entries.application: When you write your western's silence, ask what it is refusing. Tompkins's answer is not the only one, but a story with no answer has adopted a position by default.

entries.category: Belonging, Exile and the Unfit Man
entries.name: What the Killing Costs the Killer
entries.description: The genre's intuition that violence damages its agent, and the clinical literature that partly supports it.
entries.principle: The western has always held that the man who kills cannot rejoin the settled world, and there is a real clinical construct in the neighbourhood: moral injury, the lasting damage caused by acts that violate one's own moral code, which is distinguished in the literature from post-traumatic stress and is associated with guilt, shame and withdrawal. The construct is well described and increasingly well measured; its boundaries against related diagnoses are still argued over, and the genre's version is a nineteenth-century intuition rather than a clinical claim (robustness: construct robust, boundaries contested).
entries.example: The ride-out is the genre's image for this, and it predates any clinical vocabulary by a century.
entries.application: If your gunman is undamaged, that is a choice. If he is damaged, choose whether you are writing withdrawal, guilt or fear, because they behave differently on the page.

entries.category: Nostalgia, Loss and the Closed Frontier
entries.name: Two Kinds of Nostalgia
entries.description: The distinction between wanting the past back and dwelling in its irrecoverability, and why the western needs both.
entries.principle: Svetlana Boym distinguished restorative nostalgia, which wants to rebuild the lost home and tends toward the political, from reflective nostalgia, which dwells in longing and loss without expecting return and tends toward the ironic and the personal. The distinction maps almost exactly onto the difference between the political neo-western and the elegiac one, which is why it is worth having (robustness: humanities distinction, not an empirical taxonomy).
entries.example: A story that wants the country restored and a story that mourns it are doing different things, and audiences read the difference as politics whether or not the author intended one.
entries.application: Decide which nostalgia your story is in. Restorative nostalgia in a contemporary western is a political position, and readers will treat it as one.

entries.category: Nostalgia, Loss and the Closed Frontier
entries.name: Nostalgia Does Something
entries.description: The emotion is not simply a malfunction, and the research on it changed direction.
entries.principle: Nostalgia was treated for most of its history as a disorder and has since been studied as a common, largely social emotion associated with increased feelings of belonging, meaning and continuity of self, and often triggered by loneliness or disruption. The core findings replicate reasonably well; the size and durability of the benefits, and how much of the work is done by the social content rather than by the pastness, remain argued (robustness: core findings robust, magnitude contested).
