entries.example: The genre's reliability as comfort reading during periods of social disruption is consistent with this, and is a better explanation of its revivals than any account based on politics alone.
entries.application: Nostalgia is doing something for your reader other than sentiment. Knowing that it supplies continuity and belonging tells you what your elegy has to deliver.

entries.category: Nostalgia, Loss and the Closed Frontier
entries.name: The Closed Frontier as Collective Loss
entries.description: Mourning something nobody in the audience experienced, and why it works anyway.
entries.principle: The genre asks audiences to feel the loss of a world they never inhabited, and the mechanism is that the loss is not really the frontier but whatever the frontier has been made to stand for — autonomy, legibility, a country in which effort and outcome are visibly connected. That substitution is why the elegy transfers so easily across nations and decades, and why the same structure works for audiences with no relation to the American West at all (robustness: craft observation supported by the international transfer of the form).
entries.example: The Ostern, the nordestern and the Australian western all reproduce the elegiac register with entirely different content underneath it.
entries.application: Name what your frontier is standing in for. If you cannot, the elegy will read as generic, because the specificity is in the substitution rather than in the period detail.

entries.category: Myth, National Memory and the Audience
entries.name: Narrative Templates and What an Audience Already Knows
entries.description: Audiences arrive with a shape in their heads, and the shape does most of the work.
entries.principle: Collective memory research describes shared narrative templates — schematic story shapes a culture uses to organise many different events — and the western is one of the most fully specified templates any culture has produced. The consequence for a writer is that the audience supplies enormous amounts of unstated material, which is why the genre can be so compressed, and why deviation registers so strongly (robustness: template concept well established; claims about specific national templates contested).
entries.example: Four bars of score and a silhouette deliver a moral universe before a word is spoken, which no other genre manages at that speed.
entries.application: You are writing into a template. Use the compression it buys you, and remember that everything you do not specify will be filled in with the classical default.

entries.category: Myth, National Memory and the Audience
entries.name: The Legend Persists After the Correction
entries.description: Why printing the legend works, stated as the well-attested effect it is.
entries.principle: Information that has been retracted or corrected continues to influence people's judgements and inferences — the continued-influence effect — and corrections are especially weak when the original account is a coherent story and the correction is merely a denial. This is the mechanism behind the genre's most quoted line, and it explains why the western's own repeated self-corrections have not displaced the version they correct (robustness: robust and widely replicated).
entries.example: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance dramatises the effect sixty years before the literature named it, and the film's own popularity has not displaced the legend it exposes.
entries.application: A correction inside your story will not undo the version the reader arrived with unless you replace it with a story rather than a denial. Supply an alternative account, not a contradiction.

entries.category: Myth, National Memory and the Audience
entries.name: Identification, Transportation and the Difficult Protagonist
entries.description: Why readers absorbed in a story adopt its view, and what that means for a genre with compromised heroes.
entries.principle: Readers absorbed in a narrative are measurably more likely to adopt attitudes consistent with it and less likely to counter-argue while absorbed, and identification with a protagonist increases the effect. In a genre whose protagonists are frequently doing indefensible things competently, this is the central craft problem: absorption is the mechanism by which a story that means to indict can end up recruiting (robustness: transportation and narrative persuasion effects robust; durability over time contested).
entries.example: The Searchers is the standing case — a film whose audience has spent seventy years arguing about whether it indicts its protagonist, precisely because it makes him so absorbing to follow.
entries.application: If your protagonist is doing something the story condemns, build the condemnation into the structure rather than into a speech. Absorption will overwrite the speech.

entries.name: James Fenimore Cooper
entries.description: The novelist who converted the captivity narrative into romance and invented the genre's central figure a lifetime before the West it depicts.
entries.meta: American, 1789–1851. Wrote the Leatherstocking sequence across the 1820s and 1830s, decades before the events most westerns are set among, which is why the genre's oldest conventions predate its subject. Twain's essay on Cooper's literary offences is criticism and is widely quoted as fact; Cooper's own position on dispossession is more equivocal than either his admirers or Twain allow.
entries.knownFor: Natty Bumppo, the scout who belongs to neither side, and the vanishing premise arriving fully formed in fiction before it arrived in policy.
entries.signature: A frontier organised as a moral boundary, with a white protagonist competent in Indigenous skills and loyal to an order the book insists is already ending.

works.title: The Last of the Mohicans
works.note: the template, and the direct ancestor of Karl May and the DEFA cycle

works.title: The Pioneers
works.note: the settlement itself, and the first of the sequence written

works.title: The Prairie
works.note: the scout's death, and the closing of the eastern frontier

entries.name: Owen Wister
entries.description: The Harvard easterner whose one enormous novel supplied the cowboy hero the rest of the genre inherited.
entries.meta: American, 1860–1938. A friend of Theodore Roosevelt; his West is a convalescent's West, observed from outside and idealised accordingly. The pack's named-award trap in full. Wister died in 1938, and the award under either of its names did not exist until 1961, so he cannot have received it under any framing. The Virginian cannot have won a Spur: the WWA's Spur Awards date from the 1950s, and a Spur is dated to the honoured book's year and presented at the following convention, which is why 1953 and 1954 both appear in the record. The pack's standing rule for this award: name what it was called in the year concerned, note that the Owen Wister name dates from 1991 and the Saddleman lineage from 1961, and do not pick between the new-award and renamed-award framings — the WWA's own Owen Wister page lists pre-1991 Saddleman recipients under that heading, which is the body asserting continuity rather than a reference-work error.
entries.knownFor: The Virginian, which fixed the laconic gunman, the schoolteacher from the East, and the walk-down as the form's moral settlement.
entries.signature: A visiting narrator, so the reader is invited to admire the West rather than to live in it, and a hero whose reticence is presented as a moral quality.

works.title: The Virginian
works.note: the founding text of the popular western

works.title: Lin McLean
works.note: the earlier Wyoming stories, where the cowboy is still a comic regional type

works.title: Red Men and White
works.note: the frontier stories that precede the novel

entries.name: Bret Harte
entries.description: The mining-camp story-writer who gave the genre its first mass-market form and its first sentimental machinery.
entries.meta: American, 1836–1902. His Overland Monthly stories won him a contract with the Atlantic that was reported at the time as exceptional; the reputation did not survive his move east. His 1870 dialect poem about a Chinese gambler was taken up by the exclusion movement against his stated intent; the reception inversion is the citable fact rather than the intent.
entries.knownFor: The boom camp as a society with its own rules, and the redemption-by-sentiment ending that the genre spent a century unlearning.
entries.signature: A camp of disreputable men confronted with something innocent, rendered in a knowing narratorial voice that flatters the reader's sophistication.

works.title: The Luck of Roaring Camp
works.note: the camp adopting a child, and the form's commercial breakthrough

works.title: The Outcasts of Poker Flat
works.note: the expelled and what the weather does to them

works.title: Tennessee's Partner
works.note: loyalty as the camp's only enforceable law

entries.name: Mark Twain
entries.description: The founding anti-mythic voice, writing the West as boredom, fraud and failed claims while the myth was being manufactured.
entries.meta: American, 1835–1910. Went west as a young man, failed at silver mining, and turned the failure into the account that runs against the whole subsequent tradition. Roughing It is memoir-shaped and unreliable by design, and should not be cited as a record of material conditions.
entries.knownFor: A frontier of tedium, confidence tricks and worthless claims, narrated by a man cheerfully admitting he was taken in.
entries.signature: A vernacular first person whose comedy is deflationary, aimed squarely at the version of the West being sold to easterners by everyone else.

works.title: Roughing It
works.note: the anti-myth, written while the myth was still being assembled

works.title: The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County
works.note: the camp tall tale as a form

entries.name: Andy Adams
entries.description: The trail hand who wrote the drive from inside it, explicitly to refute the romance Wister had just established.
entries.meta: American, 1859–1935. Worked the trails before he wrote about them, and the difference is visible on every page. The book was written against Wister's romanticism, and naming the target is part of the card. It is also the pack's own admitted-cost case: a western with no contested title question, admitted by stretching force to the market and the weather, with the stretch visible.
entries.knownFor: The procedural baseline for the cattle drive, against which every later account is measured.
entries.signature: Unliterary on purpose — the authority is in the order of the day, the handling of stock, and the absence of a villain.

works.title: The Log of a Cowboy
works.note: the drive as work, with no antagonist and no romance

works.title: The Outlet
works.note: the contract and the market at the far end

entries.name: Frederic Remington
entries.description: The man who manufactured the iconography and then wrote the prose to match it.
entries.meta: American, 1861–1909. Painter, sculptor, illustrator and writer, whose images fixed the visual vocabulary of the West for audiences who would never see it. His racial writing, in letters and in print, is explicit and documented, and his Spanish-American War reporting is unreliable. The card states both alongside the influence rather than instead of it.
entries.knownFor: The composed West — the light, the horizon line, and the idea of what a significant frontier moment looks like.
entries.signature: A frame that selects for emptiness and action, excluding the railways, fences and towns that were already in the country he was painting.

works.title: Pony Tracks
works.note: the reporting and sketches that established the look

works.title: Crooked Trails
works.note: the frontier stories

works.title: The Way of an Indian
works.note: the late attempt at an Indigenous protagonist

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Zane Grey
entries.description: The best-selling western writer of the magazine era, and the market that turned the genre into an industry.
entries.meta: American, 1872–1939. A dentist who became one of the highest-earning novelists of his generation; over a hundred films were made from his work. His racial material is part of the record and the pack names it. The Vanishing American's ending chain is the landmine and must be stated in full: missionary pressure fell on the 1922-23 magazine serial; Grey then wrote a survival-and-marriage ending for the book; Harper's editors substituted a vaguer death for the 1925 book, reportedly without his consent. The protagonist dies in both the serial and the 1925 book; a 1982 edition restores a third state. He died in 1939 and cannot have received a Spur or an Owen Wister Award.
entries.knownFor: Riders of the Purple Sage, and a Utah-set formula of pursuit, canyon country and a gunman who lays the work down.
entries.signature: Landscape as moral force, an outsider heroine, and a plot that resolves through withdrawal into an inaccessible valley rather than through settlement.

works.title: Riders of the Purple Sage
works.note: the defining novel, and the pursuit structure the pulps ran on

works.title: The Heritage of the Desert
works.note: the earlier Utah novel that established the setting

works.title: The Vanishing American
works.note: the book version, whose ending differs from both the serial and Grey's own manuscript

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Max Brand
entries.description: The pulp system's most productive single engine, writing at industrial rate under a long list of pen names.
entries.meta: American, 1892–1944. Born Frederick Schiller Faust; produced fiction at industrial rate across westerns, medical series and adventure — the totals given for both his output and his pen names vary widely between bibliographies, and was killed by shrapnel as a war correspondent in Italy. The pen names are the landmine — Max Brand, Evan Evans, George Owen Baxter and others are all Faust, and bibliographies disagree on attributions. He died on active assignment as a correspondent, not in retirement.
entries.knownFor: Destry Rides Again, and a mythic register that owes more to classical epic than to the frontier record.
entries.signature: Heroic archetype rather than realism — outsized figures, formal cadence, and a deliberate indifference to period accuracy.

works.title: Destry Rides Again
works.note: the novel, which shares little beyond a title with the film

works.title: The Untamed
works.note: the early novel that set the mythic register

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Louis L'Amour
entries.description: The paperback West's defining career, and the settlement argument told as family continuity across three centuries.
entries.meta: American, 1908–1988. Wrote over a hundred books that have remained continuously in print; the Sackett cycle traces one family from seventeenth-century England to the closing of the frontier. The likeliest misattribution in the pack. He received the Saddleman Award in 1981 and died in 1988, so no award can have been presented to him under the Owen Wister name, which dates from 1991; the WWA's own list nonetheless carries him under that heading, and the pack states the year and the name it held then rather than adjudicating the continuity. His Congressional Gold Medal and Presidential Medal of Freedom are real, are not western prizes, and are routinely swapped for one another. His racial material is part of the record, and his account of his own early life is partly unverifiable.
entries.knownFor: Hondo and the Sackett novels, and a body of work that made the western a reliable mass-market category for four decades.
entries.signature: Competence rendered in detail — how a man tracks, camps, fights and survives — with the landscape described by someone who had walked it.

works.title: Hondo
works.note: the novel, published the same year as the film

works.title: The Daybreakers
works.note: the Sackett cycle's opening in the West

works.title: Last of the Breed
works.note: the late novel that moves the survival material to Siberia

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Ernest Haycox
entries.description: The magazine western that raised the form's prose standard, and the direct source of the genre's most consequential film.
entries.meta: American, 1899–1950. Wrote for the mass-circulation weeklies at a time when that was the western's largest market, and commanded serial rates at the top of that market. Stagecoach is based on his story, which is a separate claim from having written it; Dudley Nichols wrote the screenplay.
entries.knownFor: Stage to Lordsburg, the story behind Stagecoach, and a body of cavalry and frontier fiction with unusual attention to structure.
entries.signature: Compression and restraint — an ensemble established fast, a journey under pressure, and a prose surface plainer than his competitors'.

works.title: Stage to Lordsburg
works.note: the story Ford's film is based on

works.title: Trouble Shooter
works.note: the railroad novel

works.title: Bugles in the Afternoon
works.note: the cavalry novel

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Clarence E. Mulford
entries.description: The creator of the character that carried the B-western, the serial and then television, and who bore almost no resemblance to what the screen made of him.
entries.meta: American, 1883–1956. Wrote the Bar-20 stories from a desk in the East, researching obsessively; his creation outlived his version of it by decades. The standard error is conflating the two Cassidys. The novels' character is rough, profane, red-haired and limping; the screen version from 1935 is a different creation aimed at a family audience, and the merchandising fortune belongs to the second.
entries.knownFor: Hopalong Cassidy, and the second mode running across three media on the strength of one character.
entries.signature: A hard, profane, working outfit rendered with heavy research, which the screen adaptation replaced entirely with a clean-living family hero.

works.title: Bar-20
works.note: the outfit, and the original Cassidy

works.title: Hopalong Cassidy
works.note: the character's own novel

works.title: The Coming of Cassidy
works.note: the origin stories

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Edward L. Wheeler
entries.description: The dime novelist who invented a name that real men afterwards claimed as their own.
entries.meta: American, c.1854–1885. Almost nothing about his life is documented and his birth year is variously given as 1854 or 1855; the 1885 death year is not in dispute. He wrote thirty-three Deadwood Dick titles in under a decade. His invented Deadwood Dick collides with Nat Love's later claim to the name; the pack states both and adjudicates neither.
entries.knownFor: Deadwood Dick, the figure that demonstrates the traffic between the manufacture and the record running in both directions.
entries.signature: Serial invention at speed for a fixed price — costume, catchphrase and incident quota, with continuity maintained across dozens of titles.

works.title: Deadwood Dick, the Prince of the Road
works.note: the first of the series, and the name's origin

works.title: Deadwood Dick on Deck
works.note: the sequel that established the run

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Elmore Leonard
entries.description: The western writer who left the form and took its dialogue economy into crime fiction, and whose western period the library has never carded.
entries.meta: American, 1925–2013. Wrote westerns for the magazines and paperback houses through the 1950s before moving to crime, where his reputation was made. The mystery-crime-thriller pack cards him purely as a crime writer and does not mention his westerns anywhere, which is the gap this card fills. A frequently cited ranking of Hombre among the best western novels is a poll rather than an award, and no Spur category should be stated for him without checking the awarding body's own list for that year.
entries.knownFor: Three-Ten to Yuma and Hombre, and a spare, listening style that reads as modern half a century later.
entries.signature: Dialogue that carries the exposition, characters defined by what they decline to say, and a refusal of the moral summary the form expected.

works.title: Hombre
works.note: the novel, and the pack's claim on his western period

works.title: Three-Ten to Yuma
works.note: the story, twice filmed under the punctuated title

works.title: Valdez Is Coming
works.note: the late western novel

entries.name: John Ford
entries.description: The genre's central film-maker, who built the classical form and then spent two decades taking it apart from inside.
entries.meta: American, 1894–1973. Directed westerns across five decades; the pack's most-cited lineage node, and acknowledged as an influence by Kurosawa. The genre's most common award error. Ford won four Best Director Oscars and not one was for a western. He received a Saddleman Award in 1972 — the name the award held that year, and the name the pack uses for it, whatever the WWA's current list heading says. Liza Black's argument about Navajo cast and crew as underpaid workers on the Monument Valley productions attaches here and is about production rather than representation.
entries.knownFor: Stagecoach, The Searchers and The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance — the form's consolidation, its most argued self-criticism, and its account of how it lies.
entries.signature: Landscape shot as an actor, a doorway used as the frame's moral statement, and communities whose rituals carry more weight than their plots.

works.title: The Searchers (1956 film)
works.note: competence and hatred made inseparable, seven years before the revision is supposed to begin

works.title: Stagecoach
works.note: the year the A-western returned, and the template for two decades

works.title: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance (1962 film)
works.note: the printed legend, staged as an editorial decision

works.title: Cheyenne Autumn
works.note: the late attempt at restitution

entries.name: Howard Hawks
entries.description: The professional group's chief architect, and the maker of the film the genre's collapse test cannot dislodge.
entries.meta: American, 1896–1977. Worked across every genre; his westerns are the clearest statement of the plot structure Will Wright named professional. Red River circulates in two cuts, which differ in narration — a book versus Groot's voice-over — but share an ending; the different ending is Borden Chase's magazine serial, which ran from 1946 into January 1947 and in which Dunson is fatally wounded by Cherry and carried back to Texas to die. Any claim about the film must name the cut, and must not credit the serial's ending to either. He never won a competitive Academy Award; the 1975 award is Honorary.
entries.knownFor: Red River and Rio Bravo — the drive as a succession crisis, and competence as the entire moral content.
entries.signature: A group whose loyalty runs sideways rather than upward, dialogue overlapped and underplayed, and a community that is largely irrelevant to the people saving it.

works.title: Rio Bravo
works.note: made in explicit disagreement with High Noon, and answering it with professional sufficiency

works.title: Red River
works.note: the drive, and the rebellion against the man who started it

works.title: El Dorado
works.note: the late restatement

entries.name: Anthony Mann
entries.description: The psychological western in its purest form, with the grievance placed where the landscape used to be.
entries.meta: American, 1906–1967. Came to the western from film noir, and the debt is visible in the lighting, the pathology and the compromised protagonists. The Stewart films are a critics' cycle rather than a studio one, and were made at more than one studio. The term adult western for this material is the 1950s critical sense and should not be confused with the later paperback shelf category.
entries.knownFor: The five films made with James Stewart in the 1950s, which relocated the genre's conflict inside the protagonist.
entries.signature: A man whose motive he cannot state cleanly, physical punishment inflicted on the hero rather than by him, and country used to expose rather than to ennoble.

works.title: The Naked Spur
works.note: the wrong and the bounty placed in the same man

works.title: Winchester '73
works.note: the rifle as the object that organises a whole plot

works.title: The Man from Laramie
works.note: the late and bleakest of the cycle

entries.name: Budd Boetticher
entries.description: The most economical statement of the genre's structure anyone made in the studio era.
entries.meta: American, 1916–2001. Made a run of low-budget westerns with Randolph Scott at the end of the 1950s that critics later grouped as a cycle. The cycle name is a critics' construction from the production company's name and was never a marketing category; the card says so. Burt Kennedy wrote four of them, which is a credit this block should not swallow. The grouping itself is argued: six films are usually counted, a seventh is disputed, and only five were made by the company the cycle's name comes from.
entries.knownFor: A series of spare, short films in which a man with a grievance meets an articulate antagonist and the landscape does the rest.
entries.signature: Two men who understand each other perfectly on opposite sides of a killing, almost no incidental cast, and running times under ninety minutes.

works.title: Ride Lonesome
works.note: the structure at its most reduced

works.title: Seven Men from Now
works.note: the cycle's opening, and its best antagonist

works.title: The Tall T
works.note: the hostage situation as a moral argument between equals

entries.name: Delmer Daves
entries.description: The director of the film that opens the sympathetic-Indian studio cycle, and of the genre's tightest deadline picture.
entries.meta: American, 1904–1977. Worked across genres; his westerns are unusually interested in negotiation, obligation and the passage of time under pressure. Broken Arrow's screenplay was fronted by Michael Blankfort for the blacklisted Albert Maltz. The 1951 Academy Award nomination, in the Story category, stands under Blankfort's name and the Writers Guild restored Maltz's credit in 1991; the card states the nomination as filed and the restoration.
entries.knownFor: Broken Arrow, which made the negotiation of an agreement the climax of a western, and 3:10 to Yuma.
entries.signature: Talk rather than pursuit, an antagonist given a real position, and endings that turn on someone choosing to keep their word.

works.title: Broken Arrow
works.note: the cycle's opening, and its limit

works.title: 3:10 to Yuma
works.note: the deadline picture, from Leonard's story

works.title: The Last Wagon
works.note: the captivity material handled sympathetically

entries.name: Fred Zinnemann
entries.description: The director of the town-marshal cycle's defining entry, and of the pack's clearest counter-example to the law-arrives-later claim.
entries.meta: Austrian-born American, 1907–1997. Left Europe in the 1920s; his one western is among the most argued films the genre has produced. Four separate claims that are routinely merged. The blacklist reading of the film is Carl Foreman's; Foreman wrote it, was subpoenaed and left for Britain. Zinnemann directed. Stanley Kramer produced and later disputed Foreman's account publicly. Gary Cooper's Academy Award is for acting, at the twenty-fifth ceremony in 1953, for a 1952 film.
entries.knownFor: High Noon — a town that declines to be governed, and a deadline the audience can read off a clock.
entries.signature: Near-real-time structure, an empty street used as a verdict, and a community given reasonable arguments for its abandonment.

works.title: High Noon
works.note: the refusal that made the film an argument rather than a story

entries.name: George Stevens
entries.description: The director of the homestead-versus-open-range dispute in its most schematic and most quoted form.
entries.meta: American, 1904–1975. Came back from filming the liberation of the camps and made westerns and epics with a markedly slower, weightier hand. Shane's single Academy Award, at the twenty-sixth ceremony in 1954 for a 1953 film, is for Cinematography, Color — not for direction, writing or picture.
entries.knownFor: Shane, which puts the claim, the warrant and the hired specialist on screen with almost diagrammatic clarity.
entries.signature: Deliberate pacing, violence staged so that a single gunshot is shocking, and a child's sightline used as the film's moral instrument.

works.title: Shane (1953 film)
works.note: the range war as a title dispute, seen from a boy's height

works.title: Giant
works.note: the empire across generations, from Ferber's novel

entries.name: William A. Wellman
entries.description: The maker of the studio era's own indictment of the mob as an adjudicating authority.
entries.meta: American, 1896–1975. A prolific and unsentimental director whose westerns are among the bleakest the system permitted. Westward the Women originates in a Capra story, which is a separate claim from the direction.
entries.knownFor: The Ox-Bow Incident, which is almost entirely aftermath and gives the men who object no power to stop anything.
entries.signature: Short, cold films with no rescue, and a refusal to let the audience locate a figure who could have prevented the outcome.

works.title: The Ox-Bow Incident (1943 film)
works.note: the lynching, and the letter read aloud afterwards

works.title: Yellow Sky
works.note: the ghost-town siege

works.title: Westward the Women
works.note: a hundred and forty brides shipped west, from Frank Capra's story

entries.name: Sam Peckinpah
entries.description: The revision's centre, and the director who made the staging of violence into an argument about its cost.
entries.meta: American, 1925–1984. His films were repeatedly recut by their studios, which is why almost every claim about them has to name a version. Both The Wild Bunch and Pat Garrett circulate in materially different versions, and a claim about either must name the cut. His treatment of women on screen and on set is documented and contested, and the card states it rather than omitting it.
entries.knownFor: The Wild Bunch, which stages the largest battle in the genre in order to purchase nothing at all.
entries.signature: Multiple cameras and intercut slow motion making death take longer than the audience wants, and professional codes that survive everything they were supposed to serve.

works.title: The Wild Bunch
works.note: the code intact and its purpose removed

works.title: Ride the High Country
works.note: the elegy in miniature, two old men and a payroll

works.title: Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid
works.note: the late, most heavily recut of them

entries.name: Arthur Penn
entries.description: The director who staged the genre's most explicit contemporary transposition, alternating registers rather than blending them.
entries.meta: American, 1922–2010. Came from live television and the theatre; his westerns are formally restless in a way the studio era's were not. Little Big Man adapts Thomas Berger's 1964 novel, which is a separate claim from writing it. Chief Dan George was nominated for a supporting Academy Award for the film and did not win.
entries.knownFor: Little Big Man, which reaches the Washita through a film that has been switching between farce and horror throughout.
entries.signature: Tonal alternation used structurally, a frame narrator whose testimony is contested, and violence that arrives as rupture rather than as climax.

works.title: Little Big Man (1970 film)
works.note: the Washita staged against a contemporary war, from Berger's novel

works.title: The Left Handed Gun
works.note: the early psychological outlaw picture

works.title: The Missouri Breaks
works.note: the late, strangest entry in the cycle

entries.name: Robert Altman
entries.description: The director who put a mining corporation in the adjudicating chair and let it win.
entries.meta: American, 1925–2006. Worked against every convention of the form he touched; his two westerns are among the most complete refusals in the genre. McCabe adapts Edmund Naughton's 1959 novel and Buffalo Bill adapts Arthur Kopit's 1968 play, and both are separate claims from the direction.
entries.knownFor: McCabe & Mrs. Miller, which declines to stage its killing for pleasure and lets the company take the town without a confrontation.
entries.signature: Overlapping sound, a business partnership audible as arithmetic, and weather used to make the frontier physically miserable rather than beautiful.

works.title: McCabe & Mrs. Miller
works.note: the corporation as antagonist, from Naughton's novel

works.title: Buffalo Bill and the Indians, or Sitting Bull's History Lesson
works.note: the manufacture of the legend as a payroll

entries.name: Michael Cimino
entries.description: The director who staged the Johnson County war as class war, and whose film became the marker for the genre's collapse.
entries.meta: American, 1939–2016. Made one western, at a cost and a scale that changed how studios financed films for a decade. Animal cruelty findings on the production are documented and led directly to expanded American Humane oversight of film sets. The 1980 premiere cut, the 1981 release cut and the 2012 restoration differ substantially, so a claim must name the cut. The received account that this film killed the western attributes an industry-wide change to one production.
entries.knownFor: Heaven's Gate, which refuses to manufacture the moral clarity its material invites and lets an association with minutes and a membership list do the killing.
entries.signature: Duration and density used against legibility, an immigrant population given the story's sympathy, and enclosure shown as paperwork and hired men in the same act.

works.title: Heaven's Gate
works.note: the range war with both sides' warrants intact

entries.name: Clint Eastwood
entries.description: The only figure who spans the Italian cycle, the American revision and the elegy as a director, and who spent the persona he had built.
entries.meta: American, born 1930. Came to direction after a decade as the Italian cycle's export star, and has returned to the genre at intervals across fifty years. Two landmines. The Outlaw Josey Wales adapts a 1972 novel published by Asa Earl Carter under the false Cherokee identity Forrest Carter, which is established rather than disputed. And Unforgiven's Best Picture award at the sixty-fifth ceremony in 1993 went to Eastwood as producer, his Best Director award is separate, and the screenplay is David Webb Peoples' — three distinct claims. His star persona is carded in Craft; this card is about the direction.
entries.knownFor: Unforgiven, which restores every element of the walk-down in order to present the invoice.
entries.signature: A persona recovered in order to be charged for, physical difficulty foregrounded, and endings that neither redeem nor punish.

works.title: Unforgiven
works.note: the ritual restored and itemised, dedicated to Leone and Siegel

works.title: The Outlaw Josey Wales
works.note: the post-war revenge picture, from Asa Earl Carter's novel

works.title: High Plains Drifter
works.note: the early, most nihilistic of his westerns

works.title: Pale Rider
works.note: the preacher-gunfighter, and the mining-claim plot

entries.name: Kevin Costner
entries.description: The director whose 1990 epic reopened the studio western, and whose language decision was the most consequential thing in it.
entries.meta: American, born 1955. Directed the film that made the genre commercially viable again, and has returned to it repeatedly since at increasing scale. Doris Leader Charge coached the Lakota dialogue and Russell Means was among those who observed afterwards that male characters speak grammatically female forms, which fluent speakers hear immediately — a craft point as much as an ethical one. The Best Picture award at the sixty-third ceremony in 1991 went to the producers, of whom he was one.
entries.knownFor: Dances With Wolves, which subtitles its Lakota rather than dubbing it and gives its Lakota characters a negotiating position.
entries.signature: Length used for immersion, translation as the plot's mechanism, and an elegiac frame that its critics argue returns the authority the content removes.

works.title: Dances With Wolves
works.note: the Lakota subtitled, and the revival's opening

works.title: Open Range
works.note: free grazing against a fenced town

works.title: Horizon: An American Saga
works.note: the late multi-part return

entries.name: Kelly Reichardt
entries.description: The director who refuses the genre's compressions and makes the refusal the argument.
entries.meta: American, born 1964. Works at small scale and slow pace; her westerns withhold nearly every satisfaction the form is built to deliver. She belongs in this block rather than in the women's-tradition block, and the pack places her once.
entries.knownFor: Meek's Cutoff, which shoots in a nearly square frame so the horizon is denied to the audience as it is to the party.
entries.signature: Duration as revision, authority resting on a claim nobody can test, and women placed where the decisions are being made and not counted.

works.title: Meek's Cutoff
works.note: the crossing uncompressed, and the guide who may be wrong

works.title: First Cow
works.note: the fur-trade frontier as a small business with a fatal exposure

entries.name: Walter Van Tilburg Clark
entries.description: The novelist who turned the genre's furniture against the genre's own account of who may judge.
entries.meta: American, 1909–1971. Nevada-raised and academically trained, he wrote few books, and one of them is routinely cited as the point at which the western was first asked to carry this kind of argument.
entries.knownFor: The Ox-Bow Incident, which is almost entirely aftermath and gives the men who object no power to prevent anything.
entries.signature: A cold, unhurried narration that refuses the reader any figure capable of stopping the outcome, and an ending that supplies the confirmation of error too late.

works.title: The Ox-Bow Incident
works.note: the lynching, and the letter read aloud afterwards

works.title: The Track of the Cat
works.note: the family ranch and the animal that may not exist

works.title: The City of Trembling Leaves
works.note: the Nevada town novel

entries.name: A. B. Guthrie Jr.
entries.description: The novelist who narrated the fur trade, the wagon train and the cattle range as one continuous expropriation.
entries.meta: American, 1901–1991. A Montana newspaperman who wrote a sequence covering roughly a century of the northern plains, and who also wrote for the screen. His Pulitzer was awarded in 1950 for The Way West, published in 1949 — two years, and a card must say which. He wrote the screenplay for Shane and was nominated for an Academy Award for it, which is a separate claim from his novels.
entries.knownFor: The Big Sky and The Way West, and a body of work in which the country is destroyed by exactly the people the genre admires.
entries.signature: Men who know the country well enough that their mistakes are choices, and a chronology long enough for consequences to arrive.

works.title: The Big Sky
works.note: the fur trade, and a protagonist who can see what he is helping to end

works.title: The Way West
works.note: the wagon company as a political body, electing and reversing itself

works.title: These Thousand Hills
works.note: the cattle range, and the sequence's third stage

entries.name: Wallace Stegner
entries.description: The West's most consequential critic of its own founding myth, and the writer through whom the pack's working collection inherits Powell's aridity argument.
entries.meta: American, 1909–1993. Novelist, historian and teacher; his non-fiction on water and public land is as load-bearing for this pack as his fiction. Angle of Repose draws extensively on Mary Hallock Foote's unpublished letters and papers, and the resulting appropriation and attribution controversy is documented, has named parties on both sides, and is unresolved. The pack states it as a dispute and adjudicates nothing. His Pulitzer was awarded in 1972 for a 1971 book.
entries.knownFor: Angle of Repose, and Beyond the Hundredth Meridian, which carried Powell's case that aridity rather than character is the West's determining fact.
entries.signature: A historian's sense of consequence applied to family material, and an insistence that the region's story is one of federal water rather than individual grit.

works.title: Angle of Repose
works.note: the novel, and the dispute that attaches to it

works.title: Beyond the Hundredth Meridian
works.note: Powell, aridity, and the argument the region ignored

works.title: The Big Rock Candy Mountain
works.note: the family novel of failed western ventures

entries.name: Cormac McCarthy
entries.description: The pack's outer limit on violence as argument, and the writer whose border novels are carded in three packs at once.
entries.meta: American, 1933–2023. Wrote across Appalachia and the Southwest; the border and frontier novels are the ones this pack claims. Blood Meridian is carded in the historical and literary packs as well, which is intentional under the library's no-dedupe rule, and Western cards it from the Western contract rather than restating theirs. No Country for Old Men does not collapse on the pack's ground clause and is admitted on the lineage clause alone. His National Book Award of 1992 is for All the Pretty Horses.
entries.knownFor: Blood Meridian, in which no exchange of fire alters the moral situation, and the Border Trilogy.
entries.signature: Biblical cadence applied to atrocity, no quotation marks, and a refusal to grant violence any redemptive function at all.

works.title: Blood Meridian
works.note: the scalp-hunting novel, and the thesis of regeneration run without the renewal

works.title: All the Pretty Horses
works.note: the border crossed, and a Mexican legal system that wins

works.title: No Country for Old Men
works.note: the code meeting an economy that does not negotiate

entries.name: Larry McMurtry
entries.description: The novelist of the West after the myth has finished with it, and the author of the pack's hardest boundary case.
entries.meta: American, 1936–2021. Wrote about small-town Texas and the cattle frontier across six decades. Lonesome Dove is the pack's hardest case under its own collapse test — the Montana ground is contested by nobody, and it is admitted on lineage and on the absence of the second mode. His Pulitzer was awarded in 1986 for the 1985 novel. His Academy Award, shared with Diana Ossana at the seventy-eighth ceremony in 2006, is for the adapted screenplay of Brokeback Mountain, which the pack hands to the literary pack — it should not be attached to his western work. The 1989 Lonesome Dove is television, not film.
entries.knownFor: Lonesome Dove, and The Last Picture Show, which writes the closing of a Texas town as an ordinary economic fact.
entries.signature: Length used to let a venture turn out not to have been worth it, and comedy sitting directly against loss without either cancelling the other.

works.title: Lonesome Dove
works.note: the drive, and eight hundred pages discovering the destination was not worth it

works.title: The Last Picture Show
works.note: the town emptying, and the cinema shutting

works.title: Horseman, Pass By
works.note: the first novel, filmed as Hud

works.title: Buffalo Girls
works.note: figures who have become their own exhibits and are paid for it

entries.name: John Williams
entries.description: The author of the buffalo-hunting novel the pack names by title as its own admitted cost.
entries.meta: American, 1922–1994. Wrote four novels in very different modes and was largely rediscovered after his death. The pack's boundary rule names Butcher's Crossing as a case admitted on force and lineage rather than on a contest between claimants, with the working shown rather than hidden. Not to be confused with the composer of the same name. His National Book Award of 1973, shared, is for Augustus rather than for the western.
entries.knownFor: Butcher's Crossing, in which a hunting party is stranded by a winter with no interest in their venture and the market collapses while they are out of contact.
entries.signature: A cold, exact prose that lets an enterprise simply fail, with no antagonist and no lesson extracted.

works.title: Butcher's Crossing
works.note: the hides brought back to a market that no longer exists

works.title: Stoner
works.note: the academic novel that made his posthumous reputation

entries.name: Glendon Swarthout
entries.description: The author of the elegiac western's cleanest single statement, and the datum against which the pack's award trap is measured.
entries.meta: American, 1918–1992. Wrote across genres; The Shootist became the film that closed John Wayne's career. He was the first recipient under the Owen Wister name, in 1991 — the presentation venue is not established and should not be stated. That is a claim about the name, not about the award: every earlier recipient received a Saddleman, and whether the two are one award renamed is the framing the pack declines to pick. He also won Spur Awards, and their categories and years are unconfirmed and should not be stated without checking the awarding body's own list.
entries.knownFor: The Shootist, a dying gunman in a town where the queue of challengers is still forming, and The Homesman.
entries.signature: A premise stated with total economy and then followed to its least comfortable conclusion, with no reprieve arranged.

works.title: The Shootist
works.note: dying and being killed, racing each other

works.title: The Homesman
works.note: what the frontier did to women it had no institutions for

works.title: They Came to Cordura
works.note: cowardice and decoration on the Mexican border

entries.category: The Contemporary Novel of the West
entries.name: Charles Portis
entries.description: The genre's finest comic narrator, and a first-person voice both film versions of the novel had to find an equivalent for.
entries.meta: American, 1933–2020. An Arkansas newspaperman who wrote five novels and was for decades a writer's writer. Two films exist, from 1969 and 2010, with different fidelities to the book, and a card must name which.
entries.knownFor: True Grit, narrated by Mattie Ross in old age, whose refusal of contractions and King James cadence is the whole method.
entries.signature: A first person built entirely from syntax rather than from dialect spelling, comic and utterly unsentimental about violence.

works.title: True Grit
works.note: the narrator, and the posse of three with three incompatible warrants

works.title: Norwood
works.note: the first novel, and the same voice in a lower key

entries.category: The Contemporary Novel of the West
entries.name: Kent Haruf
entries.description: The novelist of the High Plains town after the myth has finished with it.
entries.meta: American, 1943–2014. Set almost everything in one invented Colorado town and wrote the unmythic West at greater sustained length than anyone. Plainsong was a National Book Award finalist rather than a winner.
entries.knownFor: Plainsong, and a body of work in which the western's country is a place where people simply live.
entries.signature: Plain declarative sentences, no quotation marks, and kindness treated as a plot event rather than as a sentiment.

works.title: Plainsong
works.note: the town, the pregnant girl and the two old cattlemen

works.title: Eventide
works.note: the sequel, and the same town further on

works.title: Benediction
works.note: dying in the same country

entries.category: The Contemporary Novel of the West
entries.name: Philipp Meyer
entries.description: The novelist who ran Comanche captivity, the Rangers, land theft and oil across two centuries as one family audit.
entries.meta: American, born 1974; living status not independently confirmed on the pack's research pass. The Son was a Pulitzer finalist rather than a winner, and the 2017 series adapted from it is television and a separate claim.
entries.knownFor: The Son, which follows one Texas family from a captivity in the 1840s to a petroleum fortune, and lets the reader watch the claim compound.
entries.signature: Three interleaved voices across three centuries, and an insistence that the fortune and the atrocity are the same transaction seen at different distances.

works.title: The Son
works.note: the ground clause audited across two hundred years

works.title: American Rust
works.note: the earlier novel, outside the West

entries.category: The Contemporary Novel of the West
entries.name: Ron Hansen
entries.description: The novelist who disassembled an outlaw legend while showing it being manufactured.
entries.meta: American, born 1947; living status not independently confirmed on the pack's research pass. The 2007 film of his best-known novel is based on it, which is a separate claim from writing it.
entries.knownFor: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford, which treats print celebrity as an industry with its own incentives.
entries.signature: A close, almost devotional attention to the mechanics of fame, with the killing rendered as a career decision.

works.title: The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford
works.note: the legend assembled commercially while its subject is alive to negotiate

works.title: Desperadoes
works.note: the Dalton gang, and the earlier outlaw novel

entries.category: The Contemporary Novel of the West
entries.name: Patrick deWitt
entries.description: The Canadian novelist who runs the genre's furniture as comedy without abandoning its claim.
entries.meta: Canadian, born 1975 on Vancouver Island; living status not independently confirmed on the pack's research pass. The Sisters Brothers was shortlisted for the Booker Prize rather than winning it.
entries.knownFor: The Sisters Brothers, a gold-rush picaresque in which the thing the brothers are sent for destroys the man who has it.
entries.signature: A deadpan first person that reports violence and absurdity in the same register, with a chemical claim-jumping scheme standing in for the whole apparatus of title.

works.title: The Sisters Brothers
works.note: the errand, and the arrival that is not worth it

entries.name: Frank S. Nugent
entries.description: The most consequential screenwriting career in the genre, and the one most routinely absorbed into a director's.
entries.meta: American, 1908–1965. A film critic who became John Ford's principal writer; this block exists partly to stop directors swallowing the writers who built their films. He wrote Fort Apache and, with Laurence Stallings, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon; Rio Grande was written by James Kevin McGuinness, so the trilogy is not his. The underlying stories are James Warner Bellah's, which is a separate claim again.
entries.knownFor: The Searchers, and two of the three Ford cavalry pictures.
entries.signature: Ensembles established at speed, ritual scenes given more weight than plot, and dialogue that leaves the protagonist's central motive unstated.

works.title: The Searchers (1956 film)
works.note: the screenplay that withholds what the novel states

works.title: Fort Apache
works.note: the institution built lovingly and its commander indicted

works.title: She Wore a Yellow Ribbon
works.note: the cavalry picture as a retirement

works.title: Wagon Master
works.note: the company and the strangers it takes on

entries.name: Carl Foreman
entries.description: The blacklist inside the genre, and the writer whose reading of his own film has been disputed for seventy years.
entries.meta: American, 1914–1984. Wrote High Noon while under subpoena and left for Britain; the political reading of the film is his, and Stanley Kramer publicly disputed his account for decades. The pack states the dispute and adjudicates nothing. His award for The Bridge on the River Kwai was presented to Pierre Boulle in 1958 and restored to Foreman and Michael Wilson posthumously in 1984 — one of cinema's best-documented award misattributions and directly on this pack's brief.
entries.knownFor: High Noon, and a real-time structure built entirely around a community declining to act.
entries.signature: A deadline the audience can read off a clock, and a town given reasonable arguments for its abandonment rather than mere cowardice.

works.title: High Noon
works.note: the refusal, and the reading its author never stopped defending

works.title: The Bridge on the River Kwai
works.note: written uncredited, and restored posthumously

entries.name: John Meston
entries.description: The writer who built an adult western on radio before television attempted one.
entries.meta: American, 1914–1979. Wrote roughly a hundred and eighty scripts for the radio run and a further one hundred and ninety-six television episodes of the same property — close to three hundred and eighty in total, and the radio figure alone is often misreported as the whole — and shares its creation credit with Norman Macdonnell. The description of it as the first adult western is marketing language rather than a critical finding, and the pack states it as marketing rather than repeating the priority claim.
entries.knownFor: Gunsmoke, in which the landscape is built entirely in sound effects and the violence is ugly and its aftermath played.
entries.signature: A marshal who is tired rather than heroic, a doctor used as the show's conscience, and consequences that persist between episodes.

works.title: Gunsmoke
works.note: the radio series, and where the television western's grammar was written

entries.name: David Milch
entries.description: The pack's fullest television statement of the ground clause: a camp with no legal title at all.
entries.meta: American, born 1945. Publicly diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in 2015 and in assisted living since 2019; the pack could establish no record after 2022 and treats his current status as unconfirmed, which is why nothing here is written in a confident present tense. The 2019 Deadwood film is a television film and takes the same medium value as the series.
entries.knownFor: Deadwood, whose whole subject is what fills the vacuum where title should be.
entries.signature: An elaborate, near-Jacobean register chosen because the flat screen-western idiom would have sounded modern, and politics conducted almost entirely across tables.

works.title: Deadwood
works.note: the camp on land the United States has not yet taken

works.title: Deadwood: The Movie
works.note: the television film that closes it

works.title: NYPD Blue
works.note: co-created, and outside the genre

entries.name: Taylor Sheridan
entries.description: The contemporary neo-western's dominant single author across film and television.
entries.meta: American, born 1970. Hell or High Water was nominated for the original screenplay award at the eighty-ninth ceremony in 2017 for a 2016 film and did not win. Wind River's handling of missing and murdered Indigenous women, and its casting, drew documented criticism from Native critics, which the pack states.
entries.knownFor: Hell or High Water, which restores the range war with a bank in the cattleman's place, and Yellowstone.
entries.signature: A frontier moral vocabulary meeting modern instruments — leases, agencies, banks — and losing in ways the characters can name.

works.title: Hell or High Water
works.note: the bank as land-grabber

works.title: Yellowstone
works.note: the cattle empire as a present-day going concern

works.title: Sicario
works.note: jurisdiction itself as the horror

works.title: Wind River
works.note: the reservation crime and the jurisdictional gap

entries.name: Frederick Jackson Turner
entries.description: The historian whose thesis the whole pack is organised against.
entries.meta: American, 1861–1932. His 1893 paper was delivered at the World's Columbian Exposition; its enormous influence accumulated over the following decades rather than on delivery, and dating that influence to 1893 is a common error. The pack names its specialist frontier because of this text, and treats the word as the myth under study rather than as an analytic category.
entries.knownFor: The frontier thesis — that the frontier formed American character and democracy, and that its closing ended a formative era.
entries.signature: A single organising idea applied to the whole national history, with the frontier rendered as a process rather than as a place taken from people.

works.title: The Frontier in American History
works.note: the collected argument

works.title: The Significance of the Frontier in American History
works.note: the paper itself

entries.name: Richard Slotkin
entries.description: The scholar whose trilogy supplies the structure underneath the genre, and whose argument the pack is careful not to misdescribe.
entries.meta: American, born 1942; living and publishing as recently as 2024. His argument is literary-historical and cultural-historical, built from readings of texts, and it is not a psychological finding — the pack marks it as such on every card that uses it, and cut its Psychology collection partly on that basis.
entries.knownFor: Regeneration through violence — the claim that American identity is organised around a repeating story in which violence at the edge produces renewal.
entries.signature: Enormous reading across popular and official sources, tracing one narrative structure from the captivity narrative to the twentieth-century western.

works.title: Regeneration Through Violence
works.note: the thesis, and the trilogy's opening

works.title: Gunfighter Nation
works.note: the twentieth-century volume

works.title: The Fatal Environment
works.note: the middle volume, on the industrial era

entries.name: Patricia Nelson Limerick
entries.description: The historian whose objection to the word frontier the pack adopts as a ruling.
entries.meta: American, born 1951. In September 2022 she was removed from the directorship of the centre she co-founded and its board executive committee resigned in protest — institutional rather than scholarly, and a matter of record.
entries.knownFor: The Legacy of Conquest, and the argument that frontier is a process word that functions only from the settler's side.
entries.signature: Conquest, place and continuity offered as replacement vocabulary, with the insistence that the western story does not end in 1890.

works.title: The Legacy of Conquest
works.note: the New Western History's central statement

works.title: Desert Passages
works.note: the earlier book on responses to aridity

works.title: Something in the Soil
works.note: the essays

entries.name: Richard White
entries.description: The historian who supplied the single most useful analytic import for writing across the frontier line.
entries.meta: American, born 1947; living status not independently confirmed on the pack's research pass. His middle-ground concept has been borrowed so widely that it is now routinely used against his own stated definition, so a card using it should quote the definition rather than the borrowing.
entries.knownFor: The Middle Ground, and Railroaded, which is the corporate force this pack's third question needs.
entries.signature: Accommodation and mutual misunderstanding treated as the normal condition of contact, rather than conquest as a single event.

works.title: The Middle Ground
works.note: accommodation as the actual history of contact

works.title: Railroaded
works.note: the transcontinentals as financial constructions

works.title: It's Your Misfortune and None of My Own
works.note: the regional history

entries.name: Jane Tompkins
entries.description: The critic whose argument became this pack's single most productive trope.
entries.meta: American, born 1940. Her thesis is a strong claim with named opponents, and the pack's rule that a contested card with only one side sourced does not ship applies directly to it.
entries.knownFor: West of Everything, and the argument that the western is constitutively a reaction against nineteenth-century women's sentimental fiction.
entries.signature: Close reading of the genre's silences and its aversion to interiority, treated as one gesture rather than two conventions.

works.title: West of Everything
works.note: the inner life of westerns, and the flight from the sentimental

works.title: Sensational Designs
works.note: the earlier argument about sentimental fiction

entries.name: Will Wright
entries.description: The author of the only taxonomy in the field with a stated method, which this pack cards as craft.
entries.meta: American; the pack could establish no reliable biographical record, including a birth year, and treats his living status as unconfirmed. He is not the game designer of the same name, who is a different person and far better indexed. His method — selecting films by box-office performance — is itself criticised, notably by Jim Kitses, and the criticism belongs on the card.
entries.knownFor: Sixguns and Society, and the four plot structures the pack cards in its Craft collection as classical, vengeance, transition and professional.
entries.signature: A structural analysis derived from a defined corpus rather than from a critic's preferences, which is why its conclusions can be checked.

works.title: Sixguns and Society
works.note: the four plots, and the method that makes them arguable

entries.name: Christopher Frayling
entries.description: The Italian cycle's entire scholarly substrate, and the only source that runs the Karl May to Leone line as a single argument.
entries.meta: British, born 1946; living and publishing. His 1981 subtitle carries the pack's own lineage chain from Karl May to Sergio Leone, which is exactly what the pack's lineage clause requires a card to be able to name. He was knighted in 2001, which is not a prize.
entries.knownFor: Spaghetti Westerns, and the definition of the Zapata western as a distinct strain.
entries.signature: Production history and political context handled together, with the cycle treated as a European argument rather than as an imitation.

works.title: Spaghetti Westerns
works.note: the cycle, and the lineage chain in its subtitle

works.title: Sergio Leone: Something to Do with Death
works.note: the biography

entries.name: Philip J. Deloria
entries.description: The historian whose analysis of assumed Indigenous identity is the key to the pack's hardest cases.
entries.meta: Yankton Dakota, born 1959; a descendant of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. He is a distinct figure from his father, Vine Deloria Jr., whose Custer Died for Your Sins of 1969 is also a candidate for this collection.
entries.knownFor: Playing Indian, which is the analytic key to the DEFA problem, to Iron Eyes Cody, and to the whole identity file this pack carries.
entries.signature: Assumed identity treated as a durable American practice with a politics, rather than as a series of individual impostures.

works.title: Playing Indian
works.note: the practice, and the country it is used to claim

works.title: Indians in Unexpected Places
works.note: modernity and Indigenous life

works.title: Becoming Mary Sully
works.note: the artist, and the family

entries.name: Michelle H. Raheja
entries.description: The scholar who supplied the terms the pack needs for redface and for the Indigenous counter-western, for which no substitute exists.
entries.meta: American; described in secondary sources as Seneca, which no institutional page the pack could reach states, so the card gives the sourcing rather than asserting the affiliation. No reliable birth date or current status could be established and both are treated as unconfirmed.
entries.knownFor: Reservation Reelism, and the concepts of visual sovereignty and redfacing.
entries.signature: Indigenous film-making read as an assertion of authority over representation rather than as a response to misrepresentation.

works.title: Reservation Reelism
works.note: redfacing, visual sovereignty, and Native representation on film

entries.name: Liza Black
entries.description: The historian who made Native people's labour on western productions the subject, which nothing else in the field does.
entries.meta: American; described in secondary sources as a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, which no institutional page the pack could reach states, so the card gives the sourcing rather than asserting the citizenship. No reliable birth date or current status could be established and both are treated as unconfirmed. The pack's sensitive-material section names her by name as the one prosecution line that is about production rather than representation.
entries.knownFor: Picturing Indians, which treats Native people on studio westerns as underpaid workers rather than as images.
entries.signature: Payroll records, contracts and working conditions used as the evidence, which shifts the argument from representation to employment.

works.title: Picturing Indians
works.note: Native Americans as workers on film, 1941 to 1960

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: N. Scott Momaday
entries.description: The novelist who broke the genre's monopoly on who is permitted to narrate the dispossession.
entries.meta: Kiowa, 1934–2024. His mother had English, Irish and French ancestry and a Cherokee ancestry claim; the pack cards him as Kiowa and states her descent rather than converting it into a fraction. His Pulitzer was awarded in 1969 for a 1968 book, and the two years are constantly merged.
entries.knownFor: House Made of Dawn, in which a returning veteran is unable to reoccupy ground that is legally still his people's.
entries.signature: Ceremonial and oral structures used as narrative architecture rather than as decoration, and a landscape addressed as a party to the story.

works.title: House Made of Dawn
works.note: the novel that made Native-authored prose about the West unignorable

works.title: The Way to Rainy Mountain
works.note: the Kiowa migration told three ways at once

works.title: The Names
works.note: the memoir, and the family record as a claim

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Leslie Marmon Silko
entries.description: The novelist who wrote the ground-claim story from the side that lost it, using ceremony rather than gunfire as the settlement.
entries.meta: Laguna Pueblo, born 1948. She describes herself as of mixed Laguna, Mexican and white descent and has written about that position at length; the card states her own formulation and makes no enrollment claim, which no source the pack could reach supports either way. Her 1981 MacArthur is a fellowship, not an award for a particular work.
entries.knownFor: Ceremony, in which a veteran's cure and the land's are the same operation, and uranium mining is the wound.
entries.signature: The story told as an act with consequences rather than as a report, and a plot in which healing and land are not separable subjects.

works.title: Ceremony
works.note: the counter-western's central novel

works.title: Almanac of the Dead
works.note: the borderland counter-history at continental scale

works.title: Storyteller
works.note: the mixed-form collection where the method is visible

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Louise Erdrich
entries.description: The novelist through whom the pack keeps the land-title and jurisdiction residual the genre abandoned in 1890.
entries.meta: Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians, enrolled; born 1954. Her Pulitzer was awarded in 2021 for a 2020 book. The literary-reference pack holds her with no Western hand-off, which is the collision this pack's reciprocal card repairs: Literary owns the prose, Western keeps the title-and-jurisdiction claim.
entries.knownFor: The Round House, on criminal jurisdiction over non-Natives on tribal land, and The Night Watchman, on termination.
entries.signature: A community carried across many books, and legal instruments treated as the engines of plot they are.

works.title: The Round House
works.note: the jurisdictional gap as the whole crime

works.title: The Night Watchman
works.note: termination fought in committee rooms

works.title: Love Medicine
works.note: the sequence's opening, and the method

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: James Welch
entries.description: The novelist who narrated a massacre the genre has never filmed from inside the camp it happened to.
entries.meta: Blackfeet and A'aniiih (Gros Ventre), 1940–2003. Fools Crow reconstructs Blackfeet life before and through the Marias Massacre of 1870 — the material the pack's sensitive-material section names — and his nonfiction returns to the same ground from the historian's side.
entries.knownFor: Fools Crow, the pre-reservation novel written without a settler viewpoint character anywhere in it.
entries.signature: A calm, unhurried surface under which the destruction is already arranged, and English shaped to carry Blackfeet idiom.

works.title: Fools Crow
works.note: the Marias, from inside

works.title: Winter in the Blood
works.note: the contemporary reservation novel

works.title: Killing Custer
works.note: the nonfiction account of the Little Bighorn and after

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Mourning Dove
entries.description: One of the first Native women to publish a novel, and the author of the earliest Native-authored western the pack could establish.
entries.meta: Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, Syilx (Okanagan); born Christine Quintasket, c.1884 or 1888 – 1936, the birth year disputed. How far her collaborator Lucullus V. McWhorter rewrote Cogewea is a live scholarly dispute; the pack states it as a dispute and adjudicates nothing, and treats the collaboration itself as part of the book's subject. The priority claim is also narrower than it is usually written: S. Alice Callahan's Wynema (1891) precedes Cogewea, so the card says one of the first rather than the first.
entries.knownFor: Cogewea, the Half-Blood, drafted around 1912 and published in 1927, which the pack admits on the force clause rather than the iconographic one.
entries.signature: Romance-western machinery turned on the reader, with the heroine's mixed descent used as the mechanism of exclusion rather than as colour.

works.title: Cogewea, the Half-Blood
works.note: the fair, the two races, and both purses withheld

works.title: Coyote Stories
works.note: the Sylix narrative tradition, collected

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: D'Arcy McNickle
entries.description: The novelist who wrote the ground clause in its legal form: allotment, water and jurisdiction, all of it paperwork.
entries.meta: Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, 1904–1977; enrolled by an unusual route, through his Métis mother's adoption onto the Flathead rolls, which is sometimes written up as straightforward tribal membership. He worked for the Bureau of Indian Affairs from 1936, which is part of the record and part of the fiction; the length of his service is given inconsistently and the card does not state a span.
entries.knownFor: The Surrounded, the allotment-era novel in which every avenue of return is closed by an instrument rather than by a gun.
entries.signature: Bureaucratic process rendered with the weight other westerns give to violence, and endings in which nobody is defeated by anybody visible.

works.title: The Surrounded
works.note: title, water and jurisdiction as the antagonist

works.title: Wind from an Enemy Sky
works.note: published posthumously; the dam and the sacred object

works.title: Runner in the Sun
works.note: the pre-contact novel written for young readers

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: John Joseph Mathews
entries.description: The Osage writer who was inside the headright system while it was being murdered over.
entries.meta: Osage Nation, 1894–1979; his Osage ancestry is consistently reported as one-eighth and the pack states the enrollment rather than the fraction, which is the rule and not a dispute. He served on the Osage Tribal Council. Sundown is set in the years of the murders and does not narrate them directly, which is a decision rather than an omission.
entries.knownFor: Sundown, and the oil-and-headright ground that sits underneath the entire Osage murders literature.
entries.signature: Wealth written as dispossession's next stage, and a protagonist who cannot make his education do anything for him.

works.title: Sundown
works.note: the headright generation, from inside

works.title: Wah'Kon-Tah
works.note: the agency years, from the agent's diaries

works.title: The Osages
works.note: the tribal history

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Zacharias Kunuk
entries.description: The film-maker who removed the settler frame entirely and made the genre's arrival premise unnecessary.
entries.meta: Inuk, from Igloolik, Nunavut; born 1957 and confirmed working in 2025. Atanarjuat's Caméra d'Or at Cannes in 2001 is a festival prize for a first feature — not a Cannes best-film award, and not a writing award. The film is in Inuktitut throughout, which the pack's craft collection names.
entries.knownFor: Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner, an Inuit narrative filmed in Inuktitut with no outside viewpoint offered at any point.
entries.signature: An oral tradition adapted on its own terms and at its own pace, with the landscape supplying both the threat and the law.

works.title: Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner
works.note: the story told with nobody arriving

works.title: The Journals of Knud Rasmussen
works.note: the encounter, from the other chair

works.title: One Day in the Life of Noah Piugattuk
works.note: the relocation interview as a single conversation

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Chris Eyre
entries.description: The director of the first nationally distributed feature written, directed and co-produced by Native Americans.
entries.meta: Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes, born 1968. Smoke Signals was written by Sherman Alexie from his own stories, and the pack keeps direction and writing as separate claims: what is Eyre's is the direction. The film's code-switching between registers is named in the pack's craft collection.
entries.knownFor: Smoke Signals, which uses road-movie structure against the captivity plot and is almost entirely intra-community.
entries.signature: Reservation life filmed as ordinary rather than as evidence, with comedy carrying the material a message film would have stated.

works.title: Smoke Signals
works.note: the road picture with the settlers left out of frame

works.title: Skins
works.note: Pine Ridge, two brothers, and the monument
