entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Sterlin Harjo
entries.description: The contemporary counter-western on television, made by citizens of the nations it depicts.
entries.meta: A citizen of the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma and of Muscogee descent, born 1979 — two different relations, which the card keeps apart. Reservation Dogs is co-created with Taika Waititi and must not be carded as sole authorship. Its writers' room and directing roster were Indigenous throughout, which is the production fact the pack cites rather than a claim about representation.
entries.knownFor: Reservation Dogs, in which the genre's furniture survives only as jokes and the ground is simply where everyone already lives.
entries.signature: Deadpan comedy over grief, and a community with internal politics the outside world barely enters.

works.title: Reservation Dogs
works.note: the counter-western as a hangout comedy

works.title: Mekko
works.note: the street, the camp, and the man put out of both

works.title: Four Sheets to the Wind
works.note: the first feature

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Alanis Obomsawin
entries.description: The documentarian who filmed a contested claim to ground being settled by force as it happened.
entries.meta: Abenaki, of Odanak; born 1932 in New Hampshire and raised at Odanak, and confirmed living with an active public profile. Her fifty-year run at the National Film Board of Canada is the pack's Canadian First Nations placement, and it sits in this block rather than in the international one on purpose.
entries.knownFor: Kanehsatake: 270 Years of Resistance, filmed from behind the barricades during the 1990 Oka crisis.
entries.signature: Long presence rather than access, her own narration used sparingly, and the historical claim laid out before the standoff is shown.

works.title: Kanehsatake: 270 Years of Resistance
works.note: the golf course, the pines, and the army

works.title: Incident at Restigouche
works.note: the Sûreté du Québec raid on the Mi'gmaq salmon fishery

works.title: Trick or Treaty?
works.note: Treaty No. 9 and what was signed

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Gerald Vizenor
entries.description: The critic who supplied the analytic vocabulary the pack's frontier specialist runs on.
entries.meta: Minnesota Chippewa Tribe, White Earth Reservation, enrolled; born 1934. He is equally placeable among the pack's historians and critics and is placed here once, by the tradition-blocks-take-precedence rule. His terms are coinages with definitions and should be used as he defines them or not at all. Manifest Manners is dated 1993 in many secondary sources and 1994 by its publisher; the pack takes the imprint.
entries.knownFor: Survivance and postindian — an active presence rather than survival, and the figure who exists after the invention called the Indian.
entries.signature: Terms built to make a habit of thought visible, deployed inside fiction as readily as inside criticism.

works.title: Manifest Manners
works.note: postindian survivance, and the manufacture named

works.title: Fugitive Poses
works.note: absence, presence and the simulated figure

works.title: Blue Ravens
works.note: the novel, and the White Earth family at the front

entries.category: Native and First Nations Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Tommy Orange
entries.description: The novelist who runs the line from a massacre to a school to a city, which is the aftermath the genre never shows.
entries.meta: Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes, enrolled; born 1982. There There was a Pulitzer finalist in 2019, not a winner, and is regularly misreported. Wandering Stars carries the same family from Sand Creek through the Carlisle school to contemporary Oakland.
entries.knownFor: There There, the urban Native novel that converges on a powwow, and Wandering Stars.
entries.signature: Many first-person voices assembled toward one event, and a prologue that states the history the fiction then refuses to explain again.

works.title: There There
works.note: urban Native Oakland, and the powwow it all runs at

works.title: Wandering Stars
works.note: Sand Creek, Carlisle, and the generations after

entries.name: Willa Cather
entries.description: The novelist who wrote the homestead claim as labour, weather and market rather than as a gunfight.
entries.meta: American, 1873–1947. This block is a block about white women writing the West: the pack's tradition blocks take placement precedence, so every non-white woman is claimed by one of them first, and the pack's coverage of non-white women is counted across those blocks rather than here. Her 1923 Pulitzer is for One of Ours, a First World War novel, and not for a western.
entries.knownFor: O Pioneers! and My Ántonia, in which holding the ground is a matter of decades rather than of an afternoon.
entries.signature: Long time-scales, immigrant labour treated as the frontier's actual content, and violence that arrives as an interruption rather than as a resolution.

works.title: My Ántonia
works.note: the prairie claim held across a working life

works.title: O Pioneers!
works.note: the land, and the woman who reads it correctly

works.title: Death Comes for the Archbishop
works.note: New Mexico, and the church as a settling instrument

entries.name: Mari Sandoz
entries.description: The writer who took the Nebraska settler's side and the Northern Cheyenne's with the same hand.
entries.meta: American, 1896–1966. Her Old Jules is her own father, written without protection. Award trap, and the pack's model instance of the correct handling: she received a Saddleman Award in 1964 and died in 1966, so nothing was presented to her under the Owen Wister name, which dates from 1991. The WWA's own Owen Wister page nevertheless lists her as its 1964 recipient. The name is anachronistic; whether the award is one award renamed is the framing the pack declines to pick. Ford's Cheyenne Autumn (1964) is based on her book, which is a separate claim from her having written the film.
entries.knownFor: Crazy Horse and Cheyenne Autumn, the two biographies that made the Plains wars readable from the Plains side.
entries.signature: Research at the density of a historian, delivered in a narrative voice that never pretends to neutrality.

works.title: Old Jules
works.note: the settler father, unflattered

works.title: Crazy Horse
works.note: the biography, from Lakota testimony

works.title: Cheyenne Autumn
works.note: the Northern Cheyenne exodus north

entries.name: Dorothy M. Johnson
entries.description: The short-story writer three of the genre's most-filmed westerns come out of, credited on all three as the source and on none of them as the screenwriter.
entries.meta: American, 1905–1984. The pack's clearest case of prose authorship hidden behind a screen credit. Award trap in full: a Spur for "Lost Sister", dated 1956 by the WWA's short-fiction list and 1957 elsewhere on the award-year against presentation-year split the pack has already logged; and a Levi Strauss Golden Saddleman Award in 1976. She died in 1984, so nothing reached her under the Owen Wister name. Her 1959 honorary Blackfeet membership is a tribal courtesy and not enrollment.
entries.knownFor: "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance", "A Man Called Horse" and The Hanging Tree.
entries.signature: A premise stated in a paragraph and closed in twenty pages, with the moral cost left in the reader's hands rather than resolved.

works.title: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
works.note: first published in Cosmopolitan, June 1949; the commonly cited 1953 is the Indian Country collection

works.title: A Man Called Horse
works.note: the captivity story that became the 1970 film

works.title: The Hanging Tree
works.note: the novella, and the mining camp

entries.name: B. M. Bower
entries.description: An early and unusually prolific woman writing formula westerns at commercial scale, inside the market that formed the genre.
entries.meta: American, 1871–1940; born Bertha Muzzy. She published under initials rather than under her given name, was widely assumed by readers to be a man, and is still listed as one in some indexes and reference works; the pack states the reception and does not assert a motive no source gives. She wrote at pulp rate across four decades and knew the ranch work she described.
entries.knownFor: Chip of the Flying U and the Flying U series, which established the ranch-outfit comedy as a saleable western shape.
entries.signature: An outfit rather than a lone rider, ranch labour written accurately, and romance handled without ceremony.

works.title: Chip of the Flying U
works.note: the series opener, and the outfit as the unit

works.title: The Happy Family
works.note: the ranch comedy at its most confident

works.title: The Lure of the Dim Trails
works.note: the eastern writer sent west, which is her own joke

entries.name: Mary Hallock Foote
entries.description: The novelist and illustrator who wrote the ground clause in its engineering form — mining claims, canals and title.
entries.meta: American, 1847–1938. She illustrated her own fiction and lived the mining-camp and irrigation-project West she wrote about. Dispute, stated on both cards: Wallace Stegner's Angle of Repose (1971) drew on her letters and papers, and the attribution and appropriation controversy is documented and unresolved; the pack states it and adjudicates neither side.
entries.knownFor: The Led-Horse Claim and The Chosen Valley — the claim and the water right as the things actually at stake.
entries.signature: Technical detail of extraction and irrigation carried without apology, and an eastern woman's viewpoint held rather than dissolved.

works.title: The Led-Horse Claim
works.note: the mining claim, and the two companies on it

works.title: The Chosen Valley

entries.name: Molly Gloss
entries.description: The Oregon homestead written as unmythic labour, in the block's least mythologised register.
entries.meta: American, born 1944. Her 2000 prize was the James Tiptree, Jr. Award, since renamed the Otherwise Award; the pack names the body by the name it held in that year. She writes the Pacific Northwest rather than the Southwest, which is itself a corrective to the genre's map.
entries.knownFor: The Jump-Off Creek, a woman homesteading alone in the Oregon mountains with no rescue arranged.
entries.signature: Diary and ledger rhythms, weather and stock treated as the plot, and a refusal to make endurance into triumph.

works.title: The Jump-Off Creek
works.note: the homestead, the winter, and the arithmetic

works.title: The Hearts of Horses
works.note: the horse economy and the woman breaking for it

works.title: Wild Life
works.note: the Northwest, and the edges of the plausible

entries.name: Annie Proulx
entries.description: The writer of the contemporary ranch West at its least hospitable to the myth.
entries.meta: American, born 1935 and confirmed living. Her Pulitzer (1994) and National Book Award (1993) are for The Shipping News, not for a western. The pack hands "Brokeback Mountain" to the literary-reference pack and keeps only the residual: what the Wyoming stories say about the ranch economy and about who is permitted to remain in it.
entries.knownFor: Close Range: Wyoming Stories, in which the landscape is indifferent and the economics are the antagonist.
entries.signature: Compressed violent incident, ranch and rodeo vocabulary used without glossing, and endings that decline to console.

works.title: Close Range: Wyoming Stories
works.note: the Wyoming stories, and the country that does not care

works.title: Bad Dirt
works.note: the second Wyoming collection

works.title: That Old Ace in the Hole
works.note: the panhandle, and the hog-farm buyer

entries.name: Paulette Jiles
entries.description: The novelist who reopened the captivity-return narrative, which is the genre's oldest layer.
entries.meta: American, long resident in Canada, 1943–2025. News of the World was a National Book Award finalist in 2016, not a winner, and her 1985 Governor General's Award is for poetry. Her death in July 2025 post-dates several reference works still describing her as living.
entries.knownFor: News of the World, in which the return of a captive child is a transaction, a journey and an unresolved question about where she belongs.
entries.signature: Spare declarative sentences, period detail carried lightly, and returns that are never presented as restorations.

works.title: News of the World
works.note: the captive returned, and the man paid to do it

works.title: Simon the Fiddler
works.note: the Texas of the immediate post-war years

works.title: Chenneville

entries.category: Black Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Oscar Micheaux
entries.description: The homesteader who wrote his own claim as a novel and then filmed it — the ground clause in the first person.
entries.meta: American, 1884–1951. He homesteaded in South Dakota, wrote the experience as fiction, sold the books door to door and built a film company on the proceeds. The 1919 film of The Homesteader is lost: the pack describes the novel and the production record and does not describe scenes or shots that no one can see.
entries.knownFor: The Homesteader, as novel and as the lost film, and a race-film career of some forty features.
entries.signature: Autobiography barely disguised, uplift argued directly to the audience, and production economics visible in every frame that survives.

works.title: The Homesteader
works.note: the novel of the Dakota claim

works.title: The Conquest
works.note: the first, and the most nearly documentary

works.title: Body and Soul
works.note: the surviving silent, and Robeson's first film

entries.category: Black Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Nat Love
entries.description: The trail-drive memoirist whose book is the substrate testimony under every Black-cowboy card in the pack.
entries.meta: American, born enslaved in Tennessee, 1854–1921. Name collision, stated and not adjudicated: Love claimed the name Deadwood Dick for himself in 1876, and Edward L. Wheeler's dime-novel Deadwood Dick, who is fictional and white, first appeared in 1877. The memoir is also unreliable by design, written to make a claim to standing rather than to file a record.
entries.knownFor: The Life and Adventures of Nat Love, the 1907 memoir, and a working life that ended as a Pullman porter.
entries.signature: Tall-tale rhythm used to insist on competence, and every contest presented as one he entered and won.

works.title: The Life and Adventures of Nat Love
works.note: the cattle country, and the name claimed in it

entries.category: Black Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Sidney Poitier
entries.description: The director of one of the first studio westerns made by a Black film-maker, about a Black claim to passage.
entries.meta: Bahamian-American, 1927–2022. He replaced Joseph Sargent during production of Buck and the Preacher and took the direction credit, which has a history worth stating. His Academy Award — the thirty-sixth ceremony, in 1964, for the 1963 Lilies of the Field — is not for a western.
entries.knownFor: Buck and the Preacher, in which a Black wagon train defends its right to move and the bounty men are the law.
entries.signature: Genre furniture used straight rather than parodied, with the racial arrangement of the West stated as the plot's premise rather than its theme.

works.title: Buck and the Preacher
works.note: the wagon train, the labour agents, and the road out

works.title: A Warm December
works.note: outside the genre, and the second directing credit

works.title: Uptown Saturday Night
works.note: the comedy that made the directing career commercial

entries.category: Black Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Mario Van Peebles
entries.description: The director who put Black cavalry and Black townsites back into the studio western's own iconography.
entries.meta: American, born 1957. Posse was written by Sy Richardson and Dario Scardapane; what is Van Peebles's is the direction, and the pack keeps the two claims apart. The film frames itself with documentary material about all-Black towns, which is the argument it is making about the genre.
entries.knownFor: Posse, the deliberate reinsertion — Buffalo Soldiers, a Black town, and the land speculation that took it.
entries.signature: The 1990s action register applied to the western, with historical citation used as a frame around a revenge plot.

works.title: Posse
works.note: the Black town, and who wanted the ground it stood on

works.title: Outlaw Posse
works.note: the late return to the same material

works.title: Panther
works.note: outside the genre, and the same documentary framing

entries.category: Black Writers and Film-makers of the West
entries.name: Jeymes Samuel
entries.description: The film-maker who assembled real Black western figures into an invented plot and put the fact on a title card.
entries.meta: British, born 1979, with a Nigerian mother and an Afro-Brazilian father — a Black British film-maker in a block titled "of the West", which the card states rather than letting the block name imply an American. He directed and scored The Harder They Fall and shares the screenplay credit with Boaz Yakin, so two of the three claims are his alone and the third is not.
entries.knownFor: The Harder They Fall, whose opening card says these people existed and this did not happen.
entries.signature: Documented figures used as a cast, a contemporary score run against period image, and colour used to reject the genre's dust palette.

works.title: The Harder They Fall

works.title: They Die by Dawn
works.note: the short that established the method

works.title: The Book of Clarence
works.note: outside the genre, and the same iconographic argument

entries.name: Américo Paredes
entries.description: The scholar who recovered the borderland's own counter-western from the ballads that carried it.
entries.meta: Mexican-American, of Brownsville, Texas, 1915–1999. He is equally placeable among the pack's historians and is placed here once, by the tradition-blocks-take-precedence rule. His case against the Texas Rangers' record is a scholarly argument with named opponents and the pack states it as an argument rather than as a finding.
entries.knownFor: "With His Pistol in His Hand", the study of the corrido of Gregorio Cortez — a man shot at by the Rangers and sung about by the people they were shooting at.
entries.signature: A folk form read as a historical record kept by the side that lost, with the ballad's variants treated as evidence rather than as corruption.

works.title: "With His Pistol in His Hand"
works.note: the corrido, the manhunt, and the record from the other side

works.title: George Washington Gómez
works.note: written in the 1930s and published almost sixty years later

works.title: Between Two Worlds
works.note: the poems

entries.name: Rudolfo Anaya
entries.description: The novelist of New Mexican land grants and water rights — title the 1848 treaty was supposed to protect.
entries.meta: American, Nuevo Mexicano, 1937–2020. Bless Me, Ultima is among the most frequently banned books in United States schools, which is a documented record rather than an opinion about the book. His ground is the acequia and the grant rather than the range.
entries.knownFor: Bless Me, Ultima, and a New Mexico in which the contested claim is inherited, legal and older than the state.
entries.signature: Curanderismo and Catholic practice held together without either explaining the other, and land treated as a relation rather than as an asset.

works.title: Bless Me, Ultima
works.note: the llano, the river, and the two families' claims

works.title: Heart of Aztlán
works.note: the move to the city and the loss of the grant

works.title: Alburquerque
works.note: the developer's West, in its own spelling

entries.name: Gloria Anzaldúa
entries.description: The theorist who replaced the frontier's vocabulary on the southern axis, where the line is a wound rather than an edge.
entries.meta: American, of South Texas, 1942–2004. She is not a western by iconography: the pack admits her on the ground clause and on lineage, and the card says so rather than letting the block placement imply otherwise. Borderlands mixes English, Spanish, Nahuatl and Tex-Mex within single paragraphs on purpose.
entries.knownFor: Borderlands / La Frontera, and the border read as an open wound where two worlds grate against each other.
entries.signature: Theory, memoir and poetry in one text, with the code-switching used as the argument rather than as its illustration.

works.title: Borderlands / La Frontera: The New Mestiza
works.note: the border as a wound, and the vocabulary that follows

works.title: This Bridge Called My Back
works.note: co-edited, and the anthology that made the field

entries.name: Luis Alberto Urrea
entries.description: The writer of the desert crossing, which is the ground clause in its live contemporary form.
entries.meta: American, born in Tijuana in 1955. The Devil's Highway was a Pulitzer finalist in 2005, not a winner, and the misattribution is common. He worked as a relief-crew translator on the border before he wrote about it, which is where the reporting comes from.
entries.knownFor: The Devil's Highway, the account of twenty-six men who walked into the Arizona desert in May 2001 and the fourteen who did not walk out.
entries.signature: Reconstructed interior life laid over documentary record, with the machinery — smugglers, agencies, heat — named precisely.

works.title: The Devil's Highway
works.note: the crossing, the count, and the paperwork afterwards

works.title: The Hummingbird's Daughter
works.note: the Sonoran saint, and the border before the fence

works.title: Into the Beautiful North
works.note: the crossing reversed, as comedy

entries.name: Robert Rodriguez
entries.description: The director who reproduced the Italian cycle's furniture on the border without its settlement argument.
entries.meta: American, of San Antonio, born 1968. The pack's clearest documented case of lineage acquisition on the southern axis: he takes Leone's grammar directly and applies it to a Mexican border town. The El Mariachi budget legend is an entrenched production myth with a more complicated real figure and the pack does not repeat it as fact.
entries.knownFor: The Mariachi trilogy, in which the iconography circulates freely and no claim to ground is being settled at all.
entries.signature: Extreme economy of means presented as style, and genre citation performed openly rather than absorbed.

works.title: El Mariachi
works.note: the first feature, and the method

works.title: Desperado
works.note: the studio restatement, at scale

works.title: Once Upon a Time in Mexico

entries.category: Asian American Writers of the West
entries.name: Ruthanne Lum McCunn
entries.description: The strongest single fit in the block: a woman sold into a mining camp who ends holding an Idaho homestead.
entries.meta: American, of Chinese and Scottish descent, born 1946. Thousand Pieces of Gold is a biographical novel, and the documentary record on Lalu Nathoy's sale, her marriage and the ownership of the ranch is thin and disputed; the pack does not card the novel's incidents as history. The film is a separate claim, and its year is itself contested — 1990 by its first public showing, 1991 by its general release.
entries.knownFor: Thousand Pieces of Gold, in which a claim to ground and a claim to personhood are contested in the same transaction.
entries.signature: Archival research narrated as fiction, with the gaps in the record left visible rather than filled in confidently.

works.title: Thousand Pieces of Gold
works.note: the mining camp, the saloon, and the homestead at the end

works.title: Wooden Fish Songs
works.note: the same method, told through three women

works.title: Sole Survivor
works.note: the record, and what survives of it

entries.category: Asian American Writers of the West
entries.name: Maxine Hong Kingston
entries.description: The writer who put the Sierra Nevada railroad grade back into the frontier's founding story.
entries.meta: American, born 1940. Her 1981 prize for China Men is in the nonfiction category, and in that period the National Book Awards were branded the American Book Awards — which collides directly with the Before Columbus Foundation's American Book Award named on Frank Chin's card. Name the body and the year together or not at all. Frank Chin's long public attack on her, on Amy Tan and on David Henry Hwang for what he calls stereotyping is documented, and he is carded in this same block: the pack states the dispute and does not stage it.
entries.knownFor: China Men, and the labour contract under the continental railroad the myth is built on top of.
entries.signature: Family history and legal history braided together, with statutes reproduced inside the narrative as its own kind of document.

works.title: China Men
works.note: the grade, the contract, and the men erased from the photograph

works.title: The Woman Warrior
works.note: the earlier book, and the method

works.title: Tripmaster Monkey
works.note: the novel

entries.category: Asian American Writers of the West
entries.name: Frank Chin
entries.description: The writer who put the Chinese workers back into the Promontory Summit photograph they were cropped out of.
entries.meta: American, born 1940. His three American Book Awards (1982, 1989, 2000) are from the Before Columbus Foundation, which the pack names rather than leaving as a generic honour. His attacks on Kingston, Tan and Hwang are a documented controversy and are stated on both his card and hers.
entries.knownFor: Donald Duk, in which a boy dreams the railroad his history textbook has left him out of.
entries.signature: Confrontational polemic carried inside comic fiction, with the erasure treated as an act rather than as an omission.

works.title: Donald Duk
works.note: the photograph, and who was moved out of frame

works.title: The Chickencoop Chinaman
works.note: the play, first staged at the American Place Theatre

works.title: Gunga Din Highway
works.note: Hollywood, and the parts available

entries.category: Asian American Writers of the West
entries.name: C Pam Zhang
entries.description: The novelist who wrote the gold rush from inside a Chinese mining family, in the genre's own furniture.
entries.meta: American, born 1990; her name carries no full stop after the C. How Much of These Hills Is Gold was longlisted for the Booker Prize in 2020 — not shortlisted and not a winner. All three of the pack's clauses are present in it: the prospecting claim, the burial ground, and the right to remain.
entries.knownFor: How Much of These Hills Is Gold, a novel that opens with two children carrying their father's body looking for ground to put it in.
entries.signature: Gold-rush landscape rendered as a worked-out ruin, and a family whose claim is refused in every register at once.

works.note: the claim, the body, and the ground to bury it in

works.title: Land of Milk and Honey
works.note: the later novel, outside the genre

entries.category: Australian and Aotearoa Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Warwick Thornton
entries.description: The director of the Australian frontier's most exact statement of the pack's organising claim.
entries.meta: Kaytetye, of Central Australia, born 1970 and confirmed working in 2025. He shares Sweet Country's cinematography with Dylan River; the film's use of Arrernte alongside English is named in the pack's craft collection. His Caméra d'Or at Cannes in 2009 is a first-feature festival prize and not a best-film award, and Sweet Country took the Special Jury Prize at Venice in 2017, not the Golden Lion.
entries.knownFor: Sweet Country, a Northern Territory killing, a manhunt and a trial, filmed in the genre's grammar from the other side of it.
entries.signature: No score at all, landscape shot as country rather than as scenery, and flash-forwards that tell you the verdict before the argument.

entries.category: Australian and Aotearoa Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Ivan Sen
entries.description: The maker of the Australian neo-western procedural, where the mining lease is the claim and the law is the force.
entries.meta: Gamilaraay, through his mother; born 1972. On several titles he is director, writer, cinematographer, editor and composer — five separate credits that happen to be one person, which the pack states rather than blurring into authorship. His detective works on country his own family has a claim to.
entries.knownFor: Mystery Road and Goldstone, in which an Aboriginal detective investigates crimes the mining company would prefer left alone.
entries.signature: Aerial landscape against interior close-up, long silences, and a protagonist estranged from both the police and the community.

entries.category: Australian and Aotearoa Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Rachel Perkins
entries.description: The director of the documentary that names the frontier wars as wars.
entries.meta: Arrernte and Kalkadoon, born 1970. She founded Blackfella Films, which is a production credit distinct from direction and is stated as such. One Night the Moon is a musical drama rather than a documentary and is regularly miscatalogued.
entries.knownFor: The Australian Wars, which argues that what happened on the Australian frontier was warfare and should be counted, named and memorialised as such.
entries.signature: Archival record set against country and against descendants' testimony, with the argument made in the structure rather than in narration.

entries.category: Australian and Aotearoa Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Barry Barclay
entries.description: The film-maker who supplied the theoretical frame the pack's Indigenous counter-western card runs on.
entries.meta: Ngāti Apa, Te Āti Haunui-a-Pāpārangi and Ngāti Hauiti, with Pākehā descent as well; 1944–2008. Ngati is routinely called the first feature film by an Indigenous director anywhere, which is too strong; the defensible claim is a dramatic feature written and directed by Māori — Barclay directed and Tama Poata wrote it — and the pack uses that wording, which is a collective claim rather than a claim about one person.
entries.knownFor: Fourth Cinema — film made from inside an Indigenous nation, addressed first to that nation, and answerable to it.
entries.signature: The camera positioned as a guest, community consent treated as part of the method, and the audience assumed to be the people filmed.

works.note: the coastal community; directed by Barclay, written by Tama Poata

works.title: Tangata Whenua
works.note: the series that established the practice

works.title: Our Own Image

entries.category: Australian and Aotearoa Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Jane Campion
entries.description: A Montana ranch western made by a New Zealand director and shot in New Zealand, which is why the card sits here.
entries.meta: New Zealand, born 1954. The block placement is deliberate and the card states its reason: the film is American in setting and antipodean in authorship and production throughout. Her 1993 Palme d'Or was shared with Chen Kaige's Farewell My Concubine; her Best Director Oscar is from the ninety-fourth ceremony in 2022 for a 2021 film.
entries.knownFor: The Power of the Dog, from Thomas Savage's 1967 novel — a 1925 ranch in which the contest is over the household rather than the range.
entries.signature: Landscape used as a psychological instrument, cruelty conducted in domestic registers, and a plot whose real action is only legible in retrospect.

works.note: the ranch, the brother, and the rope

works.title: The Piano
works.note: the earlier frontier film, and the settlement it depicts

works.note: the first feature

entries.category: The Italian Cycle and Its Writers
entries.name: Sergio Leone
entries.description: The centre of the Italian cycle, and the pack's model case for admission on lineage rather than on ground.
entries.meta: Italian, 1929–1989. His films substitute money for land and are admitted on the lineage clause, which the pack states rather than smuggling. The lineage citation is documented as a lawsuit: Toho sued over Per un pugno di dollari and Kurosawa's Yojimbo (1961) and the matter was settled in Toho's favour. Italian and English release titles and years differ by up to three years; the pack gives both.
entries.knownFor: The Dollars trilogy and C'era una volta il West — the western reassembled by someone who learned it from the films rather than from the country.
entries.signature: Extreme duration held against extreme close-up, ritual delay before violence, and a score written before the shoot and played on set.

works.title: C'era una volta il West
works.note: released in English as Once Upon a Time in the West; the railroad, the water, and the land

works.title: Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo
works.note: the cycle at its largest, and the war it walks through

works.title: Per un pugno di dollari
works.note: the acquisition, and the suit that followed

entries.category: The Italian Cycle and Its Writers
entries.name: Sergio Corbucci
entries.description: The cycle's political wing and its nihilist wing at once, and the maker of the one entry that inverts the ending.
entries.meta: Italian, born 6 December in either 1926 or 1927 — reputable sources give both and the pack flags the disagreement rather than picking; died 1990. The name Django was never trademarked, producing dozens of unofficial sequels with no connection to him — the count is given anywhere between thirty and fifty and the pack states none of them — and none should be attributed to him.
entries.knownFor: Django and Il grande silenzio — the coffin dragged through mud, and a snowbound west where the ending goes the other way.
entries.signature: Mud, snow and disfigurement in place of the cycle's dust and heat, and protagonists physically ruined before the last act.

works.title: Il grande silenzio
works.note: released in English as The Great Silence; the ending the genre does not permit

works.title: Django
works.note: the coffin dragged through mud, and the image the cycle returned to most

works.title: Vamos a matar, compañeros
works.note: the Zapata western at its most cheerful

entries.category: The Italian Cycle and Its Writers
entries.name: Franco Solinas
entries.description: The writer who carried the anti-colonial argument out of Algiers and into the Zapata western.
entries.meta: Italian, 1927–1982. A writer, not a director, and this block is titled "and Its Writers" for that reason. The screenplay credit on Quién sabe? is shared and contested with Salvatore Laurani, which the pack states. He wrote La battaglia di Algeri in the same period, which is where the political method comes from.
entries.knownFor: Quién sabe?, in which the American in the revolution turns out to be working for someone, and the peasant works it out too late.
entries.signature: The political relation made into the plot's actual mechanism, and the foreigner's motive withheld until it can be used.

works.title: Quién sabe?
works.note: released in English as A Bullet for the General; the Zapata western's argument, stated

entries.category: The Italian Cycle and Its Writers
entries.name: Luciano Vincenzoni
entries.description: The structural architect of the two largest films in the cycle, and the other half of its longest credit dispute.
entries.meta: Italian, 1926–2013. A writer. He and Leone publicly disputed the division of credit for decades; the pack states it as a dispute between two named parties and adopts neither account. He also brokered the American distribution deal that made the cycle internationally visible.
entries.knownFor: Per qualche dollaro in più and Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo — the two-bounty-hunter structure and the three-way search.
entries.signature: Clean commercial architecture under baroque surfaces, with the plot's engine reducible to a single sentence in every case.

works.title: Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo
works.note: the three-way structure, and the graveyard at the end of it

works.title: Per qualche dollaro in più
works.note: the partnership plot the cycle reused everywhere

works.title: Il mercenario
works.note: screenplay, with Sergio Spina, over a Solinas and Arlorio story

entries.category: The Italian Cycle and Its Writers
entries.name: Sergio Sollima
entries.description: One of the cycle's two explicitly political directors, and the maker of its ideological reversal film.
entries.meta: Italian, 1921–2015. Frequently confused with his son, the director Stefano Sollima, which is a live collision in reference works. He was a partisan during the war, which is the background his political westerns are usually read against.
entries.knownFor: Faccia a faccia, in which the professor and the bandit exchange positions completely over the course of the film.
entries.signature: Two protagonists whose politics are the actual subject, and a pursuit structure used to keep them arguing.

works.title: Faccia a faccia
works.note: released in English as Face to Face; the reversal, carried out in full

works.title: La resa dei conti
works.note: the manhunt, and who benefits from it

works.title: Corri uomo corri
works.note: the sequel, and the revolution's money

entries.category: The Italian Cycle and Its Writers
entries.name: Duccio Tessari
entries.description: The writer-director who set the cycle's commercial template, which is the industrial layer under everything else in this block.
entries.meta: Italian, 1926–1994. He co-wrote Per un pugno di dollari and then made the two Ringo films in a single year. The two Ringo pictures share a star and a year and are not a continuous story, which is a standing error in reference works.
entries.knownFor: Una pistola per Ringo and Il ritorno di Ringo — the clean, saleable version of the cycle, and a commercial template the imitators had in front of them.
entries.signature: Bright, brisk and legible where Leone is slow and monumental, with a hero who talks and a plot that resolves.

works.title: Una pistola per Ringo
works.note: the template, and the market it opened

works.title: Il ritorno di Ringo
works.note: the same star, a different story, and the Odyssey underneath it

works.title: Vivi o, preferibilmente, morti
works.note: the comic turn, before it took the cycle over

entries.category: The Italian Cycle and Its Writers
entries.name: Enzo Barboni
entries.description: The director whose comedy outgrossed the serious films and ended the cycle commercially.
entries.meta: Italian, 1922–2002. He directed under the pseudonym E. B. Clucher and worked as a cinematographer under his own name — two credits and one man, which the pack does not merge. The Trinità films are the pack's second mode inside the cycle: the iconography circulating with no settlement argument left in it at all.
entries.knownFor: Lo chiamavano Trinità, the slapstick western that sold more admissions in Italy than any western made there before it.
entries.signature: Fistfights choreographed as farce, appetite and idleness in place of the cycle's fatalism, and every ritual it inherited played for a laugh.

works.title: Lo chiamavano Trinità
works.note: the comedy that took the market

works.title: …continuavano a chiamarlo Trinità
works.note: the sequel, and the cycle's commercial end

entries.category: The German and Eastern Bloc West
entries.name: Karl May
entries.description: The European West's founding prose, and the start of the pack's longest documented lineage chain.
entries.meta: German, 1842–1912. Established and not disputed: he had never been to the American West when he wrote the books, served multiple prison terms for fraud and impersonation, and for years publicly presented himself as Old Shatterhand. Both later German cycles descend from him — the West German films to film him, and the East German Indianerfilme to answer him.
entries.knownFor: Winnetou, the Apache chief narrated by his German blood brother, and a figure still in print and in production more than a century after the books.
entries.signature: First-person adventure delivered with the authority of a witness who was never there, and a friendship across the frontier used to license everything else.

works.title: Winnetou I–III
works.note: the trilogy, and the figure Europe inherited

works.title: Der Schatz im Silbersee
works.note: the treasure hunt, and the most-filmed of them

works.title: Old Surehand
works.note: the later cycle

entries.category: The German and Eastern Bloc West
entries.name: Liselotte Welskopf-Henrich
entries.description: The classical historian whose Lakota novels the East German cycle was built from.
entries.meta: German, of the GDR, 1901–1979. A scholar of antiquity who also studied Lakota history and did fieldwork at Pine Ridge; her scholarship and her fiction are separate bodies of work with separate standards and the pack does not cite the novels as ethnography. The whole DEFA cycle begins by adapting her.
entries.knownFor: Die Söhne der Großen Bärin, the novel cycle that supplied the Indianerfilme their material and their sympathies.
entries.signature: Historical research carried into adventure fiction for young readers, with the dispossession stated as policy rather than as misfortune.

works.title: Die Söhne der Großen Bärin
works.note: the cycle's first volume; the source the film cycle opens with

works.title: Nacht über der Prärie
works.note: the first volume of the later Das Blut des Adlers cycle, set in the twentieth century

entries.category: The German and Eastern Bloc West
entries.name: Harald Reinl
entries.description: The director of the West German Karl May cycle — the commercial engine that made the Italian cycle financeable.
entries.meta: Austrian, 1908–1986. Two documented items belong on the card: his work on Leni Riefenstahl productions, including a screenwriting credit on Tiefland — which is the extent of what the record supports, and narrower than the general claim usually made — and his killing in 1986 by his wife. The Karl May films were shot largely in Yugoslavia, which is the production arrangement the Italian cycle then borrowed.
entries.knownFor: Winnetou 1. Teil and Der Schatz im Silbersee — May filmed straight, in wide colour, for a mass European audience.
entries.signature: Postcard landscape, uncomplicated heroism, and a friendship across the frontier presented without any of the period's actual politics.

works.title: Der Schatz im Silbersee
works.note: the cycle's opening, and the boom it started

works.title: Winnetou 1. Teil
works.note: the character, filmed

works.title: Winnetou und Shatterhand im Tal der Toten
works.note: the late entry

entries.category: The German and Eastern Bloc West
entries.name: Josef Mach
entries.description: The director of the first Indianerfilm, whose credit block contains the pack's entire international argument.
entries.meta: Czech, 1909–1987. The birthday coincidence given in several reference works does not survive checking — the DEFA Film Library gives 25 February 1909 and 7 July 1987 — and the pack states the years only. A Czech director working for an East German state studio, adapting a German woman's novels about Lakota people, with a Serbian actor in the lead — one credit block, four nationalities, and an American genre.
entries.knownFor: Die Söhne der großen Bärin, the 1966 film that opened the DEFA cycle and made it state policy to run it.
entries.signature: The studio western's grammar kept intact and its sympathies reversed, with the settler as the aggressor from the first scene.

works.title: Die Söhne der großen Bärin
works.note: the cycle's first, and the reversal

entries.category: The German and Eastern Bloc West
entries.name: Gottfried Kolditz
entries.description: One of the two directors who made most of the Indianerfilme, and the one who staged a named historical massacre from the Apache side.
entries.meta: German, of the GDR, 1922–1982. Apachen and Ulzana are a linked pair rather than a series with sequels. He worked across musicals and science fiction as well, which is what a state studio's contract director did.
entries.knownFor: Apachen, which reconstructs the 1837 Santa Rita del Cobre killings — the Johnson scalp-hunting massacre of Mimbreño Apache — as the work of a mining company's men.
entries.signature: Atrocity attributed to commercial rather than military actors, and an Indigenous lead given the film's entire moral authority.

works.title: Apachen
works.note: the massacre, staged from the other side

works.title: Ulzana
works.note: the linked second film, and the reservation after

works.title: Spur des Falken
works.note: the earlier entry, and the gold claim

entries.category: The German and Eastern Bloc West
entries.name: Vladimir Motyl
entries.description: The director of the Ostern's canonical entry, which the pack admits on lineage rather than on ground.
entries.meta: Soviet and Russian, 1927–2010. Beloye solntse pustyni, released in English as White Sun of the Desert, moves the form to Central Asia after the revolution, where the contested authority is revolutionary rather than juridical — which is why the pack rejected the claim that the western is a story about the time before law arrives. He grew up in the Gulag system's orbit; his father died in it.
entries.knownFor: Beloye solntse pustyni, the Red Army soldier, the harem he is made responsible for, and the desert between him and home.
entries.signature: Comic and elegiac registers held together, songs used as structure, and an ending that refuses the heroic form the state wanted.

works.title: Beloye solntse pustyni
works.note: the Ostern proper, and the form relocated

entries.category: Latin American Writers and Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Glauber Rocha
entries.description: The nordestern's central director, in a tradition the pack admits on principle rather than by exception.
entries.meta: Brazilian, 1939–1981. The sertão is contested ground and the cangaceiro and the jagunço are the tradition's own figures, so nothing has to be stretched to admit them. His estética da fome is a 1965 manifesto, not a film, and is regularly cited as though it were one; the pack gives the year and not the venue, which it could not establish. Portuguese titles and years are given alongside English release titles.
entries.knownFor: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol, in which a cowherd kills his boss and walks into a landscape offering him a prophet and a bandit.
entries.signature: Handheld camera in white light, folk ballad used as narration, and a politics stated openly inside the fiction.

works.title: Deus e o Diabo na Terra do Sol
works.note: released in English as Black God, White Devil; the sertão, the prophet and the bandit

works.title: O Dragão da Maldade contra o Santo Guerreiro
works.note: the sequel, and the killer working for both sides

works.title: Terra em Transe
works.note: outside the genre, and the politics without the ballad

entries.category: Latin American Writers and Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Emilio Fernández
entries.description: The director who built the Mexican revolutionary and charro traditions the Italian cycle later quoted.
entries.meta: Mexican, 1904–1986. Two documented items belong on the card: he shot and killed a farm worker in May 1976, was sentenced to four years and six months, and served a small part of it. The 1930s item often attached to him is not a conviction: it is his return to Mexico under the amnesty following the 1923 de la Huerta rebellion, and the pack does not convert it into one. His name "El Indio" and his claimed Kickapoo ancestry are his own account and the pack states them as his claim.
entries.knownFor: Flor Silvestre and María Candelaria — the films through which a visual grammar of low horizon and enormous sky travelled, though the grammar itself is Gabriel Figueroa's.
entries.signature: Gabriel Figueroa's clouds and silhouettes, revolution rendered as national tragedy, and peasants photographed as monuments.

works.title: Flor Silvestre
works.note: the revolution, the hacienda, and the marriage across it

works.title: María Candelaria
works.note: the village, and what it does to the woman it decides about

works.title: Enamorada
works.note: the occupied town and its two antagonists

entries.category: Latin American Writers and Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Alejandro Jodorowsky
entries.description: The acid western's defining film, and the genre's furniture turned directly against the settlement argument.
entries.meta: Chilean-French, born 1929 and confirmed living. Documented and severe, and it must be given in three positions rather than two. In the book El Topo: A Book of the Film — dated 1971 or 1972 depending on the source — he stated that he had actually raped his co-star during the filming. In a 2007 interview he revised rather than withdrew it, saying he had not raped her but had penetrated her with her consent. Later still, in 2017 and again in 2019, he described the original statement as invented provocation. All three are on the record; the pack states all three, adjudicates none, and does not omit any of them.
entries.knownFor: El Topo, the gunfighter's progress through the desert as a sequence of duels that are also a religious argument.
entries.signature: Symbolic tableau in place of scene, mutilation used as vocabulary, and a hero whose competence is the thing being dismantled.

works.title: El Topo
works.note: the desert, the four masters, and the film the term was later coined around

works.title: La montaña sagrada
works.note: released in English as The Holy Mountain; outside the genre, and the same method at full extension

works.title: Santa Sangre
works.note: the late film

entries.category: Latin American Writers and Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: José Hernández
entries.description: The author of the gaucho tradition's central claim-to-ground poem, written as a political intervention.
entries.meta: Argentine, 1834–1886. Martín Fierro is a partisan document against Sarmiento's frontier policy rather than a folk artefact, and reading it as folklore removes its argument. Conscription, the frontier fort and the gaucho's expropriation are its actual subjects.
entries.knownFor: El gaucho Martín Fierro, and the return poem that follows it seven years later with a different politics.
entries.signature: Payada verse form used as testimony, a first-person complaint sustained for thousands of lines, and the state present as the antagonist throughout.

works.title: El gaucho Martín Fierro
works.note: the conscription, the fort, and the desertion

works.title: La vuelta de Martín Fierro
works.note: the return, and the accommodation

entries.category: Latin American Writers and Film-makers of the Frontier
entries.name: Guillermo Arriaga
entries.description: The writer of the contemporary border western: a body, a burial ground, and a claim to be returned to it.
entries.meta: Mexican, born 1958. A writer, and his public credit dispute with the director Alejandro G. Iñárritu is documented and belongs on the card. His Cannes Best Screenplay in 2005 is a festival prize; The film was directed by Tommy Lee Jones, which is a separate claim.
entries.knownFor: The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada — an American film with an English original title, carded as such against the block's Spanish-title convention — in which a Texas rancher abducts the border patrolman who killed his friend and marches him into Mexico with the body.
entries.signature: Fractured chronology assembled around a single act of violence, and the border crossed in the direction the genre never films.

works.title: The Three Burials of Melquiades Estrada
works.note: the body, the burial, and the crossing south

works.title: Amores perros
works.note: the earlier structure, in the city

works.title: The Burning Plain
works.note: the border again, and the family across it

entries.category: Japanese Cinema, Manga and the Western
entries.name: Akira Kurosawa
entries.description: The one node in the pack where the lineage runs both directions with documents on both legs.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1910–1998. The exchange, not the influence: Ford's films going in by Kurosawa's own repeated statement, and two acquisitions coming out — The Magnificent Seven (1960) licensed through Lou Morheim to Yul Brynner, and Per un pugno di dollari (1964) not licensed, with Toho suing and the matter settled out of court on reported terms rather than adjudicated. Japanese titles and years are given alongside English release titles.
entries.knownFor: Shichinin no samurai and Yojimbo — the hired defenders of a village, and the man who sets two gangs against each other.
entries.signature: Group assembled and differentiated at speed, weather used as pressure, and violence staged as short, ugly and decisive.

works.title: Shichinin no samurai
works.note: released in English as Seven Samurai; the recruitment, the village, and the rain

works.title: Yojimbo
works.note: the two gangs, and the acquisition that ended in a settlement

works.title: Kakushi-toride no san-akunin
works.note: the fortress, and the two peasants

entries.category: Japanese Cinema, Manga and the Western
entries.name: Shinobu Hashimoto
entries.description: A writer of the film the entire western exchange is built on, and the author of the chanbara's hardest revision.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1918–2018. The screenplay credits on the Kurosawa films are shared with Kurosawa and Hideo Oguni and the pack does not card sole authorship. Seppuku is his own project rather than Kurosawa's, and is the direct anti-heroic answer to the form he had helped build.
entries.knownFor: Shichinin no samurai, co-written, and Seppuku, in which the ritual the genre is decorated with is shown as an administrative cruelty.
entries.signature: Structural rigour under long running times, and a plot that withholds its actual grievance until the last possible position.

works.title: Seppuku
works.note: released in English as Harakiri; the ritual, and who is being served by it

works.title: Shichinin no samurai
works.note: co-written; the structure the exchange was built on

works.title: Rashomon
works.note: the earlier collaboration, and the method

entries.category: Japanese Cinema, Manga and the Western
entries.name: Kazuo Koike
entries.description: The writer who carried the cycle's grammar back into Japanese print, and then out again into American comics.
entries.meta: Japanese, 1936–2019. A writer, not an artist: Goseki Kojima drew Kozure Ōkami, and the two claims are separate. The manga's American reprinting in the 1980s is the documented route by which the return leg reached English-language comics.
entries.knownFor: Kozure Ōkami, the disgraced executioner pushing his infant son's cart along a road of contract killings.
entries.signature: Wordless pages held for as long as a duel takes, an implacable protagonist with a stated code, and violence delivered in a single panel.

works.title: Kozure Ōkami
works.note: published in English as Lone Wolf and Cub; the road, the cart, and the contracts

works.title: Kubikiri Asa
works.note: the executioner again, and the trade

works.title: Crying Freeman
works.note: the later series, and the method exported

entries.category: Japanese Cinema, Manga and the Western
entries.name: Shinichirō Watanabe
entries.description: The pack's second mode in animation: the iconography reproduced with the settlement argument fully detached.
entries.meta: Japanese, born 1965. Cowboy Bebop is a twenty-six-episode television series and a separate 2001 film — two works with two different medium values, and the pack keeps them apart. The series knows exactly what it is quoting, which is why it is the second mode's cleanest case rather than an accident of style.
entries.knownFor: Cowboy Bebop, a bounty-hunter crew in the solar system with the western's furniture and none of its land.
entries.signature: Genre pastiche assembled per episode, jazz scoring used structurally, and a melancholy the source material never had.

works.title: Cowboy Bebop
works.note: the series; the iconography in orbit

works.title: Samurai Champloo
works.note: the same method, on the other side of the exchange

entries.name: Ramesh Sippy
entries.description: The director of the film that answers Leone and Kurosawa at once, which is the pack's stated lineage case for the dacoit western.
entries.meta: Indian, born 1947 and confirmed living. Sholay's original ending was changed by the censor board and later restored, so any description must name the cut it means. Its box-office figures vary enormously between sources and are frequently restated in unadjusted or unsourced form; the pack repeats none of them.
entries.knownFor: Sholay, in which a retired policeman hires two convicts to take a village back from a bandit.
entries.signature: Seventy-millimetre landscape and stereophonic sound applied to a village-siege plot, with comedy, song and massacre in the same picture.

works.title: Sholay
works.note: the village, the two hired men, and the bandit

works.title: Shaan
works.note: the follow-up, and the same scale

works.title: Shakti
works.note: the family drama, and the other tradition

entries.name: Salim–Javed
entries.description: The credit through which Indian screenwriting became an authorial category with a name on the poster.
entries.meta: A two-person writing unit — Salim Khan, born 1935, and Javed Akhtar, born 1945; both living. The credit reads as a single name and the pack cards the authorial unit rather than splitting a joint credit into two half-cards, which is a schema decision the build log records. Akhtar's National Film Awards are largely for lyrics, which is a separate claim from screenwriting.
entries.knownFor: Sholay and Deewaar — the bandit siege and the angry-young-man structure that dominated a decade of Indian cinema.
entries.signature: A wronged man, a stated grievance and a plot built to deliver it, with dialogue written to be quoted back before the audience leaves.

works.title: Deewaar
works.note: the same year, and the other tradition it founded

works.note: the first of the angry-young-man films; the partnership's credits begin in 1971

entries.name: Yılmaz Güney
entries.description: The Anatolian border western and its politicised successor, made by a director who wrote from prison and finished the work in exile.
entries.meta: Turkish and Kurdish, 1937–1984. A genuine attribution problem rather than a trivium: Yol was written by Güney in prison and directed by Şerif Gören; Güney escaped from İmralı in 1981 and edited the film in exile, so the direction credit is contested by construction. His imprisonment was repeated rather than continuous — 1961, 1972, an amnesty in 1974, re-arrest the same year, and the escape in 1981. Its 1982 Palme d'Or was shared with Costa-Gavras's Missing. He was convicted of killing a judge in 1974, a matter of record contested as political.
entries.knownFor: Yol, five prisoners on leave crossing a country that will not let any of them arrive.
entries.signature: The frontier as a border under guard, journeys that fail, and the state present in every frame as a permit.

works.title: Yol
works.note: the leave, the journeys, and the credit dispute built into it

works.title: Umut
works.note: the earlier film, and the treasure that is not there

works.title: Seyyit Han
works.note: the Yeşilçam border western proper

entries.name: A Narrative of the Captivity and Restoration of Mrs. Mary Rowlandson
entries.author: Mary Rowlandson
entries.description: Memoir. The genre's oldest layer, two centuries before the genre: a woman taken at Lancaster in King Philip's War, marched through the winter, and…
entries.text: Memoir. The genre's oldest layer, two centuries before the genre: a woman taken at Lancaster in King Philip's War, marched through the winter, and ransomed. The contested ground is a body and the force that settles it is war and money, which is the pack's claim in a form nobody had yet thought to call a western. Everything the captivity narrative later hands to the genre — the wilderness as a moral test, the returned captive as a problem — is already assembled here.

entries.name: The Last of the Mohicans
entries.author: James Fenimore Cooper
entries.description: Title to a continent argued through a captivity and an escort, with a scout who can move between the two claims and belongs to neither. The book…
entries.text: Title to a continent argued through a captivity and an escort, with a scout who can move between the two claims and belongs to neither. The book invents the genre's central figure roughly seventy years before the West it would be relocated to, which is why the western's oldest conventions predate its subject. Its Indigenous characters are sorted into a good nation and a bad one on a scheme the whole later tradition inherits, including the tradition that set out to reverse it.

entries.name: Malaeska: The Indian Wife of the White Hunter
entries.author: Ann S. Stephens
entries.description: Dime novel. Beadle's Dime Novel No. 1 — the industrial form's first title, written by a woman, about an Indigenous woman whose marriage the book…
entries.text: Dime novel. Beadle's Dime Novel No. 1 — the industrial form's first title, written by a woman, about an Indigenous woman whose marriage the book cannot allow to survive contact with white society. It had been serialised twenty-one years earlier and was reissued as the opening title of a production line, which is the more consequential fact: the western becomes a manufactured object here, priced, numbered and scheduled.

entries.name: The Virginian
entries.author: Owen Wister
entries.description: Range title, rustling, and a lynching the book argues for rather than deplores — Judge Henry's defence of frontier hanging as the people temporarily…
entries.text: Range title, rustling, and a lynching the book argues for rather than deplores — Judge Henry's defence of frontier hanging as the people temporarily resuming a power they had lent the courts is the genre's most explicit statement of its own legal theory. The walk-down, the laconic hero, the schoolteacher from the East and the sneering antagonist are all fixed here. Wister did not invent the cowboy hero; he industrialised a figure the dime novels had been selling for forty years.

entries.name: The Great Train Robbery
entries.author: dir. Edwin S. Porter
entries.description: Roughly twelve minutes — surviving prints vary — and the point at which the western becomes a thing you watch rather than read. The robbery, the…
entries.text: Roughly twelve minutes — surviving prints vary — and the point at which the western becomes a thing you watch rather than read. The robbery, the pursuit and the shot fired at the camera assemble a grammar the genre spent the next century elaborating, and the film was a western before there was any settled sense that westerns were a category. It is not the first narrative film, which is a claim regularly made for it and does not survive checking.

entries.name: The Log of a Cowboy
entries.author: Andy Adams
entries.description: A trail drive from the Rio Grande to Montana, told by a man who had done the work, and written in explicit irritation at Wister. There is almost no…
entries.text: A trail drive from the Rio Grande to Montana, told by a man who had done the work, and written in explicit irritation at Wister. There is almost no gunplay: the antagonists are the river crossings, the market, the weather and the arithmetic of getting three thousand cattle somewhere they can be sold. It is the purest instance of the pack's admitted cost — a western in which the force settling the claim is economic — and the pack's working collection runs on its material.

entries.name: Riders of the Purple Sage
entries.author: Zane Grey
entries.description: A Utah ranch whose title is contested by a church court, with the force arriving first as theocratic law and then as a gunman who lays the work down…
entries.text: A Utah ranch whose title is contested by a church court, with the force arriving first as theocratic law and then as a gunman who lays the work down and rolls a stone across the valley mouth. It sold enormously and set the pulp market's structure for thirty years: pursuit, canyon country, an outsider heroine and a resolution by withdrawal rather than by settlement. Its treatment of Mormons, and Grey's racial material generally, is part of the record and the pack names it rather than editing around it.

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Seth Jones; or, The Captives of the Frontier
entries.author: Edward S. Ellis
entries.description: Dime novel. Beadle's eighth number and its first runaway seller, which is what turned an experiment into a production line. The captivity plot is…
entries.text: Dime novel. Beadle's eighth number and its first runaway seller, which is what turned an experiment into a production line. The captivity plot is stripped to a chase, a rescue and a disguise, and the frontiersman is already a type rather than a person. Its commercial success is the reason the western was industrialised in prose before it was ever filmed.

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Buffalo Bill, the King of Border Men
entries.author: Ned Buntline
entries.description: Dime novel. A story-paper serial, running in the New York Weekly from December 1869 rather than issued as a book, and the manufacture of a living…
entries.text: Dime novel. A story-paper serial, running in the New York Weekly from December 1869 rather than issued as a book, and the manufacture of a living man into a property by a writer who then put him on a stage and eventually into an arena. Cody was a scout with a real if ordinary record; what the serial did was convert him into a character he then spent thirty years performing, until the performance was the primary document and the record the derivative one. The legend-and-fact machine the genre keeps examining starts here, with a named author and a publication date.

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Deadwood Dick, the Prince of the Road
entries.author: Edward L. Wheeler
entries.description: Dime novel. Black Hills claim-jumping answered by a road agent's counter-title, in the first of thirty-three titles Wheeler wrote in under a decade;…
entries.text: Dime novel. Black Hills claim-jumping answered by a road agent's counter-title, in the first of thirty-three titles Wheeler wrote in under a decade; it opened Beadle's Half-Dime Library rather than the Dime Novel line. The traffic between manufacture and record runs both ways here, and the two orders are opposite: Wheeler published the name in 1877, while Nat Love's memoir of 1907 dates his own acquisition of it to 1876. Publication order and claimed order do not agree, and the pack states both and adjudicates neither.

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: The Untamed
entries.author: Max Brand
entries.description: The pulp western's dominant voice arriving fully formed, with a hero who is barely human, a horse and a dog who are practically characters, and a…
entries.text: The pulp western's dominant voice arriving fully formed, with a hero who is barely human, a horse and a dog who are practically characters, and a whistled tune used as a leitmotif. Frederick Faust wrote it under one of a long list of pen names and at a rate no other writer in the genre approached. It is the second mode at industrial scale: iconography reproduced for a magazine schedule, with no interest in what a claim to ground actually costs.

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Destry Rides Again
entries.author: Max Brand
entries.description: A wrongful conviction, six years in prison, and a methodical claim on a town's respect pursued afterwards against the twelve men who put him there.…
entries.text: A wrongful conviction, six years in prison, and a methodical claim on a town's respect pursued afterwards against the twelve men who put him there. The 1939 film that made the title famous shares the name and very little else, and using one to describe the other is the pack's standing example of an adaptation that is not one. Faust's rate of production is the context: this is a good book from a writer producing them at industrial speed.

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Hondo
entries.author: Louis L'Amour
entries.description: Apache land, a woman holding a homestead on it, and a treaty already broken by the government that wrote it. L'Amour's dispatch rider is his most…
entries.text: Apache land, a woman holding a homestead on it, and a treaty already broken by the government that wrote it. L'Amour's dispatch rider is his most economical protagonist and the book is his cleanest single statement of a position he held throughout: the Apache have the better legal argument and it will not help them. The chain runs the other way from the usual assumption: L'Amour's 1952 story "The Gift of Cochise" was adapted by James Edward Grant into the screenplay, and the novel is a novelisation of that screenplay. It shares a year with the film, which is why the pack's namespace tiebreak has to fall on medium rather than date.

entries.category: The Pulp, Dime and Paperback West
entries.name: Longarm
entries.author: Tabor Evans
entries.description: Series paperback. A deputy US marshal, four hundred-odd titles, and a byline that is not a person: "Tabor Evans" is a publisher's house name, with…
entries.text: Series paperback. A deputy US marshal, four hundred-odd titles, and a byline that is not a person: "Tabor Evans" is a publisher's house name, with the first book written by Lou Cameron and the rest by a rotating stable. The authorship arrangement is the card's actual subject, because it shows the western's industrial layer still running long after the genre was declared dead on screen. It opens the post-1978 men's-adventure line the pack keeps distinct from the 1950s critical sense of the adult western.

entries.name: Cimarron
entries.author: Edna Ferber
entries.description: The Oklahoma land rush as a claim literally raced for, and then a forty-year argument about who keeps it, conducted largely by a woman running a…
entries.text: The Oklahoma land rush as a claim literally raced for, and then a forty-year argument about who keeps it, conducted largely by a woman running a newspaper after her husband walks out of the plot. Published as a book in 1930, which is the year the pack cards under its serialisation rule; a 1929 magazine serialisation is widely reported and the pack could not confirm the magazine or the issues. Ferber's Pulitzer is for So Big, not for this; the Academy Award belongs to the 1931 adaptation.

entries.name: Stagecoach
entries.author: dir. John Ford
entries.awards: Won two Academy Awards at the twelfth ceremony (1940) for 1939 films — Thomas Mitchell for Supporting Actor and the score. Nominated for Best Picture and Best Director; neither won.
entries.description: A passage through Apache territory in which every claim on the coach is a claim to standing in the town at either end, and the two passengers the…
entries.text: A passage through Apache territory in which every claim on the coach is a claim to standing in the town at either end, and the two passengers the town has expelled are the two who behave well. It is the film usually credited with making the western respectable again, and it is built from Ernest Haycox's 1937 story "Stage to Lordsburg", which is a separate claim from having written it. Monument Valley enters the genre here as scenery, on Navajo land, which is a fact the pack states alongside the film's reputation.

entries.name: The Ox-Bow Incident
entries.author: Walter Van Tilburg Clark
entries.description: Cattle title, a lynching, and the question of who is entitled to adjudicate — answered by a posse that hangs three men and then learns it was wrong,…
entries.text: Cattle title, a lynching, and the question of who is entitled to adjudicate — answered by a posse that hangs three men and then learns it was wrong, in a book that spends more time on the deliberation than on the killing. It reads as the direct rebuttal of The Virginian's argument for frontier hanging, though Clark did not state that intention and the pairing is a critics' construction. The 1943 film follows it closely and still cuts material — Davies's argument is shortened and the Rose Mapen strand goes.

entries.name: My Darling Clementine
entries.author: dir. John Ford
entries.description: A town's jurisdiction and a marshal's claim on it, with the gunfight arriving as an obligation rather than as a climax. The film's relationship to…
entries.text: A town's jurisdiction and a marshal's claim on it, with the gunfight arriving as an obligation rather than as a climax. The film's relationship to the documented Tombstone events is loose to the point of invention, and it is more interesting as evidence of what a studio western in 1946 wanted the West to have been — a church dance, a barber's chair, a schoolteacher — than as an account of anything. The legend-and-fact problem is inside the picture rather than announced by it.

entries.name: Red River
entries.author: dir. Howard Hawks
entries.awards: Nominated for two Academy Awards at the twenty-first ceremony (1949) for 1948 films — Motion Picture Story and Film Editing. No wins.
entries.description: Title to a herd, and to the Texas ground it came off, contested between a father and the son he raised and settled by a mutiny on the trail. It is…
entries.text: Title to a herd, and to the Texas ground it came off, contested between a father and the son he raised and settled by a mutiny on the trail. It is the professional plot's founding statement: competence is the entire moral content, and the group's loyalty runs sideways rather than upward. The film circulates in two cuts which differ in their narration — a book against Groot's voice-over — and share an ending; the different ending belongs to Borden Chase's magazine serial, which ran from 1946 into January 1947 and in which Dunson is fatally wounded by Cherry and carried back to Texas to die.

entries.name: Shane
entries.author: Jack Schaefer
entries.description: Homestead against open range, narrated by a boy who understands about half of what he is watching, which is the device the whole book runs on. It is…
entries.text: Homestead against open range, narrated by a boy who understands about half of what he is watching, which is the device the whole book runs on. It is the range-war plot in its cleanest available form: two claims to the same valley, no legal machinery capable of settling between them, and a man with a particular skill who can. It was serialised as "Rider from Nowhere" in 1946 and published as a book in 1949, which is the year the pack cards.

entries.name: Winchester '73
entries.author: dir. Anthony Mann
entries.description: A rifle passes from hand to hand across the territory and the film follows the rifle, which lets it survey an entire society by the simple method of…
entries.text: A rifle passes from hand to hand across the territory and the film follows the rifle, which lets it survey an entire society by the simple method of watching who ends up holding the object. It opens the Mann and Stewart cycle, and with it the neurotic western: a protagonist whose grievance is private, whose competence is frightening, and whose pursuit is closer to compulsion than to justice. The gun as the thing that actually circulates is the genre's most efficient single structural idea.

entries.name: High Noon
entries.author: dir. Fred Zinnemann
entries.awards: Won four Academy Awards at the twenty-fifth ceremony (1953) for 1952 films — Gary Cooper for Actor, Film Editing, Score and Song. Nominated for Best Picture and Best Director; neither won.
entries.description: A town's claim on its own marshal, refused, and a deadline the audience can read off a clock. Four separate claims about it are routinely merged:…
entries.text: A town's claim on its own marshal, refused, and a deadline the audience can read off a clock. Four separate claims about it are routinely merged: the blacklist reading belongs to Carl Foreman, who wrote it, was subpoenaed and left for Britain; Zinnemann directed; Stanley Kramer produced and later disputed Foreman's account in public. It is also the pack's counter-example to the idea that the western is set in the moment before law arrives — the law is already there, wearing a badge, and asking for help.

entries.name: Shane (1953 film)
entries.author: dir. George Stevens
entries.awards: Won one Academy Award at the twenty-sixth ceremony (1954) for 1953 films — Loyal Griggs for Cinematography, Color. Nominated in five further categories — Best Picture, Best Director, Screenplay (A. B. Guthrie Jr.) and two Supporting Actor nominations — none of which won.
entries.description: The novel filmed with the boy's viewpoint kept and the violence made deliberately ugly — Wilson's killing of Torrey is staged as a physical shock…
entries.text: The novel filmed with the boy's viewpoint kept and the violence made deliberately ugly — Wilson's killing of Torrey is staged as a physical shock rather than as a duel, and the film's gunshots were amplified for exactly that reason. Stevens gives the homesteaders' case a documentary weight the book only implies. It is the film Will Wright's classical plot is derived from, which is worth stating because the novel is frequently substituted for it in accounts of his argument.

entries.name: The Searchers
entries.author: Alan Le May
entries.description: A captivity, and a claim to a person made entirely in the language of property. The book is colder than the film and more explicit about the…
entries.text: A captivity, and a claim to a person made entirely in the language of property. The book is colder than the film and more explicit about the search's real purpose, and its ending is not the film's. Le May built it from documented captivity cases, of which the Parker abduction is the best known, and the pack keeps the novel and the film as separate entries because they resolve their central question differently.

entries.name: The Searchers (1956 film)
entries.author: dir. John Ford
entries.awards: None (verified negative; it received no Academy Award nominations).
entries.description: The most argued-over film in the genre, and the one that most rewards the argument: a search conducted for five years by a man whose intention…
entries.text: The most argued-over film in the genre, and the one that most rewards the argument: a search conducted for five years by a man whose intention toward its object he never states and the film never confirms. It withholds what the novel says outright, which is the adaptation's whole method. It received no Academy Award nominations at all, which is the pack's cleanest demonstration that award record and canonical standing are unrelated quantities.

entries.name: Rio Bravo
entries.author: dir. Howard Hawks
entries.description: A jail, a prisoner, a town and a siege — the film the pack's collapse test cannot dislodge, because removing the contested claim and the force that…
